News.title: Andy Burnham 'open' to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave trade
News.content:
Andy Burnham 'open' to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave trade

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is "open" to calls for Britain to formally apologise for its role in the slave trade, but ruled out considering financial reparations

View 3 Images Andy burnham is due to attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in the Caribbean next week

Andy Burnham has said he is "open" to calls for Britain to formally apologise for its role in the slave trade, but ruled out considering financial reparations.

‌



‌



The Prime Minister, who is due to attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in the Caribbean next week, voiced his personal "sorrow and regret" over the suffering inflicted by the transatlantic slave trade, pledging to offer a "structured dialogue" with those affected.

‌



Writing in The Guardian, he said: "Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do.

‌



View 3 Images Prime Minister Andy Burnham (L) congratulates Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey after he delivered a speech on the second day of the annual Labour Party conference (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

"Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today."

He described the trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation" of people "treated as property and worked to their deaths".

‌



"I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today," he wrote.

Caribbean nations have renewed their demands for Britain to apologise for its role in trading enslaved people for profit, as well as calls for reparations, as the King toured the region.

‌



The King has been officially welcomed to Antigua and Barbuda by the Governor-General Sir Rodney Williams after flying in from Guyana to VC Bird International Airport.

The Antigua and Barbuda Royal Police Band played the national anthems of the UK and Antigua and Barbuda on instruments including steel pans and formed a Guard of Honour. The King was then invited to inspect the ranks, walking up and down with Sir Rodney and stopping to speak to a few officers as he went.

‌



Also in the line up to meet the monarch were Minister of Foreign Affairs and Chair of the CHOGM 2026 Task Force, Chet Greene; Minister of Tourism, Civil Aviation, Transportation, and Investment, Charles Fernandez; Chief of Defence Staff, Brigadier General Telbert Benjamin; and Commissioner of Police of the Royal Police Force of Antigua and Barbuda, Everton Jeffers.

View 3 Images Charles spent two days in The Bahamas earlier this week (Image: AP Photo/Tim Aylen)

‌



The Prime Minister said: "We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them."

In line with the stance taken by his predecessors, he stopped well short of entertaining any notion of reparation payments.

‌



"Some have called for financial reparations for the slave trade. I do not believe that is the right answer. I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part."

Instead, he outlined plans to launch an initiative targeting debt-servicing, aimed at helping nations repay their debts over a longer period at more favourable rates. Chancellor John Healey, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and former prime minister Gordon Brown will join him at the summit to help with this work, he said.

Article continues below

He added that the UK will also back countries in their shift towards renewable energy, champion smaller nations on the world stage, and support efforts to educate women and girls while tackling poverty and inequality.

News.title: King Charles tries witchcraft instruments and says he wishes he'd had them before
News.content:
King Charles tries witchcraft instruments and says he wishes he'd had them before

Guyana's Tashao Derrick John said his meeting with the King was 'very amazing', adding Charles was 'very interested in the role indigenous people play in protecting our forests'

View 4 Images Charles met native communities while in Guyana (Image: Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

King Charles tried shaking indigenous maracas used for witchcraft as he met representatives of Guyana’s nine indigenous groups.

‌



‌



Taking up a hand crafted maraca, Charles gave it a shake and said that he should have had it when he took part in the Junkanoo parade in the Bahamas. Carianne Campo, 19, a Queen from the Carib tribe in Region Three, said: “It is used in witchcraft to summon the spirits. He shook it and he said he should have had this at the Junkanoo and said it was marvellous.”

‌



Later, Charles was gifted a traditional archer’s bow and arrow to take back to the UK and mimed using it before handing it to an aide for safe keeping.

‌

King Charles reflects at spot where slaves were publicly executed after uprising READ MORE :

View 4 Images Charles was at one point during the meeting gifted an archer's bow (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Other gifts included a riding crop, “Ah! If I go riding again on a horse,” the King said, and a whistle, which he said sounded like an owl.

‌



Charles arrived at the Umana Yana, meeting place for the National Tashaos Council, in the searing heat. Before going inside the traditional hut used to host meetings, he was presented with an Amerindian necklace by Aliyah Abraham, 10, who had travelled overnight from her home in Surama.

As he walked inside, Charles was accompanied by Tashao (chief) Derrick John, who visited the King’s Gloucestershire home of Highgrove last year, a meeting that was shown in the King’s Harmony film.

‌



View 4 Images Charles was warmly greeted in Guyana (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

He said of the state visit: “It’s very amazing. It’s an experience we will never forget. He was very interested in the role indigenous people play in protecting our forests and the funding that is being transferred through forest carbon credit financing to the indigenous community and how that is transforming lives.

‌



"With Guyana being a small country we are taking a bold step.” Charles then held a ten minute private conversation with indigenous Tashaos, or chiefs, although the occasional shout from protesters outside could be heard.

The King was shown around the centre where each of the nine different groups had a stall to exhibit local crafts. Charles was shown a plan for “Harmony Village”, a partnership between the Guyana government and the King’s Foundation.

‌



View 4 Images The King was shown around the centre where each of the nine different groups had a stall to exhibit local crafts (Image: Victoria Jones/Shutterstock)

Ben Bolgar, executive director of projects at the King’s foundations said that the site, which will host workshops, was “using Dumfries House as a model”.

Article continues below

Speaking later, Bolgar said: “The King and the President had this idea of Harmony Village, because the President was so inspired by Dumfries House.”

News.title: 'Troubling questions after revelation Zara Tindall has been selling controversial jewellery'
News.content:
'Troubling questions after revelation Zara Tindall has been selling controversial jewellery'

King Charles' niece has her own jewellery collection including gems from a mine where traditional Indigenous landowners have warned of serious environmental damage

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Zara must bling it on

Some of the world's most beautiful diamonds come with an ugly environmental legacy. And those paying the price deserve to have their voices heard. Our revelation that Zara Tindall has been selling jewellery containing controversial Argyle pink diamonds raises troubling questions. The King's niece has her own jewellery collection featuring gems from an Australian mine where traditional Indigenous landowners have warned of serious environmental damage. A damning report identified contamination by toxic 'forever chemicals', polluted water, severe erosion and damage to sacred sites, including burial grounds. Yet Zara, a supporter of conservation charities, has promoted jewellery containing these stones costing tens of thousands of pounds. Singer Ellie Goulding was mortified after discovering the controversy surrounding diamonds she wore. Zara should now demand answers from those supplying her collection. Above all, Indigenous communities deserve transparency, proper restoration of their land and a genuine say in its future. No glittering diamond should ever outshine the responsibility to protect our planet and its people.

‌



‌



Ballot wrong...

Donald Trump faces a humiliating reckoning in next week's US midterm elections as American voters prepare to deliver their verdict on his presidency. His war with Iran, soaring prices and punishing trade tariffs have left families furious and Republicans fighting to save their seats in Congress. Trump's increasingly chaotic campaign has hardly helped. He cancelled two final rallies, then hastily reinstated them amid questions about his willingness to support struggling candidates. Even Republican strongholds such as Texas and Kansas have become fierce battlegrounds. The President's name may be absent from Tuesday's ballot, but his record is at the heart of this election. For the rest of the world, America under Trump has become a frightening example of how quickly a great nation can lose its way.

‌



Glorious telly

The Traitors kept us gripped, guessing and shouting at our televisions until the very end. With enough backstabbing, betrayal and barefaced lies to put Westminster to shame, it was glorious entertainment. The castle doors may have closed, but we’re already desperate to be let back in.

News.title: Telephone kiosk 'at centre of Britain' protected for future generations
News.content:
Telephone kiosk 'at centre of Britain' protected for future generations

The KX100 kiosk at Dunsop Bridge in Lancashire, was the 100,000th telephone kiosk installed in the country. It was officially opened in 1992 by explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, who was the first to use it to make a call

Sir Ranulph Fiennes Interview

A telephone box at the geographic centre of Great Britain has been given Grade II-listed status.

‌



‌



The KX100 kiosk at Dunsop Bridge, in Ribble Valley in Lancashire, was the 100,000th telephone kiosk installed in the country.

‌



It was officially opened in June 1992 by explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, who made the first call from the kiosk.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

He was joined by children from nearby Thornleyholme RC Primary School.

Jayne Rimmer, Historic England's north region listing team leader, said: "As part of the last generation of the public telephone box, it is a nationally significant kiosk."

‌



The Twentieth Century Society (TCS), which champions outstanding examples of modern design, had applied for it to be listed.

Campaigns director Oli Marshall said he was "absolutely delighted" by their success.

‌



View 3 Images The KX100 kiosk at Dunsop Bridge, in Ribble Valley in Lancashire, was the 100,000th telephone kiosk installed in the country. (Image: James Maloney/Lancs Live)

Avoiding awkward conversations about money costs Brits nearly £1,600 a year READ MORE :

He said: "There's no small irony that it was the arrival of the KX100 that first spurred the Society into action back in 1985.

‌



"Once the slayer of traditional red telephone boxes, that we fought vigorously to repel, now itself being given heritage protection.

"While widely unloved and underappreciated in comparison to the classic red telephone boxes, the ugly duckling KX100 model has developed a cult following."

‌



The Tour de France is "passing through Dunsop Bridge next July," he added.

"We hope the kiosk will form the centrepiece of the village's celebrations, as well as being the centre of Great Britain".

‌



Ribble Valley Borough Council leader Simon Hore said the phone box had "a special place in local people's hearts".

View 3 Images Dunsop Bridge is at the geographical centre of Great Britain (Image: James Maloney/Lancs Live)

‌



A plaque states the payphone "marks the centre of Great Britain" First introduced in 1985, the KX100 design has large glass panels and was designed to be easier to clean and more accessible than the previous red model.

The kiosk is of particular importance as it featured "a bespoke, site-specific design" featuring "key places in Britain radiating from the BT 'Piper' marque and Dunsop Bridge".

‌



The phone box was officially opened in June 1992 by explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes.

View 3 Images Sir Ranulph Fiennes with King, then Prince Charles back in 2012. (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The Lancashire village was named as the nearest settlement to the geographical centre of Great Britain following work by national mapping agency Ordnance Survey (OS).

Its calculations put the centre at Whitendale Hanging Stones, about 4.3 miles (7km) north-west of Dunsop Bridge.

‌



The title has been disputed, with other places also making a claim, including Haltwhistle in Northumberland.

OS later stated there could be "no absolute centre for a three-dimensional land mass sitting on the surface of a sphere and surrounded by the ebb and flow of sea water" and "different projections, scales and methods of calculation will all produce different results".

Article continues below

Dunsop Bridge was the result of defining Britain as "the mainland and the 401 associated islands", a spokesperson said in 2014.

They added that "looking only at the mainland of Great Britain", the location was a little further south, lying about 2.5 miles (4km) north-west of Whalley.

News.title: Charles could be ditched as King by Bahamas as country's PM breaks silence
News.content:
Charles could be ditched as King by Bahamas as country's PM breaks silence

King Charles visited The Bahamas over two days earlier this week, with the country's Prime Minister Philip Davis saying the future of the monarchy there was "a question for my people"

Has the King done enough to acknowledge the history of slavery in the Caribbean?

The Prime Minister of The Bahamas has said he is open to losing the King as head of state and becoming a republic.

‌



‌



Charles was welcomed to the island nation over two days earlier this week, where he frequently spoke of the shared history and deep bond between our two nations.

‌



Yet, despite the warm welcome, Philip Davis has said the future of the monarchy in The Bahamas was "a question for my people" and that he would be "guided by the will" of Bahamians on whether to force a new future. The Prime Minister also addressed growing calls across the Caribbean for the King to apologise for slavery and for reparations to be paid.

‌



Sarah Ferguson seen in public for first time with Beatrice and Eugenie after fleeing UK over Epstein scandal READ MORE :

View 4 Images King Charles in The Bahamas earlier this week (Image: Ben Stansall/Press Association)

He said the King "acts on the advice of his government" and was awaiting that advice until what he called "respectful dialogue" on reparations was complete.

Mr Davis said repair "is not absolutely money, simply, money" and could mean "acknowledgement, education, training, things of that nature."

‌



He pointed to research tracing the largest export of cotton to Liverpool back to a plantation on Long Cay, near Crooked Island, and said the family "might want to consider" repair. But he admitted financial reparations could be "challenging for government", adding: "As a citizen, I would question why my tax payment ought to go to satisfy the debt of my ancestors 200 years ago."

Asked whether the slave trade was lawful at the time, he said: "I don't think so." He cited the King's Trust providing scholarships for Commonwealth citizens to study at Commonwealth universities, saying: "That could be a form of repair."

‌



View 4 Images The King with Prime Minister Philip Davis in Nassau earlier this week (Image: Chris Jackson/Press Association)

On his visit earlier this week, the King made clear that leaders at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) will discuss matters around the legacy of slavery next week in Antigua and Barbuda.

‌



His comments, made in an interview with Sky News, come days after the King began a nine-day Caribbean tour in Nassau, his first official visit to The Bahamas as monarch.

Asked whether The Bahamas still wanted the King as head of state, Mr Davis said: "I think we have some very passionate Bahamians who say we should be a republic. Equally, we have many passionate Bahamians saying that we ought not to rid ourselves of part of our history."

‌



He said any move to a republic would require a referendum, adding: "Referendum in this country is not fared well, but that question would be a question for our people."

View 4 Images The King gives a speech in Cllifford Park (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Within hours of touching down in Nassau on Tuesday, Charles made a speech at a youth rally where he said “It is only right that we acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond”.

However, before the King left Britain, talk of his visits to The Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda was dominated by calls for the monarch to deliver an apology for Britain and the monarchy's historic role in the slave trade as well as calls on the government to pay reparations. Activists in The Bahamas said the King had not gone far enough with his speech and said the issues were far from being resolved.

‌



Mr Davis, who was re-elected in May, said a vote on the monarchy was not currently on the table because "my mandate did not include a referendum on whether we should keep the King or not." But he added: "If it comes up, certainly, but again, I'll be guided by the will of my people."

View 4 Images Charles spent two days in The Bahamas earlier this week (Image: AP Photo/Tim Aylen)

‌



Pressed on his own view, he said he was "quite agnostic" about the issue. When asked whether he would be open to losing the King as head of state, he replied: "I'm open to it, yes."

And to those in Britain who believe there is no need for an apology, he said: "I think they have to appreciate the weight of that history and that ancestors like ourselves continue to bear."

‌



The Bahamas gained independence in July 1973. On his visit this week the King returned to Clifford Park, where he last officially appeared as Prince of Wales in 1973 when the country gained independence after 300 years of British rule. On that occasion he delivered a formal message from Queen Elizabeth II to Bahamians.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Mr Davis said the country had "thrived" since then. "We have a tremendous advancement, development, and you can see how we have developed," he said.

But his remarks suggest the nation's relationship with the Crown could yet take a different course, following Barbados, which became a republic in 2021.

Article continues below

After The Bahamas, the King's tour moves on to Guyana and then Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, where Queen Camilla will join him.

News.title: Farmer's 'blazing row' with dad before strangling him and leaving body in shallow grave
News.content:
Farmer's 'blazing row' with dad before strangling him and leaving body in shallow grave

Charles Wright, 52, strangled Brian Wright, 82, and left his body in a shallow grave at Hall Farm near Newark in Nottinghamshire

View 3 Images Brian Wright was 82 when he was killed by his son (Image: Nottinghamshire Police / SWNS)

A man killed his father and buried him on the family farm before taking his own life following a "blazing row" over money, an inquest heard.

‌



‌



Charles Wight, 52, saw a "flash of red" when he felt his father, Brian, 82, was "cutting him out" of the family's business. He choked him to death to death placed his body in a shallow grave at Hall Farm near Newark in Nottinghamshire.

‌



Two days later, Charles took his own life. Nottingham Coroner's Court heard today that, in a voice message left by Charles for police, he said his father was "thinking of replacing him" and "giving the lion's share of the farm to another family member".

‌



In the note, which was sent on November 22, Charles said: "I just had a flash of red and after 25 years and everything I have given him, he was just cutting me out like that. I just saw red, dragged him out of the car and throttled him."

View 3 Images Police near the scene where Brian Wright was buried in Nottinghamshire (Image: Joseph Raynor/ Reach PLC)

The inquest was told Brian had called Charles "useless" and "not capable of farming" and said it was a "mistake to let him farm that land" during the heated argument. Detective Chief Inspector Ruby Burrow, of Nottinghamshire Police, told the court of the voice message: "Charles stated that he had killed his father and intended to kill himself.

‌



"He described that his father Brian had criticised him and there had been a disagreement about finances. He stated he had buried his father Brian on the family farm."

Brian was reported missing to police shortly before midnight on November 20 as he had failed to take his wife to a hospital appointment. The next day, Charles, his brother James Wright and a colleague who worked on the family farm as a mechanic spoke to police officers.

‌



DCI Burrow told the inquest that Charles, who was interviewed the day before he took his own life, "was able to assist by describing difficult family dynamics and difficulties in relationships over the years, including issues around finances and also working arrangements on the farm". She continued: "We had a number of interactions with Charles.

"Charles provided similar contextual information about relationships within the family. He described an argument he had had with his father. He described his father had been critical towards him and he, himself, had taken some time to calm down."

‌



View 3 Images Police near the farm following the two deaths (Image: Joseph Raynor/ Reach PLC)

Charles Wright told police his father had "left in the opposite direction after the small argument", the court heard. Later on November 21, Brian's vehicle was reported as appearing "out of place" where it had been left overnight, and his body was discovered buried on the farm four days later.

‌



His cause of death was found to be pressure applied to the neck, the inquest heard. Ms Burrow said there had been a report on November 22 of "a collision between a vehicle and two gentlemen", where the vehicle was driven at them "apparently deliberately".

She stated that Charles had driven his vehicle at his brother James, who was running alongside a friend, "causing injury". Charles Wright took his own life later that same day, with his body discovered in an outbuilding area on Hall Farm.

Article continues below

Senior coroner for Nottinghamshire Mairin Casey ruled that Brian Wright had been unlawfully killed, while his son's death was concluded to be suicide. Addressing the family members present in person and those joining via video-link, she said: "The horror of this, I'm clear in my mind, will have affected all of those who have survived in a very deep and painful way."

News.title: Armenian parliament erupts into brawl over 'Ministry of Sex' as fists fly and chair hurled
News.content:
Armenian parliament erupts into brawl over 'Ministry of Sex' as fists fly and chair hurled

Footage from Yerevan shows dozens of people brawling after a trade of insults over a proposal aimed at resolving what opposition MPs said was a problem with women turning to activism

Armenian MPs in Parliament Punch Up

A meeting over a proposed 'Ministry of Sex' during an Armenian Parliamentary session descended into the third all-out brawl on the premises in a matter of days - with fists flying and an MP hurling a chair.

‌



‌



Armenian lawmakers appeared at the National Assembly in its capital, Yerevan, on Thursday for a debate over the unusual proposals. Lawmakers with the pro-Russian Strong Armenia party had put forward the idea after bizarrely claiming that a lack of sexual satisfaction was leading middle-aged women into political activism.

‌



The ruling party, Civil Contract, immediately objected to the idea - which was meant to leave “no unsatisfied women” - and demanded a public apology, after which the chamber descended into a fight.

‌



Fists fly as huge brawl breaks out in Albanian parliament over student protests READ MORE :

View 4 Images The fight began after a verbal disagreement between Taron Chakhoyan and opposition leaders

The violence erupted after Civil Contract MP Taron Chakhoyan accused opposition members of being "steeped in corruption" and demanded an apology for proposing the ministry.

Chakhoyan said: "People steeped in corruption are talking about corruption, fake accounts, and targeting family members. Mr [Narek] Karapetyan, it is not my fault that your entire extended family is involved in politics, including your uncle, your father, and your cousin, who even tried to open a ministry in our country.

‌



"It is not my fault that he wanted to open a ministry that would satisfy all women. You have still not apologised to women for that."

View 4 Images Narek Karapetyan was also involved in the trade off

‌



A shouting match followed, with Strong Armenia member Narek Karapetyan allegedly calling Chakhoyan a "mess from head to toe". The rush towards the central podium, where Chakhoyan was speaking, broke out afterwards, with members seen punching and kicking each other.

Video taken of the fight shows assembly members rushing towards the chamber's centre and brawling with one another, with fists flying.

‌



At one point, Vahagn Aleksanya, the chamber's deputy speaker and a member of Civil Contract, picks up a red chair and chucks it at the group's periphery, but they keep fighting. Chakhoyan was seen at another point pouring a glass of water on a rival.

View 4 Images The brawl enveloped all of the Parliamentary chamber

‌



According to the Daily Telegraph, other MPs joined in the chaos by throwing bottles and breaking tables before the brawl was broken up.

Armenia's prime minister Nikol Pashinyan, said in a statement after the fight that, while he condemned the violence, he supported "the measures" taken by his faction. He said Strong Armenia, a younger party which formed earlier this year, being present in Parliament "does not mean that one should become insolent".

‌



He said: “I condemn violence, but I support the measures taken by the Civil Contract faction today, because [Strong Armenia] being in the opposition does not mean that one should become insolent."

View 4 Images The brawl at one point saw a chair thrown into the crowd

‌



“Whether with a chair or something else, it is proportionate and right.” Chakhoyan later apologised to the public for the behaviour of his opponents, saying it was "hooligan" before adding: "It won’t work to provoke a fight and escape from the National Assembly session hall without getting beaten."

The Ministry of Sex row comes following two previous brawls, both of which followed Civil Contract and Strong Armenia members trading insults.

Article continues below

And it was capped off with a tongue-in-cheek comment from the prime minister, who joked on Facebook after the incident about the opposition's physical - or lack thereof - strength. He joked that, despite being called "Strong Armenia" the party's MPs were not "physically strong".

News.title: Russell Myers: King Charles in danger of being remembered as monarch who didn't apologise
News.content:
As the King stood in reflection in Georgetown, on the very ground where enslaved Africans were executed after the Demerara uprising of 1823, it was impossible not to be encapsulated by the moment.

Even before Charles' arrival in The Bahamas earlier this week and Guyana today, this tour has been dominated by the issue of slavery and reparations.

I have no doubt that Charles' personal feeling over slavery is deeply felt and perhaps, given the freedom to do so rather than being restricted by the government, he would feel moved to issue an apology for Britain and the monarchy's historic role in slavery.

King Charles reflects at spot where slaves were publicly executed after uprising READ MORE :

King Charles' popularity sinks to lowest level of reign amid Harry and Meghan return READ MORE :

View 3 Images King Charles in Guyana today (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Indeed, within hours of landing in Nassau on Tuesday, he told a youth rally: "It is only right that we acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond". Yet, however heartfelt his words, they have not quietened the clamour that has followed him across the Caribbean.

At a Junkanoo parade in Nassau, one sign in the crowd read simply: "Pay us what you owe us." In Guyana, President Irfaan Ali has welcomed the King's past expressions of regret but made clear an apology must be the next step. And today came perhaps the most striking intervention of the tour so far.

Speaking to Sky News, Bahamian Prime Minister Philip Davis said he was open to losing the King as head of state, just days after giving him the warmest of welcomes.

View 3 Images Protestors hold up posters during the King's visit to Guyana (Image: Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

‌



The future of the monarchy, he said, was "a question for my people" and he would be "guided by the will" of Bahamians. Asked directly whether he was open to it, he replied: "I'm open to it, yes."

Mr Davis was careful. He described himself as "quite agnostic", noted that a referendum was not part of his mandate and acknowledged that many Bahamians did not want to "rid ourselves of part of our history".

But his message to Britain was unmistakable. To those who see no need for an apology, he said: "I think they have to appreciate the weight of that history and that ancestors like ourselves continue to bear."

Here lies the King's dilemma. He acts on the advice of his ministers, and the Government has ruled out both an apology and reparations, fearing a legal precedent that could open the floodgates for former colonies around the world.

‌



View 3 Images Charles during a visit to Umana Yana in Guyana (Image: Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

Mr Davis himself recognises that. He said the King "acts on the advice of his government", and conceded that financial reparations could be "challenging". Repair, he suggested, might instead mean acknowledgement, education and training, even pointing to the King's Trust scholarships as "a form of repair".

That is perhaps the most hopeful note for Charles. There is a path between apology and silence, and it is one he has walked for years.

He has also confirmed that Commonwealth leaders will discuss the legacy of slavery in Antigua next week, at a summit he will preside over.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Yet the ground is shifting beneath him. Barbados left in 2021. Jamaica is pushing towards becoming a republic and now the leader of a nation that welcomed him so warmly this week admits he is open to the King's departure.

None of this is of Charles's making. He has gone further than any monarch before him in confronting the past.

But history rarely judges kings on intentions alone. If Chogm ends with warm words and little else, the danger is that his reign in the Caribbean will be remembered not for the moments of reflection, but for the apology that never came.

‌

News.title: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack
News.content:
Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, has been hit by a $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) hack - thought to be the biggest in history.

News.title: Driver guilty of hitting cyclist and dragging him to death under car
News.content:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A man has been found guilty of murdering a head teacher who was dragged to his death for more than a mile while trapped under the wheels of a car.

Simon Richardson crashed into 56-year-old Michael Mullins, who was cycling home from his job at Stretford Grammar School on the evening of 20 April in the village of Warburton in Trafford, Greater Manchester.

Prosecutors claimed Richardson, 35, fled the scene of the crash before stopping to try to dislodge the injured but still-living cyclist and then driving on with Mr Mullins still lodged underneath the vehicle.

Richardson was also convicted of dangerous driving and will return to Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court to be sentenced on Monday.

There were shouts of "Yes!" from the court's public gallery as the guilty murder verdict was announced.

Others could also be heard crying.

The judge, Mrs Justice Brunner KC, told Richardson that there was only one sentence for murder, namely life imprisonment.

News.title: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
News.content:
Ukraine is not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.

One British official told the BBC: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".

Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".

"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.

In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.

The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of midterm elections on Tuesday, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".

Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.

Still, the US State Department this week said it had approved the sale of more than $2bn worth of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for the country's air defences to protect itself from Russian attacks.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.

Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

News.title: Why MPs keep talking about an early election despite Burnham's denials
News.content:
Wander through Parliament at the moment, and there is one issue many MPs want to discuss: is there going to be an early general election?

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has nearly three years to go before he has to call an election and he has repeatedly and categorically ruled out going to the country early.

But the discussion persists - and many think it is a real possibility.

After Wednesday's Budget, that talk has only increased.

As one former Labour minister puts it: "Why would you sprinkle round a few politically smart (albeit small) giveaways now but delay all the really tough and unpopular decisions on welfare and defence to an autumn spending review if you weren't creating a window for a spring election?"

Others have also suggested to the BBC that Chancellor John Healey's plans felt like a pre-election programme.

They argue the Budget contained voter-friendly measures on the cost of living, such as Â£100 help for many with energy bills and extending VAT cuts on electricity bills. Young voters are to be offered help on to the housing ladder, through the Your First Home scheme.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has questioned why some-voter friendly measures announced by Healey will only be in place until the summer.

Could it be, she suggests, that the prime minister plans to go to the country before these measures run out?

(The counter-argument to this is that household energy pressures are less severe in the summer.)

Some MPs also point out the prime minister is popular at the moment and Labour is leading in most polls.

Reform, who had led the polls for some time, have had a difficult few months.

Will things ever look better for Burnham, they ask.

News.title: King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour
News.content:
The King has made a poignant visit to the site where a Guyanese slave rebellion was violently resisted by British authorities, making the stop during his tour of the Caribbean.

He visited Independence Park in Georgetown to remember the Demerera Slave Rebellion of 1823, which saw an uprising by thousands of enslaved people.

Accompanied by Guyana's Culture Minister, Steven Jacobs, he was told how hundreds of slaves were killed by colonial leaders during the rebellion and many of those who survived were executed close to where the King stood.

Above the King was a sign that he took time to read.

"This ground was used as a public execution site," it said, "where enslaved persons...were condemned to death and hung."

The moment of reflection was what Buckingham Palace had described as the King "not shying away from the UK's colonial legacy" and described today as a chance for the King to reflect on Guyana's history of slavery and resistance.

In 2022, Charles described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to "deepen my own understanding of slavery's enduring impact", in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.

Independence Park, which is now a sports ground, drew a crowd of dozens of schoolchildren. The King stopped to talk to many of them asking them about their homework, their holidays and if they'd had a day off school.

News.title: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
News.content:
Police Scotland is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell during their time at Balmoral Castle.

The Daily Express reported, external that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence in Aberdeenshire.

Sex offender Epstein - who died in 2019 - and Maxwell, who was jailed in 2022 for sex trafficking, are understood to have visited the castle with Mountbatten-Windsor, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Police Scotland said inquiries were at "a very early stage" and that it would be inappropriate to comment further.

Representatives of Mountbatten-Windsor have been contacted for comment.

News.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
News.content:
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).

Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.

Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.

While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.

Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.

Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday, taking more than $500bn (Â£374bn) off its market value after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.

At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.

The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.

The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.

On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.

"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.

In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.

News.title: Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86
News.content:
Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".

Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."

Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft".

"Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.

Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.

The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."

The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.

Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".

Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".

"He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

News.title: UK could see 10 days without rain after 'wettest week in two years'
News.content:
The UK could see as many as 10 consecutive days without rain after an unsettled end to October that featured back-to-back storms.

It comes after the Environment Agency said England experienced its wettest week in two years thanks to Storms Austen and Boelo.

Following this recent unsettled weather, the return of high pressure will bring a prolonged spell of largely dry and calm conditions, with very little rain in sight.

Mist and fog will remain a persistent feature, with some slow-clearing dense patches expected during the mornings.

News.title: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
News.content:
Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been told.

In her closing speech at London's Southwark Crown Court on Friday, prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC said the women had "nothing to gain" from coming forward apart from "some closure".

Speaking for the defence, Polly Dyer told jurors Brand had pleaded guilty and been fined over possession of cannabis in 1995, but had no other "convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings".

Brand, 51, is on trial facing seven charges; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. He denies the charges.

Karmy-Jones KC told the court that this case brings together six different women, none of whom knows each other.

She said that while all the alleged victims have since moved on with their lives, due to this trial they have been forced to "relive what has happened to them".

None of the women involved has "sought the limelight" or "any kind of publicity", she said, adding there was "no benefit to them from perhaps some closure."

Referring to Brand's accusers' evidence the prosecutor said "how many said he was nice and then there was a like a personality changeâ¦

"His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty," Karmy-Jones KC said.

She added that the complainant's evidence had been that "he didn't listen when I said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care, pulling pushingâ¦ thrusting".

"In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim."

The prosecutor also dismissed the idea that a documentary had caused the women to "re-invent" what actually happened.

"There is no magic force in this documentary", she added.

"What in fact happened was these women have realised they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth."

She added: "Truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years."

She told the jury: "The experience of people raped may be something that looms a little bit larger in your mind rather than the intricacies of the outfit.

"The defendant couldn't really remember anything when he was interviewed, in stark contrast to now when he suddenly seems to remember all sorts of details about the week."

News.title: Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father
News.content:
The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had decided an investigation was required into the force's "failure to pass on allegations of serious offending... to relevant overseas authorities at the time".

The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.

He has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".

On Thursday the Met said it had voluntarily referred itself to the IOPC.

The letter at the heart of the IOPC investigation was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.

The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".

Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason to not visit Thomas Markle and not allow him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.

Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".

The IOPC will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas.

The policing watchdog also said it had decided a further matter, relating to an alleged data breach in which information was passed on to a third party, "should be returned to the force to be appropriately dealt with". No details were provided about the circumstances of the alleged breach.

The Met said on Thursday that it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".

The letter was forwarded by officers to the Sussexes' royal office rather than to Meghan personally, while there have been reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to ask for one from the Sussexes.

The watchdog will have to consider how the contents of the letter were treated by the force at the time.

Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, previously told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".

"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken [and] why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies."

Reports of the Met's handling of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.

Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.

Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims. Police there have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.

However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they can examine the items.

Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha, who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

News.title: Stabbed boy felt Huntingdon train attacker 'was not sane', court hears
News.content:
A 14-year-old boy stabbed by a man who went on to attack people on a train said he did not feel the knifeman was "mentally sane", a court heard.

The teenager was attacked in Peterborough the day before Anthony Williams is accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train that had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon in November 2025.

In a video recorded interview played to jurors at Cambridge Crown Court, the boy said: "This random guyâ¦ he just pulled out a knife and stabbed me."

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder - four of which concern attacks prior to the mass train stabbing.

At the time of the attack, the boy, who cannot be named because of his age, was waiting with a friend on a footbridge over the River Nene, before going trick or treating.

Williams drew a knife from his waistband, he said, and "because I was closest to him, he's just stabbed me".

"I didn't feel like he was mentally sane. His eyes were wide open, like he was on something," he said.

"My friend said he was shouting something like 'are you involved?'."

"When he stabbed me, it's like he was there for a knife fight. Like he was waiting for me to pull out something."

The teenager said he had "so much adrenaline" that it felt "like a poke in the chest".

The jury heard the pair ran away and hid in some bushes, where they called the police.

News.title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
News.content:
Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.

"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.

He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".

In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.

Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.

The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".

Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.

He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.

The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.

News.title: Wettest week for two years but still not enough rain to get out of drought
News.content:
The recent stormy weather brought England's wettest week in two years, according to the Environment Agency.

However, despite the rain, Wales and most of England are still in drought with parts of southern England in severe drought.

Met Office provisional statistics for October show that the UK received above average rainfall.

However, the National Drought Group have said it will take sustained and above average rainfall over a seven month period for conditions to improve to normal.

Over the last week we had the first two named storms of the season - Austen and Boelo - which gave much of the UK significant and much needed rain.

Rainfall totals ranged from 38mm in central England to 87mm in the south-west and according to Enviroment Agency (EA) monitoring, it was the wettest week across England since October 2024.

In some parts of southern England there was nearly 50% more rainfall than normal throughout the month.

As a whole, England has had 111% of its long-term monthly rainfall, according to the EA.

News.title: Ministers vow online safety action after teen sextortion victim took own life
News.content:
The UK government has said it remains committed to making the online world as safe as possible for young people following the death of a teenager who took his own life after he fell victim to an online sextortion scam.

Cai Davies, 18, died in June 2025 after he had sent messages to a woman he believed had a romantic interest in him.

South Wales Central Coroner's Court heard he had been targeted by scammers operating from Africa, who demanded money from him and said intimate photos would be sent to his friends and posted on YouTube.

The coroner addressed a Regulation 28 preventing future deaths report, external to the UK and Welsh government with her concerns about how Cai had fallen victim to the scam.

Assistant coroner Rachel Knight recorded a conclusion of suicide after Davies, from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, died.

Knight said it was "more likely than not" that personal stresses in his life together with falling victim to the sextortion scam "more than minimally contributed" to his death.

She wrote of the scammers: "Conversation quickly turned sexual and she asked him for intimate images, which were then used to blackmail him for money by threatening to send the images to his family and friends, and to upload them to a YouTube channel.

"The images were indeed sent to at least one of Cai's Facebook friends by the scammer.

"Cai was bombarded with video calls and messages via Facebook Messenger and WhatsApp over a very short period of time making demands for money."

News.title: Decades after their first wins, Roger Howarth and Beth Maitland win at Daytime Emmys
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Roger Howarth and Beth Maitland of “The Young and the Restless” swept the supporting acting categories at the 53rd annual Daytime Emmys on Friday night, with both winning decades after their first triumphs.

Howarth currently plays Matt Clark on the CBS soap. He first won in 1994 in the younger actor category for his breakout role as Todd Manning on “One Life to Live.”

Maitland was honored for playing Traci Abbott, a role she originated in 1982 — the year of her first supporting actress win — and has played off and on ever since.

"I was equally as gobsmacked back then as a young actress, and I can’t tell you how meaningful it is to be here,” she said before paying tribute to her fellow nominees and actors.

“Every one of you a winner, every one of you a part of the contribution daytime makes in a world gone mad, offering just a few minutes of relief — to laugh, to cry and to celebrate."

Tracee Ellis Ross won in the travel and adventure category for her Roku show “Solo Traveling with Tracee Ellis Ross.”

“Wow, how fun is this?” Ross said, while thanking the countries of Morocco, Mexico and Spain. “I'm an Emmy winner!”

Ross was a five-time Primetime Emmy nominee for the hit ABC comedy “black-ish.”

Ambyr Michelle of “Beyond the Gates” won for emerging talent in a daytime drama, the second year the award was handed out.

“I don't just see an award,” she said. “I see a promise fulfilled.”

Sherri Shepherd won as daytime talk series host for “Sherri,” which ended its four-season run in May.

The ceremony held at the Hollywood Palladium was streamed live for the second straight year.

News.title: Fireworks warning issued after teen suffers life-changing injuries: 'His eye leaked down his face'
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Health leaders have issued a safety warning after fresh figures revealed an increase in hospital admissions for burns and injuries related to fireworks.

According to NHS England, 85 people were admitted to hospital in England last November, rising from 60 the previous year. Over the course of 2025, total admissions hit 161, compared to 120 during the preceding 12 months.

The caution follows an incident involving a family from Hartlepool, whose son Aleks Stasiukiewicz, 17, sustained life-changing injuries in November 2024.

Taken to the James Cook University Hospital in Middlesbrough, consultants confirmed he lost his left eye and part of his eyelid. Medical staff removed firework fragments before inserting a spherical prosthesis to replicate natural eye movement.

open image in gallery Aleks with his injuries ( Family handout )

Aleks said: “On the evening of the accident, I attended an organised fireworks display at a local rugby club, before joining my friends at a nearby park.

“I remember someone lighting a firework, but it didn’t go off as intended so I went over to relight it. It exploded instantly, knocking me to the floor.”

His mother, Julie, went to the scene after Aleks’ friend called her to say there had been an accident.

She said: “When I arrived, Aleks was already lying in the ambulance, I didn’t take my eyes off him, I was devastated. I had to watch as his eye leaked down the side of his face. “

Aleks said: ” When people say don’t play with fireworks, listen.

“I know it can be tempting to break the rules and have a bit of fun but fireworks are incredibly dangerous.”

Professor Frankie Swords, NHS medical director, said Bonfire Night “is a great opportunity to be with friends and family” but children can be the ones paying the price when things go wrong.

open image in gallery Specialists worked to remove fragments of fireworks from his eye socket before inserting a ball-shaped prosthesis to replicate the movement of a real eye ( Family handout )

“Some have suffered life-changing injuries, turning what should be a night of fun into a nightmare,” she said.

“So it’s vital you keep a close eye on children and loved ones to help prevent accidents like this, and know the NHS is available 24/7 if you need us.

“Call 999 in an emergency, and the NHS website also offers information on the prevention and treatment of burns, as well as first aid measures, for anyone who needs it.”

The Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (Rospa) is urging people to enjoy fireworks at professionally-organised public displays.

People buying them for home should look up and follow the firework code, which includes only buying fireworks from reputable retailers, using them one at a time, lighting them with a taper at arms length and never going back to a lit firework, it said.

Becky Guy, senior policy manager at Rospa, said: “Bonfire Night should be a time for families and communities to come together safely, but these latest figures show that far too many people are still suffering serious injuries from fireworks.

open image in gallery Bonfire Night “is a great opportunity to be with friends and family” but children can be the ones paying the price when things go wrong, the NHS said ( Family handout )

“Particularly worrying is the increase in the number of children being admitted to hospital. Fireworks are not toys.

“A moment’s carelessness can result in serious burns, eye injuries and permanent scarring.

“We highly recommend people attend organised fireworks displays wherever possible. Not only are these much safer, they are more spectacular too.

“If you can’t make it to an organised display and are planning fireworks at home, please remember some simple precautions.

“Keep children under close supervision, follow manufacturers’ instructions and think carefully about the space you have available before choosing fireworks.

“Not every garden is suitable for every type of firework, so always check the recommended safety distance before buying.

“We would also encourage people to think about neighbours, pets and wildlife by letting people know about displays in advance and considering lower-noise fireworks where possible.”

In 2022, Riley Luke, from Paisley in Renfrewshire, was just eight years old when he lost four fingers and part of his hand after a fireworks accident.

open image in gallery Riley had to learn to write with his left hand after being released from hospital (SFRS/PA)

He had been out playing in the local area when his friends found a firework and they began passing it around each other as they tried to light it.

His father Scott Luke explained: “Eventually, Riley was holding it and when it lit, it stuck to his hand.

“He was trying to get it off his hand and then within seconds it exploded, which resulted in losing four of his fingers and a good part of his palm.”

Anna Baker, clinical nurse specialist in children’s burns and plastics, said: “Always stand well away from fireworks and dispose of sparklers in cold water buckets.

“Sparklers can get up to 4,000 degrees when lit and it is where we see the most common cause of injuries during fireworks seasons.”

News.title: Nearly half of young adults who work from home feel 'lonely', data shows – and it could get worse
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Younger employees experience greater levels of isolation when working remotely compared with older generations, with the issue potentially intensifying, new research indicates.

Figures from the Bupa Wellbeing Index point to a rise in the proportion of 18 to 24-year-olds who feel remote working causes loneliness, increasing from 42% in 2025 to 47% in 2026.

In contrast, 34% of all surveyed adults in 2026 stated that working in isolation leads to loneliness, down slightly from 35% the prior year.

Among those aged 45 to 54, the figure stood at 28%, while only 18% of individuals aged 55 and over felt working alone induced loneliness.

Shazna Khanom, head of clinical mental health at Bupa, said: “As we await the final publication of the Alan Milburn review of young people and work, one thing increasingly stands out to me as a clinician.

“It’s not just about helping young people into work, we also need to create workplaces where they can feel connected, supported and able to thrive.

“While remote and flexible working can bring significant benefits, connection and mental wellbeing should remain a priority alongside them.”

open image in gallery There has been a rise in the number of 18 to 24-year-olds who feel working alone makes them lonely ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

The report also revealed that workers aged 18 to 24 face a heightened impact from workplace mental health struggles relative to the wider population.

Some 41% noted that mental wellbeing had harmed their capacity to work over the preceding 12 months, compared with 29% across all age groups surveyed.

Nearly nine in 10 (87%) younger staff also reported attending work despite managing a mental health issue, whereas the general population figure was 70%.

Furthermore, mental health proved a larger factor in young staff quitting jobs over the past year, with 35% of those aged 18 to 24 citing it as an influence, compared to 24% across all age groups surveyed.

It comes after Office for National Statistics (ONS) data from July to September showed higher feelings of loneliness generally among younger age groups.

Some 34% of people aged 16 to 29 said they always feel lonely or are lonely often or some of the time, compared to 25% of people of all ages and 22% of those aged 50 to 69, the ONS found.

open image in gallery Nearly nine in 10 (87%) younger staff also reported attending work despite managing a mental health issue ( Alamy/PA )

Ms Khanom added: “Creating mentally healthy workplaces is a shared responsibility. Employers can make a real difference by fostering environments where people feel safe discussing concerns and accessing support early.

“For those who are struggling at work because of mental health concerns, my advice would be to speak to your manager, HR team or a healthcare professional. A conversation can make all the difference in helping you to get the help you need.”

The Bupa report included data on working and feeling lonely for 5,262 people.

Kelly Nicoll, immediate past president of the Institution of Occupational Safety and Health (IOSH), said managers need to update practices “to reflect the evolving demands of a multi-generational, hybrid workforce”.

She added: “Our own research has indicated around half of 18 to 24-year-olds say home and hybrid working makes it harder to build relationships with colleagues and managers.

“More than two-fifths fear fewer face-to-face interactions are restricting their personal and professional development. A third feel demotivated.

“Managers need to build in more structured supervision time and regular check-ins with young workers and hybrid workers.

“They need to make room for daily informal catch-ups and also set weekly and monthly one-to-one sessions to cover performance and address wider issues such as health, safety and wellbeing, as well as mentoring, coaching and career development.

“Mental health risk management should be fully integrated into occupational safety systems and management practices need to be updated to reflect the evolving demands of a multigenerational, hybrid workforce.”

News.title: Graphika finds China-linked Spamouflage accounts posing as US voters on X
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The long-running influence campaign known as Spamouflage is active ahead of the midterm elections, with accounts likely linked to China posing as U.S. voters and posting divisive content about U.S. politics, social issues and the elections, analysts say.

In a blog posted on Friday, Graphika, a New York-based firm that tracks online networks, said it had identified Spamouflage-linked activity on X that closely resembles tactics documented in 2024 ahead of the U.S. presidential election.

“The accounts post content questioning election integrity and the legitimacy of U.S. democracy,” the Graphika blog said.

Intelligence and national security officials have long warned that Russia, China and Iran have run online influence operations targeting U.S. voters ahead of elections. China, rather than supporting one presidential candidate over the other, has focused its efforts on undermining confidence in elections, voting and the U.S. in general, observers have said.

The Chinese Embassy in Washington didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Darren Linvill, who co-directs Clemson University's Watt Family Innovation Center Media Forensics Hub and has tracked Spamouflage activity, said there is “no chance it tips the balance in any real political conversation.”

“Spamouflage is famously bad at mimicking real Americans," Linvill said. “It's outside their wheelhouse.”

Rather, the network has been more effective in suppressing information, Linvill said, as the accounts linked to the influence operation “very frequently attack and harass members of the Chinese diaspora community” and are part of a wider effort by Beijing to silence views it dislikes.

In its blog, Graphika said it identified an account that appears to have replaced a removed account that was linked to Spamouflage and has posted divisive U.S. political content, including attacks on Democratic Party leadership during the U.S. government shutdown in October 2025 and criticism of immigration policy.

Graphika flagged four accounts with a history of Spamouflage activity that now amplify MAGA-styled personas and another account with more than 200,000 followers that presents itself as a Philippine culture blog but now posts pro-China and divisive U.S.-focused content.

Graphika said it could not determine whether the account was hijacked or whether the original operator sold or otherwise lost control of it.
