World.title: Malawi: Police Confirm Egyptian Deputy Ambassador Beaten in Lilongwe Attack
World.content:
A senior Egyptian diplomat has been hospitalised after being attacked and beaten in Lilongwe, sparking a police investigation into the shocking assault.

National Police spokesperson Gladys Chiwaula confirmed that Egypt's Deputy Ambassador to Malawi was admitted to a hospital in the capital after the attack.

"Police are following up on the matter and will give more details later," she said.

Chiwaula gave few details.

She did not say where the attack happened, what led to it, or how serious the diplomat's injuries are. Police have also withheld the deputy ambassador's name.

Officers say they are investigating, but the incident is likely to raise alarm over the safety of foreign envoys in the country.

World.title: Africa: From Commonwealth Connections to Economic Opportunity - Expanding Africa-Caribbean Trade Linkages
World.content:
guest column

When Commonwealth leaders gather in Antigua and Barbuda this November, they will confront rising trade tensions, geopolitical shocks and supply chain disruption alongside longstanding challenges, such as high debt, limited affordable finance, climate exposure and poor connectivity.

Across Africa, the Pacific and the Caribbean, these pressures make diversifying markets, attracting productive investment and building resilience through trade even more urgent. They also increase the importance of regional and cross-regional value chains that can withstand disruptions to established trade relationships.

One opportunity lies in plain sight: stronger Africa-Caribbean economic connections. Shared history, culture and diaspora relationships provide a foundation, as do common ambitions to diversify exports, add value locally and create opportunities for small businesses, including those led by women and young entrepreneurs.

The institutional landscape is also changing. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is building a framework for trade including goods, services, investment and digital commerce, while the Caribbean is deepening the CARICOM Single Market and Economy.



Connecting these integration efforts across the Atlantic could help firms aggregate supply and demand, build scale, and develop regional value chains. and access larger markets. A bigger, more integrated market can improve the commercial case for investment and the economics of cross-regional trade.

Forthcoming analysis by the International Trade Centre (ITC), undertaken with the support of Afreximbank, points to considerable unrealised trade potential between Africa and the Caribbean. But the numbers tell only part of the story.

In a survey of 1,175 businesses and business support organisations only 10% of African companies and 12% of Caribbean companies reported trading with the other region. Yet among those that did, 79% of African firms and 82% of Caribbean firms described their experience positively or very positively. The challenge is less about potential than removing barriers to scale.

Businesses struggle to access reliable market information, trusted partners and appropriate finance, as well as to navigate standards and move goods efficiently.

These constraints are not new. Low trade volumes weaken direct transport links; poor connectivity raises costs; limited commercial relationships restrict information; and smaller transactions are harder to finance.

The priority is to tackle these challenges in a comprehensive way.

Physical distance remains particularly costly. ITC estimates freight costs on African exports to the Caribbean at almost 20% of shipment value, compared with just over 8% for African exports globally. Caribbean exports to Africa face costs approaching 22%. Limited routes and fragmented networks continue to undermine viable trade. Scheduled direct air services between Lagos and Barbados, launched in 2026, illustrate how improved connections can support business travel, tourism and wider services.

Access to finance depends not only on the availability of capital, but on whether viable opportunities can be connected to appropriate financing. Businesses need guidance on available funding and lender requirements, and financial institutions need appropriate instruments and ways to manage risk. Trade finance, working-capital facilities, guarantees and risk-sharing mechanisms can all bridge these gaps.

Payments also matter, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Slow, costly or uncertain transfers can derail transactions. More efficient cross-border payment systems would reduce both transaction costs and risks. Africa's Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) offers useful lessons for simplifying payments as financial links with the Caribbean deepen.

Beyond trade volumes, value creation extends beyond goods. Services, digital solutions and the creative industries can generate more value within both regions. Africa and the Caribbean have globally recognised cultural assets and extensive diasporas, yet much of the creative value is captured elsewhere. Creators and firms need finance, workable payments, intellectual property expertise, distribution channels and direct access to buyers and investors. Supporting creative businesses, rather than only promoting cultural exchange, would generate more revenue and help jobs remain in local economies.

Governments and institutions can create the enabling environment, but businesses will ultimately determine whether a new chapter in Africa–Caribbean economic relations succeed, especially for SMEs.

Commonwealth trade and investment platforms can connect policymakers, investors, entrepreneurs and business leaders. They offer a way to identify obstacles that no single firm or government can resolve alone. Success, however, means introductions becoming contracts, investment reaching viable enterprises and businesses entering new markets.

The Commonwealth brings an existing economic advantage to this endeavour. The opportunity is to make that advantage work more deliberately for Africa–Caribbean commerce, where physical distance, limited market information and still-thin commercial networks continue to constrain trade.

Through its Working Group on Trade and Investment, member countries are developing a workplan to expand intra-Commonwealth commerce. Cooperation on compatible regulations, mutual recognition of standards and qualifications, and simpler border procedures can help realise these gains.

Close 

ITC's work on investment promotion and digital trade to women's economic empowerment, small-state resilience and emerging Africa–Caribbean business linkages can advance this agenda. Afreximbank's Global Africa vision brings the finance, investment and commercial infrastructure required to turn diaspora ties into sustainable economic relationships.

These capabilities are complementary. Trade policy can open markets; finance helps businesses act; and enterprises sustain commercial relationships.

The practical test is clear: identify viable opportunities, mobilise investment, resolve logistics, finance and payment barriers, connect SMEs to customers and investors, use digital trade to overcome distance and retain more value within regions. Progress should then be measured in transactions, market access and sustainable business relationships.

As leaders gather in Antigua and Barbuda, they can demonstrate how a connected Commonwealth can convert partnerships into investment, enterprise and shared prosperity.

World.title: Nigeria: Gunmen Kill Police Inspector, 11 Others in Kebbi
World.content:
Residents of Karwa, Kestu and Waiwayi in Besse/Shanga riverine areas of Kebbi State have fled their communities as suspected members of the Lakurawa and Mamudawa terror groups killed 11 residents and a police inspector in a series of attacks they have launched on the communities.

The terrorists carried out a series of attacks on the communities in Besse and Shanga from the 22nd to 28 October, this year, Daily Trust gathered. During the attacks, they burnt houses and looted property as they moved along the River Niger bank from Kaoje to Besse.

A local who spoke to our corespondent, Aminu Usman, said the attack on the communities was devastating as the gunmen burnt houses and property before retreating to their hideouts.



He said, "the attack took many of the villagers unawares. No one expected that the Lakurawa terrorists would attack us. The attack was carried out in a coordinated manner. They burnt our houses and looted our property. Many people have been rendered homeless and they have fled the communities," he said.

Though the police said five people were killed in an attack on October 26, while seven others died in attacks on October 28 in the Karwa, Kestu and Waiwayi area of the state, bringing the total to 12, including a police inspector, locals who spoke under condition of anonymity said over 23 people actually lost their lives in the Lakurawa/Mamudawa attacks on the communities of Koko Besse and Shanga areas of Kebbi.

A source said, "They killed people and took their valuables. They burnt motorcycles and broke into shops and took whatever they wanted."

He added that rumour of the attacks triggered the mobilisation of vigilantes known as Yan Sakai, who allegedly attacked some Fulani traders at Samanaji Market on October 22, 2026.

A resident who spoke to our correspondent said, "I know a man who lost four of his family members in the attack. As I speak, only a few people are left in the affected communities. Some of them who fled for safety during the attack are just returning on the assurance by the security agents and government that measures are being put in place to ensure our safety."

He called on the government to come to their aid as some of the residents have nowhere to stay.

Another resident, Aliyu Tailor Besse, said the attack was carried out by the Lakurawa terrorists group.

"What happened was that after attacking communities in Kaoje area of Bagudo Local Government, they started moving along the River Niger up to Koko Besse area.They were attacking communities along the River Niger as they moved towards Besse community. Many people were killed in the attacks. Prior to the attacks, those who saw them moving along the River Niger banks had raised an alarm calling on residents of the communities along the area to vacate. Some left, but many others stayed behind," he said.

Daily Trust gathered that a few days before the Karwa, Kestu and Waiwayi attacks, suspected members of the Lakurawa group also attacked Lafagu and other communities in Boya area of Kaoje, killing the village head, Alhaji Saidu Mujeli, and six others before leaving the area through the River Niger bank to attack other communities in Besse and Shanga.

It was gathered that despite the establishment of an army battalion in Kaoje to curtail the activities of terrorists, attacks have continued.

Police confirm attacks

Speaking to our correspondent, the state Police Public Relations Officer, SP Bashir Usman, said "it's true that the attack happened but it did not happen in one day and not in one community. It started from the 22nd of this month. The casualties recorded was not in a single attack. They attacked many of the communities in the riverine area and that's why the figure of those killed rose to 12. A police inspector and 11 others were killed in the attacks."

He said members of the Lakurawa terrorists group had earlier attacked communities along the Karwa, Kestu and Waiwayi axis on 22nd of October, but security operatives repelled them. He said they later carried out attacks on the communities of Karwa, Kestu and Waiwayi on October 26 and 28.

"Although the joint security teams repelled the attacks, seven people unfortunately lost their lives, including a police inspector," he said.

He added that earlier, members of the Yan Sakai, had invaded Samanaji Market and killed Fulani traders.

"Our police tactical teams deployed by the Divisional Police Officer (DPO) in Besse, responded promptly to restore peace and prevent further carnage. However, three Fulani people lost their lives, while a police inspector sustained injuries in the line of duty," he said.

The state police spokesman said a tactical team of the police had been deployed to the troubled communities and normalcy is gradually returning to the area.

"The police have launched investigation into the attack and is following up on the attackers," he said.

'Attacks sign of frustration'

A security expert, who retired as a Captain in the Nigerian Army, Shehu Abubakar, told our correspondent that the attacks carried out by suspected members of the Lakurawa group in some communities of Kebbi, is a sign of frustration.

"You should understand that a battalion of the Nigerian Army was recently established at Kaoje area of Bagudo Local Government to curtail activities of the bandits and Lakurawa, operating in the area. The Lakurawa must leave the area to find a convenient place as base to carry out their attacks. They carried out their attack on the communities along the River Niger bank while migrating to another area to avenge the presence of the army base at Kaoje.

"They can no longer stay close to the area where the battalion is located. They migrated from Kaoje, through the bank of the River Niger, moving through communities of Samanaji, Dutsinmari, Zaria Kalakala, to where they started their attacks at Karwa, Kestu and Waiwayi. Now that they seem to have been displaced, the security agencies operating in the state should follow them up in every move they make so that they don't get a convenient place to settle. That way, they may be frustrated to move out of the state," he said.

Military bases in Kebbi

In the last two years, six Forward Operation Bases were established in Sakaba,Zuru,Yauri, Augie and Kaoje. The Battalion in Birnin Kebbi was upgraded to an Armoured Brigade, just as there is a battalion in Zuru.There are also army units in parts of Kaoje and other areas to strengthen military operations in the troubled communities of Augie, Danko Wasagu, Mahuta, Argungu, Arewa, Bagudo and Dandi, but the spate of killings occasioned by bandits and Lakurawa attacks remain a growing concern among residents.

Close 

Kebbi's killing fields

On Wednesday of last week, a large number of bandits invaded Dirin -Daji in Sakara Local Government Area of the state. It took the combined efforts of the security agencies in the area to disperse the attackers.

A week before the Kaoje district attack, three people were killed at Kasabo, a community in Saminaka, Yauri Local Government Area of the state. The community was attacked by the bandits in the early hours of the day when people were preparing to go about their daily activities. A resident, Aminu Usman, said their attackers came in large number to invade the community and that they killed three people while many others escaped through the bush.

A few days before the attack at Kasabo, suspected members of the Lakurawa terrorists group attacked the site of the construction company handling the Badagry-Ilela Supper Highway project at Gubba in Maiyama Local Government Area of the state, killing two soldiers and a Chinese national. The attackers were said to have crossed into Kebbi from Kebbe area of Sokoto, to carry out the attack, it was gathered.

Efforts to get comments from the state government proved abortive, but a top government official who does not want his name in print told our corespondent that the state government was working closely with security agencies to identify and apprehend those responsible for the attacks.

He said, "Governor Nasir Idris has been up and doing on issues of security on the state. No fewer than 109 armoured vehicles and other logistics have been procured for security agencies to fight insecurity in the state."

World.title: Africa: AFCON Every Two Years Again As CAF Reverses Decision
World.content:
The Confederation of African Football (CAF) has reversed its decision to stage the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) every four years, announcing that the tournament will return to its traditional two-year cycle.

The decision was unanimously approved by the CAF Executive Committee, with President Patrice Motsepe announcing the development after the organisation's Strategy Conference in Cabo Verde, held from October 7 to 9, 2026.

The reversal comes after CAF reviewed its earlier plan to move AFCON to a four-year schedule and introduce an Africa Nations League as a biennial competition.

CAF said the proposed Nations League would take several years to generate the financial resources and football development benefits required to make its competitions globally competitive and financially sustainable.



In a statement published on its website on Thursday, Motsepe said the decision to retain the two-year AFCON cycle was taken in the interest of African football, the confederation's 54 member associations and African players playing for clubs outside the continent.

"The decision by the CAF EXCO that the CAF AFCON should take place every Two Years was based on advancing, protecting and promoting the interest of African Football and CAF's 54 Member Associations, as well as the interest of African players employed by Football Clubs outside Africa," he said.

Motsepe added that CAF was concerned about the time it would take for the proposed Africa Nations League to deliver the financial and developmental gains initially expected from the competition.

He said the new tournament was intended to mirror the existing AFCON format and take place every two years, but would not provide the required support for African football in the immediate future.

Under the revised calendar, the next AFCON will take place in 2027, with Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda jointly hosting the tournament.

The subsequent editions are scheduled for 2028, 2031 and 2033, with CAF maintaining that the competition will not be staged in a FIFA World Cup year.

Motsepe expressed confidence in the three East African countries' ability to deliver a successful tournament in 2027.

He also described AFCON as more than a football competition, saying it provides an opportunity to celebrate Africa's cultures and bring people from across the continent and the diaspora together.

"The AFCON competition is also about celebrating African Football and Africa's rich and diverse cultures, customs and traditions and bringing people together from Africa's 54 Countries, the African Diaspora and throughout the world," he said.

"The CAF EXCO decision is in the best interest of African Football and CAF's 54 Member Associations and will also contribute significantly to the development and growth of football in Africa," he added.

World.title: Ethiopia: As Tens of Thousands Flee Ethiopia to Kenya, UN Agency Warns of Growing Humanitarian Needs
World.content:
A map showing the location of Kenya (in orange) and Ethiopia (in green).

Geneva — The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) says humanitarian needs are growing in an unfolding crisis on the Kenya–Ethiopia border as ongoing clashes on the Ethiopian side have forced tens of thousands of people to cross into Kenya in search of safety.

Significant cross-border movements at Moyale have been reported since Oct. 22.

“According to local authorities, up to an estimated 50,000 people have crossed into Kenya,” said Fatima Mohammed-Cole, the UNHCR Representative in Kenya.

“The figure remains fluid as registration and verification efforts continue, amid reports of further crossings,” she said in a statement.



Many of those fleeing are women and children.

The UN official said that while some affected people are staying with relatives and in host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations such as schools and churches.

- FOOD: THE URGENT NEED

“Food remains the most urgent need, alongside safe drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and health care,” said Mohammed-Cole.

UNHCR has deployed an emergency team to Moyale and is working closely with the Kenyan government.

It is working alongside the UN migration agency, IOM; the UN children’s agency, UNICEF, the UN World Food Programme, the Kenya Red Cross Society, and other humanitarian partners, to support the national and local response.

UNHCR said it is mobilising emergency relief supplies, including essential household items and temporary shelter materials, to support nearly 12,000 people, with efforts underway to increase assistance as needs grow.

The agency is supporting ongoing assessments of protection and humanitarian needs.

“We are also working with the authorities and partners to identify safer accommodation options, further away from the border, for those fleeing violence,” the UNHCR official said.

According to Chatham House researchers, “Although Tigray has seen conflict before, this time there is a risk that hostilities could extend into Eritrea and Sudan,” they wrote.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Global Nursing Head Flags Dangers of Misinformation After Killing of Congo Ebola Nurse
World.content:
A nurse prepares a bed for a suspected case of Ebola in the isolation unit at Bwera Hospital, Kasese District (file photo).

Geneva — The International Council of Nurses (ICN) head has warned of the lethal dangers that misinformation poses to the nursing profession following the killing of a nurse in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo), who was responding to an Ebola case.

ICN chief executive Howard Catton said the "tragic news" was a reminder that prevalent misinformation was particularly dangerous for healthcare staff after young men armed with machetes killed the nurse.

"Health misinformation and the breakdown of trust in science is now a deadly risk for nurses and health workers," Catton posted on the media platform X on Oct. 29.

The UN's Ebola coordinator and the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) on Oct. 29 deplored the killing of the nurse working to fight the disease in the DRC four days earlier.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In an interview with AllAfrica, Catton also warned that community health workers often supplant nurses and may be seen as an easy, cheap substitute for a skilled nursing workforce in parts of Africa.

"There is both the migration of registered nurses from the continent of Africa and unemployment of nurses in Africa," said Catton.

"So, as we see this growth in community health workers, we also know that registered nurses continue to leave Africa for high-income countries in Europe or North America."

At the same time, many nurses on the continent remain unemployed.

Catton cited UN figures showing Africa's health workforce grew to 5.72 million in 2024, up from 4.3 million in 2018, noting that such progress is not keeping pace with demand.

ONLY 46 PERCENT OF WORKFORCE NEEDS

"The African region currently has only 46 percent of the health workers it needs," said the head of the international nursing group.

Catton visited African countries last year, and some leaders said what is happening is making it harder for them to improve their healthcare systems.

"To us, this is starting to feel like a form of neo-colonialism because we're having valuable resources which are being taken; we're not being adequately compensated for them," said the nursing head, conveying the sentiment some African leaders expressed to him.

The WHO's Africa 2026 report says an estimated 943,000 trained health workers across the African region were unemployed in 2024.

That is, as the continent faces severe staffing shortages and meets only 46 per cent of its overall health workforce needs.

"We are training more health workers than ever before, yet too many remain unemployed while millions go without care," said Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa.

"Without bold investment and coordinated reform to plan, train and retain health workers, progress toward universal health coverage will remain out of reach," said Dr Janabi, speaking in Ghana in May.

Close 

The WHO estimates a global shortage of at least ten million healthcare workers by 2030, and some organizations project an even larger shortfall, writes Pooja Kumar, a global leader at the McKinsey Health Institute.

She notes, though, that the global healthcare workforce shortage is not evenly distributed.

"For example," Pooja says, "Africa has 17 percent of the world's population but accounts for 52 percent of the global shortage."

World.title: Chad: France and Chad Rebuild Military Ties With Planned Air Force Training
World.content:
Two French fighter jets and a transport aircraft will soon make a stopover in Chad and carry out "training activities", the French army has said, as the two countries seek to rebuild ties.

The stopover will take place as part of a joint military exercise involving the armed forces of Côte d'Ivoire, Gabon and France in November.

Xavier Rival, a spokesman for the French chief of defence staff, said Thursday that two French Mirage 2000 fighter jets and a French CASA transport aircraft would make a technical stopover in Chad.

"It will be a short visit that will also provide an opportunity to conduct training activities," he said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Relations between France and Chad began to deteriorate in mid-2024.

They reached breaking point when Chad's leader Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno formally terminated his country's military cooperation agreement with France in November 2024.

The move led to the complete withdrawal of French troops from the country in early 2025.

Mending ties

Rival said France's cooperation with Chad had resumed, "in full respect of Chad's sovereignty".

He said the French armed forces would help develop the capabilities of the Chadian air force.

"France's objective is to contribute to efforts against regional instability," he added.

Chad had been one of France's last military footholds in the Sahel, a region where Paris once deployed more than 5,000 soldiers as part of its anti-jihadist Operation Barkhane, which ended in November 2022.

Coups between 2020 and 2023 forced France to withdraw from Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, as the juntas in those countries drew closer to Russia.

France and Chad have since sought to revive their ties, while expanding them to include economic and cultural cooperation as well as military assistance.

Algeria and Chad cement stategic partnership with raft of bilateral deals

'New step forward'

President Emmanuel Macron hosted Déby for talks in mid-October as part of ongoing efforts to rebuild the relationship. It followed another visit in January.

During Déby's most recent trip, France and Chad signed a declaration of intent to renew their defence cooperation.

"We are taking a new step forward and formalising the strengthening of our defence partnership, in line with a renewed relationship," Macron posted on social media platform X, after hosting Déby at the Élysée Palace.

Close 

"We are building a partnership based on mutual respect and practical cooperation for the benefit of our peoples."

France and Chad sign 'renewed' defence partnership following two-year hiatus

Macron has sought to renew France's engagement with Africa after years of strained ties with former French-speaking colonies.

On the economic front, France's main employers' federation Medef hosted a France-Chad business forum in September, bringing together 250 companies to encourage investment.

The Élysée said Medef is planning to send a delegation to Chad in the coming months.

Under an ambitious national development plan to diversify its economy, Chad says it aims to raise €26.5 billion in public and private investment and boost its GDP by 60 percent by 2030.

(with newswires)

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 30, 2026
World.content:
Rwandan Man Convicted in U.S. for Lying About 1994 Genocide Role

A Rwandan man, Eric Nshimiye, has been convicted in the United States of perjury and obstruction of justice after lying under oath about his involvement in the 1994 Rwandan genocide. A federal jury in Boston found that Nshimiye concealed his alleged participation in attacks against the Tutsi community while testifying in the 2019 immigration fraud trial of his former university classmate, Jean Leonard Teganya. Nshimiye fled Rwanda for Kenya in 1994 and was admitted to the U.S. as a refugee the following year. Evidence presented at his trial showed that, while a student at the University of Rwanda in Butare, he took part in attacks on the Tutsi people, including by striking them on the head with a club. Nshimiye faces up to five years in prison for each of four perjury counts and up to 10 years for obstruction of justice. He is expected to be sentenced on 26 January 2027.

Tinubu Heads to Saudi Arabia to Pray for Nigeria



Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has travelled to Saudi Arabia to perform the lesser Hajj pilgrimage, known as Umrah, where he is expected to pray for Nigeria's peace, unity and stability. The presidency said that the visit will provide an opportunity for spiritual reflection and prayers for the country's continued progress. Tinubu's trip comes as Nigeria prepares for general elections, with insecurity and economic challenges expected to dominate the campaign. His media aide has dismissed speculation that the visit is intended for medical checks, insisting that it is a religious journey. The next elections are scheduled for 16 January 2027. Tinubu's main challengers will again be former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi.

U.S. Seizes $750,000 in Kenyan-Linked Student Aid Fraud Probe

US authorities have seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency linked to an alleged international student financial aid fraud scheme involving Kenyan nationals. The seizure forms part of Operation Ghostbusters, an investigation into a network accused of using stolen American identities to submit fraudulent student aid applications and divert millions of dollars in grants and loan refunds. The US Justice Department has charged five defendants, with investigators alleging that Kenyan-based conspirators worked with individuals in the US to transfer proceeds through bank accounts and overseas networks. Authorities said that the wider investigation has identified more than $32 million in losses. Cooperation with Kenyan law enforcement agencies is continuing to trace funds and pursue suspects.

Rights Group Urges Mali to Release Missing Junta Critic and Son

Human Rights Watch has called on Mali's military authorities to disclose the whereabouts of former government minister and junta critic Mountaga Tall and his son, Cheick Mamadou Tall, six months after their abductions. Unidentified gunmen reportedly seized Mountaga in Bamako on 2 May. His son disappeared two weeks later after being told he could deliver belongings to his father. Their whereabouts and condition remain unknown, with authorities yet to acknowledge detaining them. Human Rights Watch said that the disappearances reflect a wider crackdown on political opposition and dissent under Mali's military junta. He urged authorities to ensure their safety and release them.

Sudan Accuses Ethiopia of Backing Drone Attacks

Sudanese authorities claim that 162 drone attacks launched from Ethiopian territory have killed more than 400 civilians and 102 military personnel, amid allegations that Ethiopia is supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Officials said that the attacks have targeted several locations across Sudan, destroying schools, hospitals, health centres and fuel stations. However, the claims have not been independently verified. Sudan has accused Ethiopia of allowing drones to operate from bases near its border. He warned that the attacks threaten regional stability and efforts to enable displaced people to return home. Ethiopia has previously rejected allegations of supporting the RSF, describing them as unfounded. Sudan's Defence Minister has also accused more than 20 countries of providing the paramilitary group with logistical support, funding, mercenaries and drones.

Close 

Guinea-Bissau Busts Trafficking Ring Behind Fake Migration Scheme



Police in Guinea-Bissau have dismantled an alleged human trafficking network that lured approximately 70 people from across West Africa with promises of employment and opportunities to migrate to Europe. More than five suspects have been arrested following an operation on 21 October. Authorities allege that victims from countries including Mali, Sierra Leone, Guinea, Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire were defrauded, held against their will and pressured into recruiting others into fraudulent pyramid schemes. Some women were reportedly threatened with sexual exploitation and prostitution. Victims have been rescued; however, many remain stranded in Guinea-Bissau because they cannot afford to return home. Human rights organisations have raised concerns about inadequate shelters, psychological support, and financial assistance for survivors.

Watkins' first two seasons with the USC Trojans saw her score an average of 25.6 points per game. Now, she returns to a talented supporting cast as the No. 3 Trojans pursue their first national championship since 1984.

PACERS STAR TYRESE HALIBURTON MOVED TO TEARS AFTER LONG-AWAITED RETURN FROM ACHILLES INJURY

Watkins added that she's already imagined what it will feel like to see her first basket go in.

NEW FACES, NEW PLACES: FIVE TRANSFER PORTAL PLAYERS POISED FOR SUCCESS THIS COMING SEASON

"They have proven that they’re going to be really impactful players at a high level," coach Lindsay Gottlieb said.

Last season, Watkins would set up chairs in the locker room for the team talk on the road. It was one of the small ways she found to be useful without being on the court.

"I was able to take on a leadership role for sure, and I can’t say I really owned that role prior to that," she said. "Being able to do that and also see the game from a different perspective and seeing how can I help my team really helped grow my IQ and leadership skills."

One month after she and her husband were arrested for the alleged murder of their trans New York Times executive son-in-law, Shili Chen claims in new legal documents that her husband is the one to blame, according to reports.

Shili Chen, 77, and Shouyong Zhang were arrested Sept. 26 for allegedly shooting Jonathan McKinsey, 40, in a crowded park in Dublin, California.

In a new bail filing, Chen’s lawyers claim the 77-year-old watched her husband fire the fatal shots at McKinsey at the Dublin Sports Grounds from inside her car, according to the San Francisco Chronicle.

FATHER-IN-LAW OF TRANS NYT EXEC ADMITTED KILLING HIM, WORKED 'IN CONCERT' WITH MOTHER-IN-LAW: DOCS

Her lawyer, Curtis Briggs, argued that Chen only got out of the car "to protect her husband from what she feared was an assault by Mr. McKinsey," the California Post reported.

She was allegedly seen on surveillance video firing a gun at McKinsey after Zhang fired the shots that killed him.

Chen’s lawyers argued she was kept "in the dark" while Zhang planned McKinsey’s murder.

Zhang allegedly admitted to the fatal shooting just days after when video footage of the attack was shown to him, court documents obtained by Fox News Digital showed.

Zhang told police he asked his wife to drive to the park but didn’t explain why, according to the Chronicle.

Prosecutors accused the couple of "lying in wait" at the park for McKinsey before the shooting, but her lawyer claims there isn’t enough evidence to prove that.

That special circumstance has been used to hold the couple without bail.

In a separate filing, Zhang’s public defender argued that he didn’t pose a threat because of his age and health and because the shooting was an isolated family incident.

Chen’s lawyer argues that she wasn’t the "actual killer" since she shot McKinsey when he was already dead.

Several 911 callers reported gunfire at the Dublin Sports Grounds before a Dublin Police Services sergeant arrived and found McKinsey lying face up with multiple gunshot wounds. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Witnesses pointed police toward a black Honda Civic leaving the parking lot, leading officers to conduct a high-risk traffic stop nearby, the filings state.

Chen was driving and allegedly had a firearm in her possession when she was detained, while Zhang was in the passenger seat.

Three witnesses identified Chen and Zhang as the shooters, while surveillance video allegedly captured the couple opening fire "in concert" on McKinsey.

Police said the couple started shooting in a crowded park's parking lot with "blatant disregard for public safety," even as several children were nearby.

OREGON TEACHER WHO WRESTLED SHOTGUN FROM SCHOOL GUNMAN SHARES EMOTIONAL MESSAGE AFTER ATTACK

Police later searched the Honda and recovered a second firearm that Zhang allegedly admitted using in the shooting.

The complaint alleges the killing involved "great violence" and acts showing a "high degree of cruelty, viciousness, or callousness." Prosecutors also allege both defendants were armed or used a weapon during the killing.

McKinsey's killing came amid a bitter divorce and custody battle with Chen and Zhang's daughter, Candice Jang.

McKinsey accused Chen of directing anti-LGBTQ slurs at him and one of his children and alleged Zhang struck him in the chest while he was recovering from double mastectomy surgery, The Mercury News reported. Jang made competing allegations of domestic violence and child abuse against McKinsey, which he disputed.

The Pima County Sheriff’s Department gave an update on the Nancy Guthrie missing person’s case Friday, saying the department continues to work with the Nancy Guthrie Task Force on DNA analysis in an effort to advance the case.

The law enforcement agency reminded the public that no tip is too small.

NANCY GUTHRIE CASE: UNCLAIMED $1.2M REWARD SUGGESTS 'VERY SMALL CIRCLE' OF SUSPECTS, RETIRED FBI AGENT SAYS

Authorities have struggled to identify a suspect or person of interest in her disappearance despite a masked man appearing on Guthrie's Ring doorbell camera.

Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos , in the days following Guthrie's disappearance, confirmed that she was taken, telling reporters during a news briefing, "She did not leave on her own. We know that."

NANCY GUTHRIE INVESTIGATORS SEE UPTICK IN TIPS AFTER RANSOM NOTES RELEASE: SHERIFF

World.title: 'The View' co-hosts agree Democrats should not impeach Trump if party wins back control of Congress
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"The View" co-hosts agreed with former Vice President Kamala Harris Friday that impeachment would not be a good use of the Democratic Party’s time and resources if the party wins back control of Congress in the midterm elections.

"I think that going on in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea," Harris warned Tuesday on "The Parnas Perspective" podcast. "OK, just to be honest with you. Because we have limited resources, and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations. And that's where the time should be spent. Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-round and the votes aren't there, right? So, that's how I feel."

After playing a clip of Harris' comments, "The View" co-hosts agreed with her assessment.

KAMALA HARRIS BREAKS WITH LEFT FLANK, WARNS DEMS THAT IMPEACHING TRUMP IS 'NOT A GOOD IDEA'

"In terms of Trump, no, I don't think that's what should be on the agenda," co-host Sunny Hostin said. "Hakeem Jeffries — who I believe will be the next speaker of the House, after November — he has a plan for 100 days which includes tax credits, taking care of the tax credits, limiting ICE and also stock trades.

"And then he's got a plan for the first 100 hours, which would include, you know, just undoing a lot of unpopular Trump policies. So, I think there is a plan in place that Democrats have, and it may not include impeaching Trump."

"I think that Democrats have to be realistic of what's achievable," co-host Ana Navarro said. "We are four days away from the election. So, before we start talking about what Democrats are going to do once they win, they've got to make sure they win.

"People have to focus not on all of the conversation about impeachment and what is going to happen but rather on getting out the vote and getting people to the polls so that the American people decide who they want in power in the House and in the Senate.

"There's a limit to what Democrats are going to be able to do even if they win the House, even if they win the House and the Senate, because Donald Trump is still president," she continued. "Legislation in this country needs to be signed by the president. If not, it needs to have a veto-proof majority. And I think that's going to be very difficult to achieve. I'm completely against impeachment.

"There's 100 other ways to hold Donald Trump and his administration accountable," Navarro added. "Impeachment is an exercise that's moot if you don't have the 67 votes in the Senate required to indict."

Joy Behar pointed to former President Richard Nixon's resignation from office after Republican lawmakers warned him that he lacked sufficient Senate support to avoid conviction if impeached and said of Trump, "If we don't have the votes to convict, there's no point in impeaching."

DEM MAKING SENATE COMEBACK BID SAYS HE WOULDN'T SUPPORT A TRUMP IMPEACHMENT PUSH

Sara Haines also agreed, arguing that many of Trump’s supporters are now angry with him for breaking campaign promises and that Democrats could capitalize on their dissatisfaction by delivering on their own promises.

"It's important to recognize the moment," she said. "Donald Trump was elected and promised things he never touched. He's been remodeling, redecorating, working to revenge, all the things. The voters were left high and dry, which is why we're seeing some red states flip full to blue," she said. "That's why we are watching this campaigning.

"They need to see someone get in there, hold them accountable, do the investigations, fine," Haines continued. "But really show the American people that what they promised, to fix all these things, that immediately there's action taken. Even if it can't get past the president. Spin the wheels. Show the people that you are putting up policy, that you are taking things to vote, that you are actually acting for the people that put you there."

"Impeachment is not where the focus should be," Alyssa Farah Griffin said. "It costs actually a lot of money to do a trial, do the investigation.

"What I think is important is there are day one things that would be beneficial for all Americans and a lot of Republicans would be on board with that a Democratic Congress could do," she continued.

"Repealing Trump's tariffs, that is the power of the purse controlled by Congress and trying to wind down or pause the war in Iran. Those are things you should get Republican votes to do. That will bring down people's fuel prices. Those are where the focus should be."

Earlier this month, veteran Democratic strategist James Carville also warned Democrats against impeaching Trump if the party wins control of Congress in the midterms.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Democratic strategist and co-host of "The Huddle" podcast Dan Turrentine told Fox News Digital, "Neither the Senate arithmetic nor the American people are there. Folks are angry with the president about the economy, tariffs, healthcare, the war with Iran, corruption. They feel he is focused on everything but them.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Our job is to fight for the real lives of real people, solving their problems, while providing appropriate oversight of the executive branch and trusting the electorate provides accountability," he added.

"The quickest path back to the minority or continuing to be on the outside, looking into the White House, is to focus on revenge and score settling."

World.title: Judge orders Trump administration to stop threatening election officials
World.content:
A federal judge issued a sweeping order Friday night blocking the Trump administration from threatening or intimidating election officials amid pressure tactics used by the administration in the weeks leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

The eight-page order prohibits any action that may “threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots of any registered voter solely on the basis that the ballot belongs to an individual alleged by [the administration] to be ineligible to vote.”

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson, who’s based in California, wrote, “In the lead-up to the election, high-ranking DOJ and DHS officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election.”

The order comes in the wake of efforts to require states like California and Washington to separate out ballots the administration says could be cast by noncitizens. An appeals court ruled against the administration in California this week; the Washington case is pending.

“Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” Thompson wrote Friday.

The judge’s order extends through Nov. 16, nearly two weeks after Election Day.

World.title: Appeals court again rejects DOJ’s bid to segregate over 20,000 alleged noncitizen ballots in California
World.content:
A federal appeals court on Friday rejected the Trump administration’s latest bid to force California to set aside ballots from over 20,000 people it alleges might be noncitizens.

The “United States has not made the required showing that such extraordinary relief, during an ongoing election, is clearly required by law,” a 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals panel found in a 2-1 ruling.

“As the district court found—and we discern no clear error—there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system.”

The dissenting judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, wrote that what the government had been suggesting is a “modest” remedy.

“The federal government and the States can work together. California decided long ago that aliens can’t vote in its elections. Today, the federal government merely seeks to safeguard that decision. We should have let them try,” he wrote.

The majority judges were Mark Bennet, another Trump nominee, and Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden nominee.

It was the second time in a week the appeals court panel had rejected a request from the administration to intervene in the case.

The administration filed suit earlier this month demanding California election officials set aside over 20,000 ballots it contended may have been sent from noncitizens.

In a ruling Wednesday, U.S. District Judge David Carter found the request “violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections.”

“If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process,” he ruled.

Carter also questioned the administration’s methodology in coming up with its list of names, and noted that the Department of Homeland Security had claimed in July that the number of noncitizens who were registered to vote in California was closer to 200,000.

“Given the vagueness of Plaintiff’s descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states, the Court cannot conclude that Plaintiff’s process is credible,” the judge wrote.

He also pointed to similar claims the administration had made in Nevada, where it had alleged there were 15,903 registered voters as noncitizens. They “later reduced that number to 6,218, and then to 185 after conducting its manual review. Nevada officials later confirmed that all 185 individuals were citizens,” the judge wrote.

In its earlier ruling, the appeals court judges also pushed back on the government’s claim it needed to step in on an emergency basis, saying it was “at least in part, a self-constructed one” because it had waited it until far too close to the election to intervene.

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling or whether it planned to file an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court.

Kristen Clarke, general counsel of the NAACP, which was involved in defending the case, said in a statement, “The Department of Justice sought to throw out the voices of more than 20,000 Californians without credible evidence and outside the established safeguards that protect voters’ rights.”

“Today’s decision sends a clear message: our elections must be governed by facts, law, and constitutional principles, not political interference or voter suppression,” the statement said.

World.title: U.S. set to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan, despite risk they’ll be returned to Taliban
World.content:
The Trump administration is preparing to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum seekers to Pakistan on the first such flight of its kind, a senior administration official told NBC News — a move critics say could put their lives at risk.

The proposed deportation flight, which has not been publicly announced, could take place as early as Monday, according to rights advocates and families of detainees.

Among those facing deportation are relatives of Afghans who worked with the U.S. military in its 20-year war against the Taliban, which is now back in power. The deportees could face severe repercussions should Pakistan return them to Taliban-ruled Afghanistan as is widely expected.

Afghans driven from their country by war and political instability have been welcomed by the U.S. for decades, including tens of thousands who fled the country following the chaotic withdrawal of U.S.-led forces in 2021. President Donald Trump halted admissions for Afghans and other refugees when he returned to office last year as part of a broader immigration crackdown.

His administration has deported thousands of people to countries that are not their own, many of them in Africa, in what immigration lawyers say is an effort to skirt international laws against returning asylum seekers to the countries they fled from. The legality of these so-called third-country deportation agreements is set to be debated by the Supreme Court in December.

It is not clear what kind of formal agreement the U.S. may have with Pakistan, but the senior administration official said the U.S. charter flight would not be able to land there without the Pakistan government’s knowledge and approval. The deportation plan was earlier reported by Bloomberg and The New York Times.

Bloomberg cited a federal government official familiar with the plans as a source for its report, while The New York Times cited three U.S. officials.

Shawn VanDiver, president of the San Diego-based advocacy group AfghanEvac, said it had confirmed that in recent days at least 80 Afghans have been moved to Louisiana from 34 other ICE facilities around the country, 19 of them without legal representation.

He said it was possible that there were hundreds of Afghans at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center, which has served as a hub for ICE detainees before their deportation from the U.S.

If the U.S. sends Afghan detainees to Pakistan, they are not likely to be there long. Pakistan, which has hosted millions of Afghan refugees for decades, launched a sweeping crackdown in 2023, pressuring hundreds of thousands of Afghans to leave the country and forcibly deporting others.

They are arriving to an Afghanistan battered by multiple humanitarian crises, including widespread malnutrition, as well as an ongoing military conflict with neighboring Pakistan and a dramatic rollback of women’s rights under the Taliban’s hard-line Islamic policies.

VanDiver said the Trump administration would most likely be aware that Afghans sent to Pakistan would be at high risk of being returned to Afghanistan.

“You don’t have to be that smart to figure out that they’re sending them to Pakistan so that Pakistan will finish the job,” he said.

Regardless of whether they worked with the U.S. military, VanDiver said, any Afghans flown from the U.S. would be viewed with suspicion by the Taliban and at risk of persecution, imprisonment or worse.

That does not appear to be a major concern for the White House, said the senior administration official, who declined to be identified because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

“The administration’s position is, ‘These individuals do not have status in our country, therefore we don’t really care what happens to them,’” the official said.

VanDiver and others say the Trump administration’s treatment of Afghan allies could also have long-term consequences for U.S. national security by discouraging people in other countries from working with U.S. forces in future conflicts.

Asked whether the Trump administration was concerned about that, the official said, “I don’t think they care.”

The White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.” ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

A State Department spokesperson said the agency had “no plans to announce.”

“We reaffirm our position that all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security and prosperity of their citizens,” the spokesperson said.

Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.

The senior administration official said the Afghans on the flight could include people with deportation orders, people who were turned down for asylum and people whose temporary protected status was terminated by the Trump administration. Many of the Afghans facing deportation requested asylum after crossing into the U.S. from Mexico, VanDiver said, and some of their cases are still pending.

‘We just sat there and cried’

Charlotte, a U.S. citizen whose Afghan husband has been in ICE detention since early 2025, said he had been moved to the Louisiana facility from Pennsylvania this month and told he would be deported in early November. She declined to be identified by her full name out of concern that her husband could be targeted by the Taliban.

Charlotte said she and her husband, whose asylum case has been pending for nine years, were visiting family in Maryland last year when he accidentally crossed into West Virginia and was pulled over. Though he was carrying his valid Illinois driver’s license, he did not have his work permit with him.

“When he was pulled over,” she said, “the sheriff actually said, ‘I’m an ICE agent. You’re going to immigration custody. I don’t care if the charges are dismissed, or I don’t care if you have a five-year work permit or Social Security card. I don’t care if you’re legal. Trump’s administration just took over — you’re going directly to immigration custody.’”

Charlotte sold their home in Illinois and moved to Maryland with their son, now 6, in order to be able to visit her husband at the ICE facility where he was held in Pennsylvania, about 100 miles away.

“I lost my nice house, our car, we left everything behind,” she said.

Over the next 20 months, when she took her son to see his father at the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, they were always separated by plexiglass.

“They never let him hug him one time,” Charlotte said. “We just sat there and cried every time.”

But at least they knew where he was and that he was OK, she said. Now that he’s in Louisiana, she said, “we can’t even visit or even say goodbye, he’s over 1,200 miles away.”

With her husband potentially being sent to Pakistan or Afghanistan — a country he hasn’t been to since 2016 — the uncertainty is even greater; Charlotte said he is growing his beard to comply with the Taliban’s strict rules for men’s facial hair.

“I’m just terrified that he’s not going to be safe,” she said, “or he’s going to be held in the jail and there’s nothing I can do.”

Charlotte said she believed her husband had been targeted for deportation because of a past conviction for a nonviolent crime that has since been resolved.

“I still don’t think this should end our entire life, for a child not to see his dad,” she said.

“He’s completely devastated and traumatized,” she said of their son. “He wants to fight. He wants to go protest. He wants to speak to Donald Trump. He basically knows so much more than he should.”

The preparations for the deportation flight come nearly a year after a shooting in Washington that killed one National Guard member and seriously injured another. The suspect, an Afghan national who served alongside U.S. troops in Afghanistan and was evacuated to the U.S. in 2021, had been granted asylum by the Trump administration. Immigration restrictions were tightened after the shooting.

VanDiver said the Trump administration may also be using the Pakistan flight as a test case for Camp As Sayliyah, a U.S.-run camp in Qatar where more than 1,000 Afghans who had been slated for resettlement in the U.S. have been stranded since Trump returned to office last year.

Asked about VanDiver’s claim, the White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson again said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.”

According to AfghanEvac, the camp was housing 287 men as of July, 319 women and 433 children. Most of them have been approved for U.S. resettlement after extensive vetting, and many of the adults worked alongside U.S. forces in Afghanistan.

The group at Camp As Sayliyah also includes 150 relatives of U.S. military service members, AfghanEvac said.

00:39 Afghan refugees in Qatar protest over travel suspension 00:00 00:00

The State Department said earlier this year that everyone would be removed from the camp by March 31, a deadline that was later extended to Sept. 30. In September, the Trump administration delayed its closure by another nine months, The Associated Press reported.

Earlier this year, the administration considered sending the Afghans at Camp As Sayliyah to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which is experiencing the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

In a statement on Friday, AfghanEvac accused the Trump administration of planning the Afghan deportation flight as the country is distracted by next week’s midterm election, “hoping no one is watching.”

“The government won’t say where these flights land, because it knows what happens to the people on them when they do,” the group said. “A government confident in what it is doing does not hide it.”

World.title: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
World.content:
ROME — Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.

The demonstrations were largely peaceful but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protestors and groups of police charging to disperse protestors in Rome on Friday night.

After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe, more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.

The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France, where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.

Demonstrators gather at the Piazza della Repubblica in Rome on Friday. Sara Monetta / NBC News

Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.

In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.

00:40 Protesters storm the Colosseum in Rome 00:00 00:00

Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”

The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”

Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”

“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” added Luca, who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.

Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.

They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.

Student protesters in Rome on Friday. Sara Monetta / NBC News

Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.

Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.

But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.

A man draped in the Palestinian flag joins a protest at the Piazza della Repubblica in Rome on Friday. Sara Monetta / NBC News

“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.

The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.

World.title: Outcry prompts ‘Call of Duty’ to cut Seoul tragedy footage
World.content:
American video game publisher Activision said Friday that it was removing controversial footage from its newly released “Call of Duty” game after an outcry in South Korea over the inclusion of real-life footage from a deadly 2022 Halloween crowd crush in Seoul.

Last week’s global release of “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” came days before the Oct. 29 anniversary of the disaster in the South Korean capital’s nightlife district of Itaewon, where a crowd of tens of thousands of partygoers surged beyond control in a narrow alley, causing nearly 160 deaths.

The game, which takes place amid a fictional North Korean invasion of the South, features about 10 seconds of heavily edited footage of the tragedy to illustrate what the aftermath of a Pyongyang attack might look like, though it does not refer to the Itaewon crowd crush directly.

Groups representing families of the crowd crush victims had demanded that the footage be removed, saying it was appalling that the game had directly reproduced actual scenes of people performing CPR “while victims lay on the cold streets amid chaos and desperation.”

“If the game developer has even the slightest sense of respect and empathy for the victims of the Itaewon disaster, it should promptly take corrective action,” the Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association and Itaewon Disaster Citizens’ Countermeasures Committee said in a joint statement Friday.

The California-based game publisher, Activision, apologized in a statement and said the footage would be completely removed through a game update scheduled for release Nov. 12.

“This game is a fictional work created to provide a realistic and immersive experience,” the company said, according to the South Korean public broadcaster MBC. “In using actual news footage in the game, we never intended to evoke any tragic incident, including the Itaewon disaster, or to trivialize the suffering associated with such tragedies.”

The controversy came as grieving families are still waiting for answers about authorities’ failure to prevent the disaster four years ago. Nearly two dozen officials have been charged in the investigation, which is still underway, while three former police officers have been jailed.

On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung vowed that his government would “uncover the truth.”

World.title: Family of real estate CEO wounded in Toronto home invasion, officials say
World.content:
A search is underway for three armed men who broke into a mansion in Toronto, Canada, belonging to a real estate CEO in the early morning hours Thursday and attacked and injured the family inside, authorities said.

The suspects, who were masked, forced their way through a back entrance of the five-bedroom home in the Bridle Path neighborhood at around 3:40 a.m. local time, wielding guns and a hammer, Toronto police said.

Once inside, police said they went to the second floor of the home and confronted 75-year-old David Morton, his wife, 64-year-old Doriana Morton, and their two adult daughters, Maggie and Cristina.

"There was a demand made for valuables from within the home," Toronto Police Service Inspector Kristy Smith told reporters. "Whether or not they escaped with anything is uncertain at this point."



Police said David Morton, CEO of the MAC Group, and his daughters, ages 28 and 26, tried to fight off the intruders when shots were fired.

All three sustained gunshot wounds, Smith disclosed. And in a separate statement Friday, David Morton said that all four family members were also attacked by the suspects with the hammer.

David Morton said that he and his two daughters were still hospitalized Friday with gunshot wounds, but he did not provide details on their conditions.

"What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience," David Morton said in his statement. "... It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home."

The three male suspects, all believed to be in their 20s and wearing dark clothing, fled the scene in an SUV, police said.

"All these houses have good security," Cecil Hawkins, a former resident of Bridle Path, said. "So I'm kind of surprised. Shooting people in the house, it just seems mind-boggling."

According to Toronto police, there have been 119 home invasions so far in 2026, up 32.2% over this time last year.

Thursday's home invasion happened in the same neighborhood where a mansion belonging to rapper Drake was targeted in multiple break-in attempts in May 2024. A security guard for Drake was also wounded in a shooting outside the home at that time.

World.title: DOJ calls Alaska Senate allegations "troubling," asks to segregate ballots
World.content:
Anchorage, Alaska — The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska said new reporting on the origins of an independent candidate's Senate campaign "has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets" to the state, as federal officials in a separate civil case seek to segregate some of Alaska's Senate ballots.

Michael Heyman, the U.S. attorney for the District of Alaska, called the allegations about how Daniel J. Sullivan — a man with the same first and last name as incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan — ended up on the ballot "troubling."

"We are aware of the recent New York Times reporting regarding the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, that they orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J. Sullivan as a sham candidate, and we are taking that extremely seriously," he said in a press conference in Anchorage.

But Heyman declined to detail what specific crimes are being investigated, saying he's "not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not."

"That's what we do, is we investigate whether a crime has been committed under several theories, so I'm not going to comment on what those theories are, and I'm also not going to put the cart before the horse," he said.

Asked by CBS News why the Justice Department is choosing to escalate the case ahead of the election, Heyman said, "We're not escalating anything except to the extent that a new article came out."

"This has been going on sort of quietly for several months, with the intent not to escalate anything," he said, adding that investigators are going to take allegations involving election integrity seriously, even if a few days before the election.

Republicans have claimed that Daniel J. Sullivan is a plant by Democrats to confuse voters and boost the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, in one of the most competitive Senate races in the country.

Peltola and national Democrats have strongly denied any involvement in his campaign. Peltola said Thursday she is "not interested in tricking voters" and "knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent."

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has argued Republicans have been linked to their own efforts to stack the Alaska ballot in order to help their preferred candidates, including in this year's Senate primary and in other elections.

State election officials initially determined Daniel J. Sullivan was not eligible to appear on the ballot, accusing him of a "deliberate attempt" to confuse Alaska voters. But the decision was overturned by state courts, which ruled that state officials didn't have the authority to exclude a candidate based on their interpretation of "good faith."

The controversy drew renewed scrutiny after the New York Times reported that operatives linked to Peltola's campaign helped recruit the second Sullivan to run. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into the matter and the Justice Department has issued subpoenas targeting several Democratic officials.

In a separate civil case, the Trump administration has sued to block Alaska from certifying the results of the Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses because of "voter confusion."

On Friday, the Justice Department asked for a preliminary injunction, saying it wants to "ensure the preservation and segregation of ballots that may be impacted by voter confusion." The government also asked for expedited discovery for the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, and requested that a judge rule on the matter by Monday. The filings heavily rely on The New York Times' reporting.

"Daniel J. Sullivan does not seek to serve in the U.S. Senate but rather seeks to confuse voters," the filing says. "Accordingly, there will indeed be voter confusion caused by this frivolous candidacy."

Federal government lawyers said they want to "preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary."

The state of Alaska opposed the request, arguing the Justice Department's lawsuit "lacks any merit." They also said votes are "comingled in the ballot box on Election Day" and therefore can't be segregated without violating ballot secrecy requirements, and noted that "the ballots (whether segregated or not) will not reveal any voter's reasons for voting for Daniel J."

And they said an order to preserve ballots is unnecessary since the state already saves ballots for 22 months.

"The United States' delay further undermines its request for expedited consideration. It waited until two weeks before Election Day to file a lawsuit about issues that arose months ago," the state said.

During the news conference, Heyman also said that he had been recused from the matter some time ago, but that the recusal "has officially been rescinded." Heyman said he had been recused because he was being considered for a judicial nomination, which is no longer the case.

World.title: El-Sayed and Stevens feud ahead of key Michigan Senate race
World.content:
Washington — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his Democratic primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, clashed Friday ahead of a Sunday campaign event where both were expected to make a rare appearance together.

The public rift between the two Democrats comes just days before one of the country's most hotly contested Senate races, as Republican nominee Mike Rogers seeks to peel off centrist Democratic voters. El-Sayed and the more moderate Stevens offered starkly differing visions for the future of the party during the primary, and although Stevens endorsed El-Sayed after he won the nomination, the two largely haven't campaigned alongside each other.

In a statement Friday evening, El-Sayed said Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago."

The dig came hours after Stevens demanded that El-Sayed — a vehement critic of U.S. aid to Israel — apologize for suggesting during the campaign that "Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, health care, and child care."

"Abdul promises to get money out of politics," Stevens said in the statement. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford."

She also urged El-Sayed to condemn an ad from an outside PAC that she said was antisemitic. The video ad features a couple in a grocery store talking about needing to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf because "we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians." The man and woman in the ad then complain about the billions in military support that the U.S. has provided Israel.

El-Sayed's campaign said earlier this week it was not affiliated "in any way" with the ad, which was created by the political action committee Rebellion PAC.

"No one speaks for Abdul but himself and his campaign," his campaign said in a statement.

In her Friday statement, Stevens also called on El-Sayed to take down his own ad featuring the far-right podcaster and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson.

It's unclear what the dustup means for their Sunday appearance.

Stevens said she planned to appear with El-Sayed at a Detroit church, alongside South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. An announcement from El-Sayed's campaign about his appearance with Clyburn did not mention Stevens.

Earlier this week, Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Later that day, Stevens said in a CNN interview that she would vote for El-Sayed, saying "we're a household divided," but she called on his campaign "to shut out the hate and to call it out."
