World.title: Bitcoin Slides Toward US$77,000 After Binance Hack
World.content:
Key Facts Bitcoin closed Friday at US$77,192, down 0.75%, after a sharp drop on Thursday; the week’s loss from the 23 October close was 4.79%.

Ethereum closed at US$2,210, down 1.74%, its lowest close in at least three months and 7.28% below last Friday.

XRP and Solana last settled on Thursday: XRP at US$1.23 and Solana at US$95.49, down 6.75% and 6.66% on the day.

The trigger was a theft of about US$6.3 billion at Binance, a major crypto exchange, the largest on record; Binance says it will cover all losses.

A stock sell-off added to the pressure: on Friday the tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell 2.86% and the broad S&P 500 index lost 1.82%.

For US investors: the IBIT fund, a US-listed holder of the original coin, fell 5.14% to US$43.36, and shares of Coinbase, a US crypto exchange, lost 10.62%.

Today’s Focus A weekly loss of 4.79% left bitcoin at US$77,192 on Friday, after a fall of 0.75% on the day. Most of the damage came on Thursday, when the price lost 4.30% as news of a US$6.3 billion theft at Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, spread. Hourly prices show the break clearly: bitcoin traded at US$80,746 at 19:00 UTC on Thursday, US$78,771 at 20:00 UTC and US$77,788 at 23:00 UTC. TRM Labs, a blockchain-analysis firm, says the money began leaving Binance wallets at 20:05 UTC and that a second wave followed around 23:05 UTC. Friday added a second shock from Wall Street, where the Nasdaq fell 2.86% and the S&P 500 lost 1.82%, its worst day since June. Crypto now trades like a high-risk tech stock, so a falling Nasdaq pulls it down even when the news from the crypto industry is not new. Ethereum and the smaller coins fell further than bitcoin, which is normal when investors cut risk: Ethereum closed at its lowest in at least three months. Solana and XRP have no Friday close in our records yet, so their figures here are Thursday’s. What matters today. Bitcoin needs to hold above US$76,418, Friday’s low, and Binance needs to reopen withdrawals on schedule; a break of either would extend the slide.

01 The Week in One Read

Bitcoin ended the week at US$77,192, its lowest close in a month and 10.9% below its 12-month high of US$86,603 on 21 September. A week earlier it had closed at US$81,074, so the week’s loss was 4.79%.

The week was quiet until Thursday evening, when the theft at Binance broke a range of US$79,000 to US$81,000 that had held since 24 October. After that, a second shock arrived on Friday, when a sell-off in US technology shares sent investors toward cash.

For US readers the practical point is that crypto no longer moves on its own news. It reacts to the same fear that moves the Nasdaq, and on Friday the two fell together.

Assessment — A hack on top of a weak week MEDIUM We rank three causes: the Binance theft, which hit confidence on Thursday; the equity sell-off, which hit risk appetite on Friday; and a Federal Reserve that has not ruled out another rate rise. Confidence is medium because the timing of Thursday’s fall matches the theft, but the stock rout and the Fed worry arrived at the same time and cannot be separated. The variable to watch is Binance itself: whether withdrawals reopen as promised and whether the roughly US$2.4 billion that TRM Labs says issuers cannot freeze starts to move. A flood of stolen coins sold into the market would be the clearest new reason for further selling.

02 The Board

The board shows bitcoin at US$77,192, down 0.75%, and Ethereum at US$2,210, down 1.74%. The last closes on record for the two smaller coins are from Thursday: Solana at US$95.49 (down 6.66%) and, separately, XRP at US$1.23 (down 6.75%).

The US-listed proxies fell harder than the coins on Friday. 03 Why It Moved

The first and heaviest cause is the Binance theft. Hackers took about US$6.3 billion on Thursday 29 October, which Binance estimates and TRM Labs puts at US$6.36 billion, and Binance paused withdrawals on several networks as a precaution.

Binance says user funds are safe and that it will cover all losses from company funds and its SAFU reserve, a fund set aside for such events. TRM Labs says about US$2.7 billion was frozen by 00:30 UTC on Friday, mostly stablecoins frozen by their issuers, while about US$2.4 billion sits in assets that issuers cannot freeze.

The second cause is the stock market. The Nasdaq fell 2.86% and the S&P 500 1.82% on Friday after Intel’s weak guidance and Amazon’s heavy AI spending plans, and the VIX, a gauge of expected stock swings, rose 12.91% to 19.42, which pushed investors to cut their riskiest holdings first.

The third cause is the Federal Reserve, the US central bank: it held its rate at 3.75% to 4.00% on Wednesday 28 October, two officials voted for an immediate rise, and Polymarket, a prediction market, gives 71.5% to another rise this year. A higher rate makes coins that pay no interest less attractive.

Friday’s data added to the rate story, because the Employment Cost Index, a quarterly gauge of US labour costs, rose 0.8% in the third quarter, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the US statistics agency. Wages rose 0.7% and benefits 0.9%, which gives rate-rise bets more support, while the Chicago PMI factory survey and the Baker Hughes oil rig count, also due that day, had no confirmed reading when we closed.

One signal conflicts with the story: the dollar index slipped 0.07% and the 10-year Treasury yield held at 4.93%, so the usual dollar-and-yields explanation covers little of the fall. Our confidence in the theft as the lead cause is medium: the fall began in the hour of the first outflows, but we cannot prove how much of it was forced selling by funds and how much was fear.

04 The Trend Behind It

This is a deepening slide, not a new one. The 20-session loss is 6.90% for the largest coin, against 11.72% for the second-largest, Ethereum.

Ethereum, Solana and XRP all closed at their lowest in at least three months. Solana sits 21.8% below its September high and XRP 21.4% below, so the smaller coins have fallen about twice as far from their peaks as the largest coin has.

Our own price history since 2010 gives a base rate, not a forecast. After earlier falls as large as bitcoin’s 20-session drop, it was higher 20 sessions later in 60 of 130 cases (46%), with a median change of minus 1.8%, a worst case of minus 47.3% and a best case of plus 68.6%.

For Ethereum the odds are similar. After earlier falls as large as its own, it was higher 20 sessions later in 40 of 84 cases (48%), with a median change of minus 1.2%.

05 What It Means for Latin America

Latin American savers use crypto mostly as a way to hold dollars, through dollar-pegged tokens called stablecoins, and as a cheap way to send money home. A hack at an exchange that many of them use raises the risk that withdrawals are delayed just when they need the money.

Binance has published no breakdown of affected customers by country, so we cannot say how many Latin American accounts are involved. Readers who hold coins on any exchange should know that Binance says user funds are safe, but that a pause on withdrawals can last days.

The price channel is simpler. Where local currencies are weak against the dollar, a US$77,192 bitcoin that is 4.79% cheaper than a week ago looks like a bargain to some buyers, though the base rates above show that falls of this size are followed by gains less than half of the time.

06 The Names to Watch

The first name is Binance, whose co-chief executive Yi He has said that withdrawals should return soon, and whose promised new Proof of Reserves, a public audit of its holdings, will test whether users trust it again. The second is Tether, the issuer of the largest stablecoin, one of the issuers that froze stolen funds.

The US-listed names show how investors are positioning. Coinbase lost 10.62% on Friday and Strategy, which holds bitcoin on its balance sheet, lost 7.84%, both more than bitcoin itself, which tells us that equity investors are selling the most borrowed-money route into crypto first.

07 What Would End It

The selling should end when the stolen funds stop moving and stock markets stabilise. Bitcoin needs to hold Friday’s low of US$76,418 and then reclaim US$80,000, which lies inside the range that broke on Thursday.

Binance said withdrawals should resume by Sunday 1 November, and a clean reopening would remove the main source of fear. The US midterm elections follow on Tuesday 3 November, the jobs report is due on Friday 6 November and the Federal Reserve meets on 8 and 9 December.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a prediction market, traders put the chance that bitcoin falls to US$70,000 at some point in 2026 at 48.5%, and the chance it rises to US$90,000 at 26.5%. About US$80.2 million has been traded on this market, as of 30 October 2026, 8:08 pm ET.

For the Fed, a separate Polymarket market gives 71.5% to another rate rise in 2026. Prices on prediction markets are bets, not polls or forecasts by officials.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

08 What to watch

Binance withdrawals, Sunday 1 November: A reopening on schedule and a new Proof of Reserves would calm the market, while a delay would suggest the damage is larger than reported.

A reopening on schedule and a new Proof of Reserves would calm the market, while a delay would suggest the damage is larger than reported. US midterm elections, Tuesday 3 November: Voters choose Congress, and traders will judge whether the result changes the budget and rate outlook that crypto depends on.

Voters choose Congress, and traders will judge whether the result changes the budget and rate outlook that crypto depends on. US jobs report, Friday 6 November: Strong hiring would add to rate-rise bets and weigh on bitcoin, while a weak report could cool the case for a December increase.

Strong hiring would add to rate-rise bets and weigh on bitcoin, while a weak report could cool the case for a December increase. Bitcoin at US$76,418 and US$80,000: A close below Friday’s low would extend the slide, while a close above US$80,000 would put bitcoin back inside its old range.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did bitcoin fall this week?

A US$6.3 billion theft at Binance hit confidence on Thursday, and a US stock sell-off added to the pressure on Friday. A weekly loss of 4.79% left bitcoin at US$77,192.

Is my money safe on Binance?

Binance says user funds are safe and that it will cover all losses with company funds. It has paused withdrawals on several networks, so access, not safety, is the near-term issue.

Who was behind the Binance hack?

TRM Labs, a blockchain-analysis firm, attributes it with high confidence to a North Korean hacking unit. Binance has named no suspect, and no government has confirmed the link.

Will bitcoin recover?

Nobody can say. After earlier falls this large, bitcoin was higher 20 sessions later in 46% of cases, so the odds are close to a coin toss.

World.title: Two Sick Venezuelan Inmates Die in Custody
World.content:
Security: Venezuela

Key Facts —Who. Two inmates, Rendy Ramón Ladera Araujo and Ildelfonzo Gil, died on 26 and 27 October 2026. —Where. Santa Ana prison in Táchira state, and police cells in Puerto Ordaz, Bolívar state, Venezuela. —Why it matters. The Venezuelan Prison Observatory (OVP), a prisons monitor, wants impartial investigations into their medical care. —As of 31 October 2026, 00:30 GMT

A Venezuelan prisons monitor says two seriously ill men died in custody within two days, and it wants impartial investigations into their care.

Two sick men held in Venezuelan custody died on 26 and 27 October 2026, according to the Venezuelan Prison Observatory (OVP). The OVP is a Venezuelan non-governmental group that monitors prisons and reports on the rights of inmates.

The deaths matter to readers in the United States, who follow Venezuela’s human rights record and prison conditions closely. The OVP says the two cases raise hard questions about medical care in custody.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Venezuela ranks 13th of 14 with 27.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (81); weakest: economic relationships (0). Alignment group: Closer to Beijing. Some pillar data are incomplete for Venezuela; see the index notes. WatchSovereign in selective default; inflation of 252%; public debt at 309% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Venezuelan media reported the OVP statement on 30 October 2026. The group named both men and described their illnesses.

What We Know

Rendy Ramón Ladera Araujo was an inmate at the Santa Ana prison, officially called Centro Penitenciario de Occidente I. The prison is in Táchira state, in western Venezuela.

He died on Monday, 26 October 2026, at the Central Hospital of San Cristóbal, the capital of Táchira state. According to information received by the OVP, he suffered from leukemia, a cancer of the blood.

Ildelfonzo Gil was held in preventive detention at the Guaiparo police holding cells in Puerto Ordaz, in Bolívar state. He died on Tuesday, 27 October 2026, of advanced facial cancer, according to the OVP.

The OVP questions why earlier requests for a humanitarian measure for Gil, such as release or house arrest on health grounds, were rejected. It also asks how a house arrest order appeared when Gil had already died.

In plain English: the OVP is a Venezuelan group that monitors prisons, and preventive detention means being held in custody before any conviction. A house arrest measure is a court decision that lets a detainee stay at home instead of in a cell.

Humberto Prado, the OVP director, demanded immediate, exhaustive and impartial investigations. He wants to know what medical care both men received and whether delays or omissions compromised their lives.

File photo: the Federal Legislative Palace in Caracas. It is not connected to the prisons in this story.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Is Not Known

The reports of the OVP statement contained no official government response. What the authorities say about the two cases is therefore unknown.

The exact dates when each man fell ill are also unknown. So is the treatment each man received before he died.

Whether any delay or omission in care played a part in either death has not been established. That is the question the OVP wants investigators to answer.

The reports do not say whether the two men were political prisoners, so we do not suggest it. We also do not know how the house arrest order for Gil came to be issued after his death.

Why Prison Conditions Matter

The OVP says the Santa Ana prison holds more than 1,300 inmates in a facility with capacity for 800. That is about 162% of its intended capacity.

The OVP also cites two earlier deaths at Santa Ana, those of Francisco Orellano in May and Yonny José Bastidas Briceño in June. Each death is a separate case with its own circumstances.

Capacity figures matter because they show how many people one prison must feed, guard and treat. The OVP did not say how crowding affected these two men.

Monitors such as the OVP ask for open inquiries into inmate health care for a simple reason. Families and the public cannot judge what happened without answers from the authorities.

What It Means for US Readers

For readers in the United States, this is mainly a human rights and accountability story rather than a market story. Those who follow Venezuela often treat the state of its prisons as one test of its human rights record.

Any official answers on these two cases will show how Venezuelan authorities handle complaints about care in custody. Until then, the facts here are limited to what the OVP has reported.

Readers following the story can watch for an official statement, an announced investigation and further OVP reports. Until then, the picture stays incomplete.

Two men are dead, and the questions about their care remain open. Clear answers from the authorities would help their families and the public understand what happened.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who are the two men who died?

Rendy Ramón Ladera Araujo died on 26 October 2026 at the Central Hospital of San Cristóbal, the capital of Táchira state. Ildelfonzo Gil died on 27 October 2026, held in the Guaiparo police cells in Puerto Ordaz.

What is the OVP?

The Venezuelan Prison Observatory (OVP) is a Venezuelan non-governmental group that monitors prisons and reports on inmates’ conditions. Its director is Humberto Prado.

What does the OVP demand?

It demands immediate, exhaustive and impartial investigations into the medical care both men received. It also asks whether delays or omissions compromised their lives.

Has the Venezuelan government responded?

No official government response was found in the reports of 30 October 2026. Whether authorities have commented since then is unknown to us.

Sources: Venezuelan Prison Observatory (OVP) statement of 30 October 2026; Venezuelan press reports of the same date.

World.title: Argentina Stocks Fall as Risk Gauge Jumps | Argentina Market Report, Oct 30
World.content:
Key Facts Argentina’s main stock index fell about 2.6% to roughly 92,080 points on Friday, its fifth lower close in a row.

on Friday, its fifth lower close in a row. Country risk jumped more than 40 points to 787, the highest close of 2026, while the official dollar fell 0.29% to 1,534 pesos.

while the official dollar fell 0.29% to 1,534 pesos. Utilities and the stock exchange fell most: gas pipeline operator TGS lost 5.5%, exchange operator BYMA 5.2% and electricity distributor Edenor 4.4%.

gas pipeline operator TGS lost 5.5%, exchange operator BYMA 5.2% and electricity distributor Edenor 4.4%. For US investors: the Global X MSCI Argentina ETF (ARGT) lost 2.82% to US$79.18, and the New York shares of Galicia, the largest private bank, 4.24% to US$32.30.

the Global X MSCI Argentina ETF (ARGT) lost 2.82% to US$79.18, and the New York shares of Galicia, the largest private bank, 4.24% to US$32.30. Prediction markets: Polymarket, a prediction market, puts 48.0% on October inflation of 1.6% to 1.8%, as of 30 October 2026, 7:48 pm ET.

Today’s Focus Argentina’s main stock index, the Merval, had its fifth lower close in a row on Friday 30 October, a day of heavy selling across risk assets. The index lost 2.59% to 92,079 points from 94,530 on Thursday, a fall of about 2.6%. Country risk, the extra yield investors demand to hold Argentine dollar bonds instead of US Treasuries, rose more than 40 points to 787 basis points. That is the highest close of 2026 and a gain of 170 to 180 points, nearly 30%, in October alone. Two outside shocks hit together: Wall Street fell as doubts about artificial-intelligence spending spread, and Brazil’s currency kept sliding after President Lula’s re-election on 25 October. A home-made doubt sits underneath, whether the government can keep financing itself and rebuild reserves in 2027 while activity is weak. What matters today. For a US investor in Argentine shares, the jump in country risk matters more than the steady peso, because it raises borrowing costs for the state and for companies, and the next test is Monday 2 November.

Argentina’s Merval and the peso.

01 The session in one read

Argentine shares ended a difficult month with another heavy loss on Friday 30 October, when the main index closed at roughly 92,080 points, down about 2.6% from 94,530 on Thursday, which was itself a 1% fall. For the month the index lost 6% to 7%, depending on the measure.

Country risk closed at 787 basis points after touching 790 during the day. It was 741 to 746 on Thursday, depending on the calculation, so the day alone added 41 to 46 points.

The official peso did the opposite of what stress usually brings: the dollar fell 0.29% to 1,534 pesos. The stress therefore showed up in shares and bonds.

Assessment — Global shock on fragile credit MEDIUM We rank the causes by weight. The first, with high confidence, is the Wall Street sell-off, because the S&P 500 fell 1.82% and Argentine US-listed shares fell 1.7% to 4.2% on the same day, and the second, with medium confidence, is the spill-over from Brazil. The third, with lower confidence, is a local credit doubt that has built through October. The variable to watch is country risk: a close back below 741, Thursday’s level, would show the scare is fading.

The global dollar index barely moved, so the day was not a story of a strong US dollar. The US 10-year Treasury yield stayed near 4.93%, the price of dollar borrowing, so the pressure came through risk appetite and not through US interest rates.

The steady official rate hides the stress. Investors sold shares and bonds rather than the currency, which is why country risk is the better gauge today.

03 Why it moved — a global sell-off, Brazil and credit doubts

The main cause is the sell-off in US technology shares. The S&P 500 fell 1.82% to 7,580 and the Nasdaq 2.86% to 25,437 after chip and artificial-intelligence spending worries spread, and Argentine shares followed because they trade as a risk-on bet.

The size of the fall in New York shows the link: Galicia’s New York shares lost 4.24%, those of oil company YPF 1.69% and the ARGT fund 2.82%. Because ADRs, New York-listed receipts of Argentine shares, are the main way US investors own the country, a global sell-off hits them first.

The second cause is Brazil. President Lula’s re-election on 25 October reversed part of the regional rally, the Brazilian real lost 1.12% on Friday to 5.44 per US dollar, and investors cut exposure to the biggest economies of South America together.

The third cause is the domestic credit story. Markets are focused on whether the government can sustain its financing programme and build reserves in 2027 while economic activity is weak, and that doubt pushed country risk up about 180 points in October.

A decree published on Friday adds to the fiscal worry. Decree 1305/2026 delays a scheduled rise in fuel taxes and the carbon dioxide tax from 1 November to 1 December, a one-month postponement that costs revenue while the government works with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), a global lender, on a US$20 billion programme.

The delay helps drivers and inflation in the short run, because pump prices stay lower, but it hurts the budget, because a tax the law says should rise with prices keeps being put off. Repeated postponements since 2025 are why investors read each one as a small test of fiscal discipline.

Politics adds a regional edge. On Thursday 29 October Brazil’s foreign ministry summoned Argentina’s chargé d’affaires to ask what role Buenos Aires played in helping Flávio Bolsonaro leave Brazil after the 25 October runoff, and neither government has announced any trade measure.

Brazil is Argentina’s biggest trading partner, so a dispute could matter for exporters if it grows, but today it is a political risk and not an economic one. It explains the mood more than the price move.

The official peso held at 1,534 even as shares and bonds fell. A steady rate alongside falling assets shows that the stress is being absorbed by prices and not by the currency.

The pattern is a broad sell-off led by companies that depend on the local economy and on foreign investors: utilities, the exchange, banks and telecoms. YPF, an oil producer that earns dollars, fell the least.

In New York the Galicia shares lost 4.24% to US$32.30 and YPF 1.69% to US$47.00, while MercadoLibre, the region’s e-commerce group, fell 2.14% to US$1,624.53. The ARGT fund lost 2.82% to US$79.18.

Currencies split: the Argentine dollar fell 0.29% against the peso, the Brazilian real lost 1.12% and the Colombian peso 1.83%. Argentina’s stress is therefore a credit and share-price story, not a currency story.

06 The technical picture

The index closed at roughly 92,080, below Thursday’s 94,530. We have no verified long price history for the index in this report, so we give no 12-month range.

For country risk, the nearest levels are the 741 close of Thursday, which is the first level to win back, and the 790 touched on Friday. A close above 800 would be a new stress zone not seen in 2026.

The official dollar closed at 1,534 pesos, 0.5% below its 12-month high of 1,542 from 28 October and 13.2% above its 12-month low of 1,355 from 13 April. Over 20 sessions it is up 0.60%, so the peso has weakened only slowly.

World.title: CSN Sinks 8% as Wall Street Rout Hits Steel Stocks
World.content:
Key Facts CSN (Companhia Siderúrgica Nacional) fell 8.31%. Brazil’s flat-steel maker closed at US$0.72 in New York, its fifth straight loss and a 12-month low.

Gerdau slipped 1.69%. Brazil’s long-steel maker closed at US$4.66, down from its 20 October high of US$5.24.

Ternium lost 2.39%. The Mexico-focused steelmaker closed at US$52.77 as US steel tariffs stay in force.

CSN’s cement sale is moving. Chinese cement group Huaxin gets ten exclusive days to buy its cement unit for US$2.3 billion (R$12.7 billion).

Brazil’s tariff shield is under pressure. A 25% tariff applies above import quotas, yet steelmakers still call imports a threat.

The SLX steel fund hit a three-month low. The exchange-traded fund fell 1.88% to US$99.40, 12.5% below its June high.

Today’s Focus Latin American steel shares fell with Wall Street on Friday, and Brazil’s CSN suffered most. Its New York shares dropped 8.31% to US$0.72, the fifth loss in a row, leaving them 39.4% lower over five sessions. Two forces collided. A US stock-market rout, led by results and AI-spending plans from chipmaker Intel and online retailer Amazon, took the S&P 500 (the main US stock index) down 1.82%, and CSN’s heavy debt turned a market dip into a rout after S&P Global Ratings, a credit-rating agency, cut its credit grade deeper into junk territory on 20 October. Gerdau fell 1.69% and Ternium 2.39%, far less than CSN, because their earnings are tied to construction and cars rather than to a heavy debt load. That gap shows the sell-off was broad but that debt decided the size of the loss. For US readers, the 50% US tariff on imported steel and Brazil’s own import tariffs decide who earns money, not global demand. Ternium and Gerdau sell into protected markets, while CSN carries the debt. What matters today. In steel, balance sheets decide who falls hardest: CSN’s debt, not demand for steel, most likely drove an 8.31% one-day loss.

01 The Session in One Read

Steel stocks across Latin America fell on Friday 30 October as the US sell-off spread, and CSN fell hardest with an 8.31% loss to US$0.72. It was the fifth consecutive down session for the Brazilian flat-steel maker and its lowest close in at least six months.

The SLX exchange-traded fund, a basket of steel stocks, slid 1.88% to US$99.40, its third straight decline. Producers with debt were punished, and producers with steady local demand held up better.

CSN is now 66.3% below its 28 January high of US$2.12, and it has lost 38.3% over 20 sessions and 23.9% over 60 sessions. Gerdau, by contrast, fell 1.69% to US$4.66 and Ternium 2.39% to US$52.77, both far smaller losses than CSN’s.

Assessment — Debt and Wall Street, not steel demand MEDIUM We rank the causes by weight: the US stock-market rout (HIGH confidence) as the common cause, CSN’s debt and credit downgrade (MEDIUM) as the reason it fell almost five times as hard as Gerdau, and the cement-sale terms (LOW). The exclusivity announcement came the same day, but we cannot tell whether investors judged the price disappointing. The variable to watch is whether CSN signs the cement sale within the ten-day window, because the proceeds would cut net debt of R$42.1 billion at the end of June. A signed deal would help the shares, while a collapse of talks would hurt them.

Steel — the daily wrap.

03 Why Steel Shares Fell on Friday

The common cause was the US stock-market rout, because investors sold cyclical shares after Intel and Amazon updated their results and AI-spending plans. The S&P 500 fell 1.82%, its worst day since June, and steel producers are among the most sensitive to a slowing economy.

CSN fell almost five times as far as Gerdau because of its debt. S&P Global Ratings cut its credit grade from B to B- on 20 October with a negative outlook, citing weaker mining results and a heavy debt load, and net debt was R$42.1 billion (about US$7.7 billion) at the end of June.

On Friday CSN also announced ten days of exclusivity for Huaxin, a Chinese cement group, to buy CSN Cimentos at an enterprise value (price including debt) of R$12.7 billion (about US$2.3 billion). The sale would cut debt, though the deal is not yet signed.

Import competition is the slow-moving cause. China supplies about half of Brazil’s rolled-steel imports, and the industry body Aço Brasil expects them to fall about 15% to 4.9 million tonnes in 2026 after new anti-dumping duties (penalties on below-cost imports), yet it still sees imports as a threat.

We have HIGH confidence in the market-wide cause, MEDIUM in the debt explanation for CSN and LOW in the cement-sale reading. The conflicting signal is that the cement sale is good news for debt, so Friday’s fall looks more like market-wide selling than a verdict on the deal.

04 The Trend Behind It

This is a continuation for CSN and a new low for the sector ETF. CSN fell 8.31% on Friday and has now lost five sessions in a row, a slide of 39.4% that erased the rebound on hopes of the cement sale.

Our own price history shows how rare this is: after CSN’s earlier falls of this size, it was higher 20 sessions later in only 3 of 9 cases (33%), with a median change of minus 2.8%. History is not a forecast, and nine cases is a small sample.

The long-steel maker shows the opposite pattern: it fell 7.0% over 20 sessions but remains 42.9% above its 20 March low of US$3.26. In its own history, falls of that size were followed by gains in 64 of 124 cases (52%), which is close to a coin flip.

05 What It Means for Latin America

For Brazil, steel is a story of protection: a 25% tariff applies above import quotas on 19 products, renewed in May through June 2027, and anti-dumping duties cover Chinese coated and cold-rolled steel. That keeps domestic prices above import parity, which helps Gerdau and hurts Brazilian builders and carmakers who buy steel.

For Mexico, the US tariff of 50% caps steel exports and weighs on Ternium. Mexico’s Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard wants Washington to lower the rate, but no deal or legal text has been published.

For US readers, the 50% Section 232 tariff (a US trade-law duty on steel imports) means American buyers pay more for Brazilian and Mexican steel, and it raises costs for manufacturers who buy it. It also keeps Latin American mills focused on their home markets, where Chinese imports are the main threat.

06 The Names to Watch

CSN, which trades in New York as SID, is the high-risk name: at US$0.72 it trades like a stressed-debt bet, and the cement sale is the one event that could change that. Investors should read its next quarterly report for the net-debt figure after the sale.

Gerdau at US$4.66 is the better-protected producer, with Brazilian construction demand and the 25% above-quota tariff behind it. It reported third-quarter adjusted profit of about R$1.5 billion (about US$276 million) on 26 October, with its highest margin since the second quarter of 2023.

Ternium at US$52.77 is the Mexico bet and depends on the outcome of the US tariff talks. For a bet on the whole group, the steel ETF is the simplest tool.

07 What Would End It

The slide in CSN would stall if it signs binding cement-sale documents inside the ten-day window, which runs to about 9 November. Even a price near R$12.7 billion would remove a large part of the debt worry, because it equals roughly 30% of the June net debt.

For the group, SLX needs a close back above Thursday’s US$101.30 to show the sell-off is over, while resistance is the US$113.57 June high. The next dated tests are the interest-rate decision of Copom, Brazil’s central-bank rate committee, on Wednesday 4 November and the US jobs report on Friday 6 November.

The honest answer is that the market-wide part of the fall should fade when Wall Street steadies, while CSN’s part will not until its balance sheet improves. A change in Brazil’s import quotas or a US-Mexico tariff deal would shift the picture for the whole group.

08 What to watch

CSN cement sale: Binding documents with Huaxin inside ten days, to about 9 November, would cut debt and could end the slide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did CSN shares fall 8.31%?

A Wall Street sell-off hit cyclical stocks, and CSN’s heavy debt and S&P Global Ratings downgrade made it the most exposed. Its cement-sale news did not lift the shares.

Why did Gerdau fall less?

Gerdau earns from construction steel behind a 25% above-quota tariff and has far less debt pressure. It also reported its best margin since 2023 on 26 October.

How does the US steel tariff matter?

The 50% Section 232 tariff caps Mexican and Brazilian exports to American buyers. Mexico wants it lowered, but no deal exists yet.

What would end the slide?

A signed CSN cement sale would cut its R$42.1 billion debt. A steadier Wall Street would ease the wider sell-off.

World.title: Costa Rica Hotel Wins Two World Travel Awards, Putting Tárcoles in the Spotlight
World.content:
A hotel on Costa Rica’s Central Pacific coast has won two international tourism awards, bringing attention to Tárcoles, a area known for its crocodile-filled river, fishing traditions and surrounding tropical forests. Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda, part of Marriott International’s Autograph Collection, was named Costa Rica’s Leading Boutique Hotel 2026 and Mexico & Central America’s Leading New Hotel 2026 at the World Travel Awards.

The recognition comes less than a year after the hotel opened in January 2026 and marks an early achievement for a property competing in Costa Rica’s established tourism industry. The awards were announced at the World Travel Awards Caribbean and Americas ceremony, held in Jamaica on October 11.

Established in 1993, the World Travel Awards recognize hotels, airlines, destinations and other tourism businesses through online voting by travel industry professionals and the public. Verified industry professionals receive double voting weight, and awards are presented in national, regional and worldwide categories.

Santa Lucía’s two victories were in the national boutique hotel category and the regional new hotel category, placing it ahead of other nominated properties in Costa Rica, Mexico and Central America. José Eduardo Arteaga, general manager of Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda, welcomed the recognition, saying it provides an opportunity to introduce more international travelers to Tárcoles and Costa Rica’s Central Pacific region.

Arteaga said the awards also help showcase the variety of tourism experiences available in Costa Rica, particularly in communities outside the best-known tourist destinations. Near Carara National Park and the Tárcoles River in Puntarenas province, the hotel has 84 guest rooms on a 150-hectare (371-acre) property surrounded by tropical forest.

The property combines traditional Costa Rican hacienda-style architecture with modern rooms and activities focused on nature and local culture. Guests can participate in birdwatching, guided nature experiences, traditional Costa Rican cooking and cultural activities. The hotel also offers restaurants, a spa and other amenities.

Its location provides access to Carara National Park, known for its scarlet macaws and diverse birdlife, as well as the Tárcoles River, where visitors frequently see large American crocodiles along the riverbanks. The surrounding region offers beaches, wildlife tours and outdoor activities, making Tárcoles an accessible destination for travelers exploring the Central Pacific coast.

Beyond attracting visitors, the hotel says its operations support the surrounding economy through employment in hospitality, food service, maintenance and other services. The company also reports purchasing goods and services from businesses in the area. Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda promotes what it calls regenerative tourism, an approach intended to support forest conservation and strengthen connections with nearby communities. The extent of those environmental and economic benefits has not been independently quantified.

The awards come as Costa Rica’s tourism industry continues to report growth in international arrivals and visitor spending. According to the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT), Costa Rica welcomed 1,733,596 international visitors during the first six months of 2026, an increase of 7% compared with the same period in 2025.

Of those visitors, 1,605,360 arrived by air, representing year-over-year growth of 7.8%. Meanwhile, figures from the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) show that foreign visitors spent approximately $3.356 billion during the first half of 2026, an increase of 8.5% compared with the previous year.

Tourism also remains an important source of employment, accounting for 167,661 direct jobs during the second quarter of 2026, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC). For Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda, the two awards offer international recognition during its first year of operation. For Tárcoles, they provide another opportunity to draw attention to a part of Costa Rica where wildlife, local traditions and tourism remain closely connected.

World.title: For First Time, Costa Rica Votes Against UN Call to End US Embargo on Cuba
World.content:
Costa Rica voted against the annual United Nations resolution calling on the United States to lift its economic embargo on Cuba, the first time the country has opposed the measure since the General Assembly began voting on it in 1992.The resolution passed on Wednesday with 130 votes in favor, 17 against and 25 abstentions. General Assembly resolutions are not binding, and the embargo remains in place.

Costa Rica was the only Central American country to vote no. Nicaragua and Panama voted in favor, Honduras abstained, and Guatemala and El Salvador did not take part.The vote completes a gradual shift. Costa Rica abstained in 1992 and then backed the resolution for more than three decades. In October 2025 it abstained for the first time in that span, and in July 2026 it was one of nine countries to vote against a procedural motion to reopen debate on the embargo.

The change follows a sharp break with Havana. In March, under then-President Rodrigo Chaves, Costa Rica closed its embassy in Cuba and asked Cuban diplomats to leave, citing growing restrictions on freedoms and worsening living conditions on the island. The government later reaffirmed the split.

In September, then-Foreign Minister Manuel Tovar said a review of Costa Rica’s position would mean changing how the country votes on the resolution. He said the government views the hardship facing Cubans as imposed by their own government, argued that Latin American governments had been too lukewarm toward Havana, and ruled out restoring diplomatic ties until Cuba is free. Tovar made the remarks shortly after meeting US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington.

Wednesday’s vote was the first on the resolution under President Laura Fernández, who took office in May. It came two weeks after Ana Elena Pinto became foreign minister on Oct. 15, during a month of turnover in the country’s diplomatic and trade leadership that included the dismissal of the trade minister. The Foreign Ministry has not published an explanation of the vote.

Costa Rica joined a bloc of opponents that grew from seven countries in 2025 to 17 this year. Alongside the United States and Israel, it included Argentina, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Hungary and Ukraine. Support for the resolution fell from 165 votes in 2025 and 187 in 2024. Germany and Italy, which had previously voted in favor, abstained.

US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz rejected the idea that the embargo is the only cause of Cuba’s economic problems, arguing that there is no blockade and pointing to Cuba’s trade with other countries and some US exports to the island. He said the number of countries changing their position had tripled and that he expected it to keep growing.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla said the sanctions directly harm the Cuban people, mainly by restricting access to food, medicine and fuel, and said US pressure would not prevail over the facts. Cuban officials accused Washington of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions and other penalties if they supported the resolution.

The General Assembly has passed versions of the resolution regularly since 1992. The votes carry political weight but have no power to lift the embargo.

World.title: Four Detained in Costa Rica Over Sedative-Spiked Rides From Bars
World.content:
Costa Rican authorities detained four men yesterday who are suspected of offering rides to people leaving bars in San José, drugging them with a sedative and then using their phones and bank cards to empty their accounts. Agents from the theft section of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) and prosecutors from the specialized cybercrime unit raided homes in Grecia, in Alajuela province, and in Aserrí, south of the capital.

The suspects are two brothers plus two other men and authorities have identified eight victims so far. Losses are put at about 10 million colones, or roughly $22,000. According to investigators, the suspects approached people who had been drinking outside bars in San Jose during the early morning hours and offered them a private transport service. During the ride, the victims were allegedly given water mixed with drops of clonazepam, a prescription sedative.

Once the drug took effect, the group allegedly took the victims’ cell phones and bank cards. Investigators say the cards were then used for purchases and cash withdrawals, and the victims were left next to the road. The four men are under investigation for alleged computer fraud and aggravated robbery however they have not been charged and the case remains open.

Authorities have not disclosed which bars or neighborhoods were involved, the ages of the suspects, or whether any of the victims were foreign visitors. The case is the latest in a series of thefts in Costa Rica that rely on speed and surprise rather than force, including one this week in which thieves emptied a rental car in eight minutes.

Anyone who believes they were targeted in a similar way can report it to the OIJ through its confidential line at 800-8000-645.

World.title: Costa Rica Celebrates National Masquerade Day With Traditional Parades and Music
World.content:
Costa Rica is celebrating one of its most colorful traditions this weekend as giant masks, lively marching bands and characters from local folklore take over streets and public spaces across Costa Rica. National Traditional Masquerade Day, observed every October 31, brings communities together for a celebration that has been part of Costa Rican culture for generations.

The Ministry of Culture and Youth has organized a series of free activities for today and tomorrow including street parades, musical performances, workshops and cultural exhibitions. The main celebration is scheduled for Friday in downtown San José, where three groups of traditional masked performers and musicians began marching at 11 a.m. from Plaza de la Democracia, Parque Morazán and the Simón Bolívar Urban Nature Park.

The groups then make their way through the capital before gathering around noon at the National Center for Culture (CENAC), across from Parque España. The event is open to the public and will feature the oversized masks and traditional music that have made these celebrations a familiar part of life in Costa Rica.

Unlike Halloween, which shares the same date, Costa Rica’s masquerade tradition has its own history and characters. The masks represent figures from local legends, including La Segua, La Llorona, the Devil, Death and La Giganta, along with a collection of other characters that have entertained and occasionally frightened generations of children.

Some of the figures tower over spectators, with enormous heads and exaggerated facial features made from papier-mâché, fiberglass or other materials. Beneath the masks are performers who dance, chase spectators and interact with the crowds as traditional marching bands, known locally as cimarronas, provide the music.

The bands typically include trumpets, trombones, drums and other instruments, producing the loud, energetic rhythms associated with Costa Rican town festivals. For many Costa Ricans, the sound of a cimarrona approaching is enough to bring back childhood memories of neighborhood celebrations, school festivals and the excitement of watching the masked characters move through the streets.

The tradition has roots in colonial-era celebrations, particularly in Cartago, where Spanish festivities gradually mixed with Indigenous customs and local folklore. Over time, communities such as Barva, Aserrí, Escazú and Cartago became important centers for the creation and performance of traditional masquerades.

The modern national celebration began in Aserrí on October 31, 1996, when local cultural organizers and artisans held a parade to promote Costa Rican traditions at a time when Halloween was becoming increasingly popular. The following year, the government officially declared October 31 National Traditional Masquerade Day through an Executive Decree.

The celebration received further recognition in 2022 when Costa Rica’s Legislative Assembly declared traditional masquerades a national symbol under Law 10239, acknowledging their importance to o cultural identity. Today, the tradition remains an important source of work for artisans who design, sculpt and paint the masks, often teaching their techniques to younger generations.

Acting Culture Minister Sally Molina Villalobos has emphasized that the celebrations are not simply about entertainment. They also recognize the craftsmanship and dedication required to keep the tradition alive. This weekend’s activities extend well beyond San José. In Cartago, a free masquerade and cimarrona festival is scheduled for Friday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Plaza Mayor, with traditional performances and workshops.

In Limón, the Civic Center for Peace will offer mask painting, traditional Costa Rican games, storytelling and a parade accompanied by a cimarrona on Friday afternoon, from 4 p.m. to approximately 6:20 p.m. The Public Library in Liberia, Guanacaste, will host a free afternoon of Costa Rican legends on Friday from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m., inviting community members to share traditional stories.

On Saturday, the celebration continues in Escazú, where Escazú Village will host free activities from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. The program includes traditional masked characters, a cimarrona performance, children’s mask-making workshops and costume competitions. Families attending the Escazú event will also find activities designed to introduce younger children to the history and artistic traditions behind the masks.

In the San Carlos area, the community of Marsella will hold traditional games, mask-making activities and a neighborhood parade on Saturday morning. Other cultural institutions are participating with exhibitions and special events, including an artisan mask display at the José Figueres Ferrer Cultural and Historical Center in San Ramón, which continues through November 6.

Not every event is free. The National Band of Guanacaste will perform a special concert at the National Theater in San José on Saturday at 7 p.m., with general admission tickets priced at ₡4,000 and discounted tickets at ₡2,500 for students and older adults. The weekend’s celebrations come at a time when Costa Rica continues working to preserve its traditional arts and customs while welcoming cultural influences from abroad.

For residents and visitors unfamiliar with masquerades, the events offer a chance to experience a side of Costa Rica that goes beyond beaches, rainforests and national parks. World.title: Lufthansa to Drop Costa Rica Route in 2027 as Sister Airline Adds More Flights
World.content:
German airline Lufthansa will stop operating its flights to Costa Rica in December 2027, but travelers will not lose the connection to Europe. Instead, sister airline Discover Airlines will take over the Frankfurt–San José route and increase service from five to six flights per week. The change, announced on October 29, will take effect on December 14, 2027, with Discover Airlines operating flights to Juan Santamaría International Airport using Airbus A350-900 aircraft.

The Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) confirmed that Lufthansa will continue operating the route through December 13, 2027, before handing it over to Discover, which belongs to the same airline group. For anyone flying here, the important point is that the route is not disappearing. Lufthansa Group will continue to fly to Costa Rica from Germany, although the airline operating the flights will change.

However, there is one important difference in the new schedule. Of the six weekly flights, four will operate nonstop between Frankfurt and San José. The other two will follow a route that takes passengers from Frankfurt to San José, continues to Belize City and then returns to Germany. That means passengers leaving Costa Rica for Frankfurt will need to pay attention when booking. Although the total number of weekly flights will increase, two of the return services will include a stop in Belize.

The change follows negotiations between the ICT and Lufthansa Group that began more than a year ago. Tourism officials said the goal was to move the route to an airline more focused on vacation travelers, which better matches Costa Rica’s tourism market. Discover Airlines specializes in leisure travel and operates from Frankfurt and Munich, serving destinations popular with tourists. It is part of Lufthansa Group, allowing passengers to continue using Frankfurt as a connection point for other destinations in Europe and beyond.

Another significant change will be the aircraft itself. Discover plans to introduce the Airbus A350-900 on the Costa Rica route, replacing the aircraft currently used by Lufthansa. The A350 is a modern long-distance aircraft designed to carry passengers across continents with improved fuel efficiency. Discover expects to receive its first A350 in June 2027 and a second aircraft in December, when the Costa Rica service is scheduled to begin.

The airline is gradually expanding its long-distance fleet, with additional A350 aircraft expected in 2028. The announcement comes as Lufthansa is already increasing its presence in Costa Rica. For the current European winter season, which began October 25, the airline expanded its Frankfurt service from three to five weekly flights and introduced Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner aircraft with its newer Allegris cabin design.

Germany remains Costa Rica’s largest source of European tourists. According to ICT figures, 54,794 German visitors arrived in Costa Rica between January and September 2026, an increase of 8.1% compared with the same period in 2025. The Frankfurt connection is particularly important because it serves both German vacationers and travelers connecting through one of Europe’s busiest international airports.

For Costa Rica’s tourism industry, the planned increase in weekly service provides another opportunity to attract European visitors, especially during the busy winter travel season. Passengers planning trips for late 2027 should keep an eye on the new schedules as Discover Airlines updates its booking system. The airline has confirmed the planned route changes, but final operating details and aircraft assignments may still be adjusted before the service begins.

World.title: High Tides Flood Homes in Costa Rica’s Puntarenas
World.content:
High tides flooded homes in Puntarenas on Thursday, October 29, with authorities warning that elevated tides could continue along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast through Saturday, October 31. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) reported flooding in Barrio El Carmen and the community of 20 de Noviembre in Chacarita.

Seawater entered homes, and photographs from the affected areas showed flooded patios and corridors, with furniture and household belongings standing in water. Members of the Puntarenas Municipal Emergency Committee visited the communities to assess damage, identify families’ needs and coordinate assistance. Initial reports did not specify the number of homes affected or provide an estimate of financial losses.

Thursday’s flooding followed repeated high tides earlier in the week. Residents of El Carmen described moving appliances and other belongings off the floor and staying awake to monitor water entering their homes. Flooding was also reported earlier in the week at Playa Zancudo in Golfito and Playa Preciosa in Puerto Jiménez, extending the effects beyond the city of Puntarenas.

The University of Costa Rica’s Oceanographic Information Module, known as MIO-Cimar, warned that the period of unusually high tides could last through Saturday. The CNE urged residents of coastal communities with a history of tidal flooding to watch local conditions and take steps to protect their belongings.

The conditions are associated with spring tides, the higher tides that occur around the new and full moon when the gravitational effects of the Sun and Moon reinforce one another. These events occur regularly and are unrelated to the spring season. MIO-Cimar coordinator Rodney Mora said warmer Pacific waters associated with El Niño were also contributing to higher sea levels, worsening the effects in vulnerable coastal communities. Water expands as it warms, allowing high tides to reach farther into low-lying areas.

El Niño does not cause spring tides, but the combination can increase the risk of flooding along the coast. Mora also warned that similar conditions could recur in November and December, urging coastal residents to prepare for further episodes.

World.title: Costa Rica Gas Prices Jump Sharply as Regular Fuel Becomes More Expensive Than Premium
World.content:
Drivers in Costa Rica will soon be paying considerably more at the pump after the public services regulator approved yet another round of fuel price increases, including a 12.38% jump in regular gasoline that will make it more expensive than premium fuel. The Public Services Regulatory Authority (ARESEP) approved the adjustment a couple of days ago, with the new prices announced yesterday. Regular gasoline will increase by ₡89 per liter, climbing from ₡719 to ₡808, while premium gasoline will rise by ₡42, from ₡764 to ₡806.

That creates an unusual situation at Costa Rica’s gas stations. Regular gasoline, traditionally the cheaper option, will cost ₡2 more per liter than premium, while diesel will also reach ₡808 following an increase of ₡23. The higher prices have been approved but will not take effect until the regulatory resolution is published in the official government newspaper, La Gaceta. Under the resolution, the new rates begin the following day. An exact implementation date had not been confirmed as of Friday morning.

At the new price, filling a 40-liter (10.6-gallon) tank with regular gasoline will cost ₡32,320 (about $71), up from ₡28,760 (about $64) today, an increase of ₡3,560 (about $8) per fill-up and with regular. Drivers filling a larger 60-liter (15.9-gallon) tank will pay ₡5,340 more than before.

For those who commute daily, operate delivery vehicles or regularly travel between Costa Rica’s major cities, the additional expense could quickly add up. The increases are not limited to gasoline and diesel. Households that use propane gas for cooking will also face higher costs, with the price of a standard 25-pound cylinder rising by ₡549, from ₡7,172 to ₡7,721.

ARESEP estimates that approximately 53% of Costa Rican households use this type of cooking gas. Restaurants, small food businesses and other commercial establishments that depend on propane will also be affected. The regulator says the adjustments reflect rising international fuel costs, which have been influenced by instability in global energy markets.

Costa Rica imports all of its finished petroleum fuels, making domestic prices especially sensitive to changes in international supply, shipping costs and the exchange rate between the colón and the U.S. dollar. Energy officials pointed to disruptions involving oil shipments from the Middle East, declining global inventories and higher refining and transportation costs. Diesel supplies have faced particular pressure as demand and supply conditions fluctuate internationally.

The latest adjustment was calculated using fuel purchases made by the Costa Rican Petroleum Refinery (RECOPE) between September 11 and October 8. The exchange rate also played a role. ARESEP used an average rate of ₡456.66 per dollar for the new calculation, compared with ₡450.41 in the previous adjustment. Because fuel purchases are made in dollars, that difference increases the amount paid in colones even when the international price of a product remains unchanged.

For Costa Rican businesses, higher fuel prices can create expenses that extend well beyond the cost of filling a vehicle. Transportation companies, agricultural producers, delivery services and businesses that distribute goods throughout Costa Rica depend heavily on diesel and gasoline. When those costs rise, companies may face pressure to adjust their operating budgets or eventually pass some of the increases on to customers.

Tourism operators could also feel the effects. Rental car companies, shuttle services and tour providers frequently travel long distances between Juan Santamaría International Airport, the Central Valley and popular destinations such as La Fortuna, Manuel Antonio, Tamarindo and the southern Pacific coast.

Tourists coming here and are renting cars will find the same regulated fuel prices as Costa Rican motorists. However, any increase in tour prices, transportation fares or rental rates would depend on decisions by individual businesses and where applicable, additional regulatory approvals.

The latest adjustment comes after earlier fuel increases in October, adding to transportation expenses as Costa Rica approaches the busy end-of-year holiday and tourism season. The approved changes also highlight how fuel prices can move differently depending on the type of petroleum product. Although regular gasoline is typically cheaper than premium, international market conditions and the formulas used to calculate domestic prices can occasionally reverse that relationship.

For those who don’t have a diesel car, once the new rates become effective, premium gasoline will actually be slightly cheaper than regular gasoline, but you should still follow the fuel specifications recommended by your vehicle manufacturer. The regulator’s decision covers nearly two million vehicles circulating in Costa Rica, including private cars, motorcycles, buses, trucks and other commercial transportation.

While our government regulates retail fuel prices, those prices are reviewed periodically and can increase or decrease depending on the cost of imported petroleum products and other factors included in the pricing formula. For now, drivers have a short period before the latest adjustment takes effect. Once the new prices are officially published and implemented, a liter of regular gasoline and diesel will both cost ₡808, marking another increase in the cost of getting around Costa Rica.

World.title: Heading Out for Halloween in Costa Rica? Expect More Police on Patrol
World.content:
Heading to a costume party, a beach bash or a masquerade parade this Saturday? Expect to see more police than usual. Costa Rica’s national police are stepping up patrols across our country for Halloween and they will concentrate on the places where crowds gather. The Public Security Ministry said officers will focus on cemeteries, churches, shopping centers and the streets around bars hosting costume parties.

The goal is to prevent vandalism, spot unauthorized parties and head off trouble at large gatherings. When the national police first outlined the plan, it said it would deploy 1,500 officers from today through Sunday. The ministry’s latest statement, issued yesterday, did not give a number of officers.

Because halloween falls on a Saturday, many parties start Friday night, and that three-day window is meant to cover them. Why cemeteries and churches? Police said incidents in past years, including vandalism and rituals at cemeteries, are the reason officers will patrol them through the weekend. César Anchía, deputy director general of the national police, outlined the weekend operations.

If you’re going out, expect police at the party too. Themed Halloween events and other mass gatherings will see preventive checks and patrols at venues and meeting points. Part of the aim is to catch parties held without permits. Shopping centers, which draw families in costume on Halloween, are also on the patrol list.

If you’re driving, watch for the Caravana del Payaso, or Clown Caravan, a Halloween ride that draws hundreds of motorcyclists. Police will watch the route and the gathering points, and the ministry said highway patrols are meant to prevent crashes. Give riders room and allow extra time where the caravan passes.

Taking kids trick-or-treating? Police are asking parents to stay with their children and keep them in sight the whole time they go door to door. Before you head home, make sure the car you get into is the ride you actually booked. Lat night, the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) said it had detained four men suspected of drugging and robbing people outside bars and nightclubs in San José.

According to the OIJ, one of the suspects allegedly posed as the ride-hailing driver victims had requested, then offered them drinks laced with a sedative. Investigators said other members of the group then withdrew cash and moved money out of victims’ accounts and spent it on goods and services, including fuel.

Saturday is also Costa Rica’s National Masquerade Day, when towns celebrate with giant-headed mascareros, cimarrona bands and dancing in the streets. Police said those community events fall under the same security operation. In beach towns, Halloween runs all weekend. Tamarindo has costume surfing, parades and beach parties on the calendar. Big crowds also draw thieves, so keep valuables with you and out of parked cars, where a rental can be emptied in minutes. In an emergency, call 911.

Halloween has grown steadily in Costa Rica alongside our own masquerade tradition, blending a centuries-old holiday with local customs. Authorities are betting that a visible police presence will keep this year’s celebrations safe for everyone who takes part.

World.title: Quadruple Murder: Police identify four victims of Coastal Plain Highway massacre, including 16-year-old boy; five men detained as investigators probe possible links to recent shootings
World.content:
Quadruple Murder: Police identify four victims of Coastal Plain Highway massacre, including 16-year-old boy; five men detained as investigators probe possible links to recent shootings

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have officially confirmed the identities of four persons murdered in Friday morning’s deadly shooting along the Coastal Plain Highway, including a 16-year-old boy, as new information obtained by Breaking Belize News raises questions about possible connections to Thursday’s murder of 19-year-old Dodrick Madrill and what sources suggest may be an internal gang conflict involving a struggle for leadership of the “Through The Park Gang”.

The victims have been identified as 16-year-old David Usher of Freedom Street, Belize City; 33-year-old Lloyd Leslie of Armadillo Street, Belize City; 23-year-old Robert Gladden of Freedom Street, Belize City; and 23-year-old Dayton Palacio, also of Freedom Street.

During Friday evening’s police press briefing, Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith confirmed that the Major Crimes Unit launched its investigation around 8:15 a.m. after receiving reports of a shooting between Miles 21 and 22 of the Coastal Plain Highway.

Responding officers discovered a red Ford Escape overturned with numerous apparent bullet holes. Three men were found unresponsive at the scene, while a fourth victim, identified as Palacio, was transported to the Southern Regional Hospital, where he was subsequently pronounced dead.

Police have since intercepted a vehicle of interest travelling toward Belize City and detained five Belize City men for questioning. No firearms were recovered from the intercepted vehicle.

However, a potentially significant connection has emerged between two of Friday’s murder victims and 19-year-old Dodrick Salvador Miguel Madrill, who was gunned down on Freedom Street in Belize City on Thursday morning.

Breaking Belize News has established that three of the five men murdered across the two incidents were jointly charged in the same firearms case in February 2025.

According to a Breaking Belize News court report published on February 1, 2025, Madrill was charged alongside Robert Lincoln Gladden, then 22, Dayton Daniel Palacio, then 21, and Emily Angelica Lopez, 49, following the discovery of an unlicensed 9mm pistol and 13 live rounds of ammunition inside a residence on Freedom Street.

Madrill, who was 18 at the time, pleaded guilty and accepted responsibility for the weapon, while Gladden, Palacio and Lopez pleaded not guilty. Madrill was subsequently remanded to prison pending sentencing.

The previous case establishes a documented association between Madrill, Gladden and Palacio, who have now been murdered in separate shootings occurring less than 24 hours apart.

The connection is particularly noteworthy amid growing concerns about possible retaliatory violence and divisions within criminal groups.

A source who spoke to Breaking Belize News suggests that the recent killings may be connected to an internal dispute involving persons associated with the same gang.

According to the source, the violence may stem from a struggle for power and leadership within the group rather than a conventional conflict between rival gangs. However, the source stressed that the information remains unconfirmed, and BBN has not independently established the motive behind the killings.

Interestingly, during Friday’s police briefing, Smith also raised the possibility of internal gang conflicts and leadership struggles while discussing the recent violence.

Asked whether the killings were retaliatory or connected to other recent shootings, Smith acknowledged that investigators had not established a definitive link but suggested that police were considering the broader pattern of violence.

“We are not so daft to think that there is no nexus between these incidents,” Smith remarked, while emphasizing that police could not officially confirm a connection.

She explained that gang violence is not always the result of rivalry between opposing groups and can sometimes originate from disputes among members of the same organization.

“When it reaches a situation where there is an internal conflict, or a struggle for leadership, or an implosion, that makes policing these incidents even more difficult,” Smith explained.

She noted that individuals involved in such internal disputes are often familiar with one another’s movements, territories and methods of operation, making it easier for them to target each other.

While Smith did not confirm that an internal leadership dispute was responsible for the latest killings, her remarks are consistent with one of the possible explanations being examined in connection with the recent bloodshed.

The developments also follow Wednesday’s shooting at a Belmopan residence reportedly associated with paralyzed street figure Ronlee Petillo, which left a 19-year-old woman injured.

When questioned directly about a possible connection between that shooting and Friday’s quadruple murder, Smith acknowledged that police had taken note of the incidents and the individuals involved, but said investigators had not established a motive or confirmed any connection.

Investigators are also reviewing surveillance footage from cameras positioned at the La Democracia junction and another junction connecting the Coastal Plain Highway to southern Belize.

Meanwhile, police have already implemented strategic changes to their deployment and are considering additional measures to prevent further violence.

Smith said the department intends to use every available resource and legal mechanism to pursue those responsible for the recent killings, including individuals who may have assisted the perpetrators before or after the crimes.

The latest murders bring renewed attention to the possibility of an escalating internal conflict among criminal elements, although police have yet to officially determine whether the shootings are connected.

Investigations remain ongoing.

World.title: Belize joins Global initiative to strengthen women’s leadership in Ocean Conservation
World.content:
Belize joins Global initiative to strengthen women’s leadership in Ocean Conservation

By Zoila Palma: Belize has joined Madagascar and 14 other countries in pledging to strengthen women’s leadership in marine conservation and blue economy development through the Women Ocean Guardians Initiative.

The commitment was announced at the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (CBD CoP17), adding Belize to a growing coalition focused on placing women at the forefront of ocean governance and the sustainable management of marine resources.

Minister of Sustainable Development and Climate Change, Orlando Habet, highlighted the important role Belizean women play in protecting the country’s marine environment. “Belize has always punched above its weight in marine conservation,” Habet said. “But our success has never been an accident of geography—it is the result of the dedication, wisdom, and leadership of our women on the coast.”

The latest commitments bring the initiative’s support to more than 50 signed pledges, including 16 governments and over 30 partner organizations. The coalition’s progress is credited to the collective leadership of 75 women ocean guardians from 33 countries.

The initiative seeks to address gaps in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, particularly Target 23, which focuses on gender equality, and Target 3, which aims to protect 30 percent of the world’s land and ocean areas by 2030. Reports indicate that gender-responsive approaches remain among the least advanced areas of the global biodiversity commitments, while inclusive governance and effective management continue to pose challenges to the 30×30 target.

The Women Ocean Guardians Initiative was convened by the Wildlife Conservation Society, Conservation International and the Global Environment Facility (GEF) to create opportunities for women working on the frontlines of conservation to influence decisions and lead marine protection efforts.

GEF CEO Diego Mesa Puyo said the initiative demonstrates the importance of bringing together financing, policy and community leadership. Wildlife Conservation Society Marine 30×30 Director Pamela Castillo also emphasized that women’s participation is essential to achieving global ocean conservation goals, stating, “We cannot protect the ocean without the women ocean guardians.”

The initiative has established three regional hubs covering Southeast Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Africa.

World.title: Mayor Wagner takes Belize City’s voice to the Commonwealth
World.content:
Mayor Wagner takes Belize City’s voice to the Commonwealth

By Zoila Palma: Belize City Mayor Bernard Wagner has called for greater authority, financial resources, and climate resilience for local governments while representing Belize at the Wilton Park Dialogue on Sustainable Urbanisation in Georgetown, Guyana.

The event brought together Commonwealth leaders, policymakers, and urban development experts ahead of the 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

Mayor Wagner who also chairs the Commonwealth Local Government Forum (CLGF), challenged governments to reconsider how cities are financed and empowered to respond to rapid urbanisation and climate change.

Drawing on Belize City’s experiences with flooding, informal settlements, and infrastructure challenges, he emphasized the importance of stronger partnerships between national and municipal governments.

Wagner also highlighted Belize City’s municipal bond initiative and its contribution to the development of Belize’s Municipal Securities Act, pointing to the initiative as an example of how local government innovation can influence national policy. He called for greater municipal autonomy and innovative financing mechanisms to ensure cities have the resources needed to address their development challenges.

Mayor Wagner met with several regional and international urban development leaders, including Guyana’s Minister of Culture, Youth and Sport, Charles Ramson Jr.; Beth Chitekwe-Biti of Slum Dwellers International; urban economist Astrid Haas; Montego Bay Mayor Richard Vernon; and Professor Clyde Phillip of Trinidad and Tobago.

World.title: International News: Flavio Bolsonaro ally blames ChatGPT for deleted ‘President-Elect’ claim
World.content:
International News: Flavio Bolsonaro ally blames ChatGPT for deleted ‘President-Elect’ claim

By Zoila Palma: A close ally of Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro is blaming ChatGPT for language in a now-deleted social media letter in which the right-wing politician described himself as Brazil’s rightful “president-elect.”

The explanation came after Bolsonaro sparked controversy by questioning the legitimacy of the country’s recent presidential election, despite losing to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than four million votes.

Bolsonaro initially shared the letter on Wednesday, alleging without evidence that the election had been marred by fraud and presenting himself as the country’s legitimate president-elect.

About an hour later, he deleted the document and posted a revised version, replacing the phrase “president-elect” with “leader of Brazil,” prompting speculation about the sudden change, Reuters report.

Paulo Figueiredo, a right-wing influencer and podcast host who serves as an unofficial spokesperson for the Bolsonaro family in the United States, said the wording was mistakenly included during the document’s preparation.

According to Figueiredo, Eduardo Bolsonaro, Flavio’s younger brother and a former congressman, had used ChatGPT to help finalize the letter. He claimed the chatbot incorporated an earlier draft containing the disputed wording, along with an outdated version of Brazil’s coat of arms.

Figueiredo said the errors were only noticed after the document had been distributed to journalists and described the revision as minor.

He maintained, however, that the senator’s position had not changed and that Bolsonaro continued to reject the election result.

World.title: Belize strengthens regional preparedness for El Niño 2026–2027
World.content:
Belize strengthens regional preparedness for El Niño 2026–2027

By Zoila Palma: On October 29, 2026, the Government of Belize, through the Ministry of Economic Transformation, participated in the regional workshops on the 2026–2027 El Niño phenomenon, held under the Regional Action Plan promoted by the General Secretariat of the Central American Integration System (SG-SICA), CEPREDENAC and the Regional Committee for Hydraulic Resources (CRRH), in collaboration with COSEFIN and with support from the World Bank.

The workshops brought together representatives from Ministries of Finance and Economy, regional institutions and development partners to discuss the potential impacts of El Niño, including drought, water shortages, agricultural losses, and the resulting pressures on economic activity and public finances.

Through the leadership of Dr. Osmond Martinez, Minister of Economic Transformation and Pro Tempore President of COSEFIN, Minister Martinez highlighted the importance of taking a coordinated and forward-looking approach to the potential impacts of El Niño, emphasizing that:

“Preparing for climate-related events requires us to look beyond the immediate impacts and consider the wider implications for our economies and public finances. By working together, sharing knowledge and strengthening our financial preparedness, we can better protect our communities, support vulnerable sectors and build resilience across the region,” Martinez said.

The Ministry noted that through its COSEFIN Pro Tempore Presidency, Belize remains committed to strengthening regional cooperation, promoting knowledge-sharing and advancing practical solutions to improve fiscal preparedness and resilience against climate-related risks.

World.title: International News: Mexican Mayor who took on cartels was murdered; his assassination still haunts his city
World.content:
International News: Mexican Mayor who took on cartels was murdered; his assassination still haunts his city

By Zoila Palma: Mayor Grecia Quiroz of Uruapan, Mexico, is living under heavy security nearly a year after her partner, former mayor Carlos Alberto Manzo, was gunned down during Day of the Dead celebrations.

Quiroz is now escorted by approximately 60 federally appointed bodyguards, armored vehicles, and military trucks as concerns over political violence and cartel activity continue to grip the region, AP reports.

Manzo gained national attention for his outspoken campaign against criminal groups and his confrontational approach to security. His assassination in a crowded public plaza shocked Mexico and intensified concerns about the dangers facing local leaders who challenge powerful criminal organizations.

Authorities have detained 34 people in connection with Manzo’s killing, including members of his security detail and individuals accused of leaking his movements or helping plan the assassination.

Prosecutors have described a possible conspiracy involving people close to the former mayor, while federal and state authorities have blamed the killing on the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

World.title: Mark the 2027 holiday dates on your calendar!
World.content:
Mark the 2027 holiday dates on your calendar!

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize has announced the official schedule of public and bank holidays for 2027.

The schedule was issued in Belmopan in accordance with the Holidays Act, Chapter 289 of the Laws of Belize.

The year will begin with New Year’s Day on Friday, January 1, followed by George Price Day on Friday, January 15.

National Heroes and Benefactors Day will be observed on Monday, March 8, in lieu of March 9. The Easter holiday period will include Good Friday on March 26, Holy Saturday on March 27, and Easter Monday on March 29.
