- Would you call Azerbaijan an example for democracy?

- No, no, never. Would you call your country an example for democracy?

- Somehow yes.

- But you ban opposition rallies.

- No, actually not.

- Yes, yes. Those extremists who wanted to have a rally, I forgot the name. You banned them.

- I don’t know about that. I mean even during those corona times they were doing demonstrations.

- No. it was before corona times. We are not, and we do not pretend to be. But there are countries which pretend to be, but they killed protesters. Do you know how many people were killed during these yellow-vest protests? Do you know? More than ten killed.

- But we are not talking about France.

- No, no, let’s talk about Europe.

- About Azerbaijan…

- No, let’s talk about those who pretend to be democrats. We are not pretending. Yes, we have shortcomings.

- I will ask Mr. Macron about this.

- But those who kill protesters, who kill protestors on the street, ten of them killed. We look how in Europe you beat protesters, you beat them by forces. You bring dogs and this is considered democracy.

- How important is the country-where we came from right now-Türkiye for you and especially during this military operation during this war? I mean there are Turkish soldiers here. Yesterday, we talked to some of them and they told us they are from Türkiye.

- You talked to soldiers?

- Yes.

- On the battlefield?

- No, no, not on the battlefield

- But where?

- In the city of Baku.

-They are fighting here, in Baku?

- No, they are here. Nevertheless, they are here.

- There can be German soldiers here now.

- You are doing military exercises together.

- Yes, we do.

- If, a third country would get involved into this conflict, do you expect the help from Türkiye?

- We do not expect any third country to be involved. We do not see which country can be involved, because the countries which surround us are our partners and friends. We know that Armenians want to involve some of them into this battle. But I am sure it will not happen. It’s a battle between us and Armenia. And everybody should stay away from that. Turkish soldiers can be here, yes. Last year we had ten joint military trainings. But also, we have military trainings with other countries. We are part of the NATO partnership peace program. Nothing strange. You saw them in Baku, you didn’t see them in the battle.

- Do you feel safer with Turkish F-16s here in Azerbaijan?

- Turkish F-16s came here as a result of the military training and they stayed here because the Armenians launched an attack on us. And they are here as a sign of solidarity. They are not participating in any battle, and there are not a plan to be part of that.

- 3 times ceasefires were broken. One negotiated by France, one negotiated by Russia one negotiated by the USA. Which international power could stop this war?

- I think, Armenia should stop it. International power-these 3 countries which you mentioned are co-chairs of the Minsk Group. They are leading countries of the world, members of the UN Security Council, permanent members. These countries adopted four resolutions demanding withdrawal of Armenian troops. But these countries did not do anything in order to implement these resolutions. These resolutions were on paper. That shows that this mediation was not efficient. But at the same time, we cannot think about some other countries which can be more powerful. Therefore, the only way to stop war is for Armenia to stop, to admit its defeat, to admit our victory and then to commit to liberation of the part of the territories. We will liberate them anyway. They did not believe when we started counter-attack. We said we will liberate, stop it now. They could have stopped even when we took Fuzuli back.

- Do you have the feeling that they are not very interested in this conflict?

- Whom do you mean?

- Those three countries for example?

- Well, no, I don’t have this feeling, because if they were not interested, they wouldn’t have been mediators. They have a mandate from the OSCE.

- But the mediation wasn’t successful.

- Yes it wasn’t successful. Because they did not put sanctions on Armenia. I raised it many times. Armenia should have been sanctioned like Iraq was sanctioned when Saddam Hussein occupied Kuwait, immediately. And there were serious sanctions against Iraq. If the same happened to Armenia, then they would have moved the forces back.

- So they closed their eyes?

- Yes, they closed their eyes. They, I would say, not closed their eyes, they were always saying there is no military solution. They wanted that this situation continued more or less the same way. I think they were fine with the fact that the conflict seemed to be frozen. They thought that it may be frozen forever, and they only tried to think about some confidence-building measures, some monitors, so that there’s no outbreak. But they did not implement their mandate, in accordance with the OSCE decision and they should have forced Armenia. I think each of these countries unilaterally can send such a message to Armenia that it should listen to it, but they did not.

- Are you listening to them?

- I am listening to every partner. But it depends what I do after I listen. But I am listening.

- Two days ago, I heard you in the radio asking the question where has Armenia the money from to do this war? What is the answer?

- No answer. I’ve been asking this question for a month. We made a preliminary calculations.

- I mean, somebody asking this question continuously somehow has an answer in mind.

- Well, if I had an answer I would not have asked. If I am still asking, it means that I did not get an answer. We made a preliminary calculation about minimum, by the way, I did not disclose all of what we have destroyed. That will come. 2.7 billion dollars, cost of the ammunition which we destroyed and which we took as a trophy. Where the money comes from? Armenia is a poor country, its budget is less than 2 billion dollars. Its foreign debt is 8 billion dollars.

- They are supported by Russia.

- That’s your opinion.

- This is official. This is no secret. Somebody else?

- Maybe, I don’t know. So, I am asking but nobody is responding. So I will continue to ask.

- Your Excellency, Mr. President, thank you very much for the interview.

- Thank you.

World.title: Poland temporarily suspends Constitutional Tribunal president from duties
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. The website of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal has published a notice announcing the temporary suspension of its President, Bogdan Święczkowski, and Deputy President, Bartosz Sochański, from performing their official duties for a period of one month.

According to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who has the longest tenure at the tribunal, will lead the institution during this period.

The stated grounds for the decision include, among other things, actions by the President and Deputy President that obstructed the convening of a general assembly of tribunal judges with the participation of all judges elected by parliament. Violations in the formation of judicial panels were also cited.

Following the publication of the announcement, large crowds of protesters gathered outside the tribunal building. Police officers subsequently entered the premises.

World.title: Uzbekistan’s regional loan portfolio reaches $30.17B, accounting for 54.9%
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. Regions outside Tashkent city accounted for 361.6 trillion soums (about $30.17 billion), or 54.9% of Uzbekistan’s total banking loan portfolio of 659.1 trillion soums (about $55 billion) as of October 1, 2026.

This was reflected in the statement by the Central Bank of Uzbekistan.

Regions outside Tashkent city accounted for 361.6 trillion soums (about $30.17 billion), or 54.9% of the country’s total loan portfolio, highlighting the significant role of regional markets in the banking system, according to Trend's calculations.

Loans to individuals made up a substantial portion of regional lending. Nationwide, outstanding loans to individuals totaled 248.4 trillion soums (about $20.7 billion), of which 175.1 trillion soums (about $14.6 billion), or 70.5%, was attributable to regions outside Tashkent city.

This means that regional borrowers accounted for more than two-thirds of all outstanding loans to individuals nationwide, underscoring the importance of household lending in the distribution of credit across Uzbekistan.

Among the regions outside the capital, Fergana region had the largest loan portfolio, at 38.7 trillion soums (about $3.2 billion). Samarkand region ranked second with 34.5 trillion soums (about $2.87 billion), followed by Tashkent region at 31.4 trillion soums (about $2.6 billion), Andijan region at 31.2 trillion soums (about $2.6 billion), and Kashkadarya region at 31 trillion soums (about $2.58 billion).

Combined, these five regions accounted for 166.8 trillion soums (approx. $13.9 billion), or approximately 46.1% of the loan portfolio outside Tashkent city.

Regional differences were also evident in deposit distribution. Outstanding deposits in areas outside Tashkent city totaled 118.1 trillion soums (about $9.8 billion). Of this amount, 84.5 trillion soums (about $7 billion), or 71.6%, represented deposits held by individuals.

The figures highlight the importance of household savings in regional banking resources, alongside the significant contribution of lending to individuals to regional credit activity.

Overall, the data show that regions outside Tashkent city accounted for more than half of Uzbekistan’s outstanding loans, while individual borrowers and depositors represented major components of regional banking activity.

World.title: Azerbaijani banks’ net foreign assets rise 22.6% year over year
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. The net foreign assets of Azerbaijani banks reached 32.78 billion manat ($19.28 billion) as of October 1, 2026, according to the Central Bank of Azerbaijan’s (CBA) monetary survey.

The figure increased by 322.6 million manat ($189.7 million), or nearly 1%, in September, the CBA reported. Compared with October 1, 2025, net foreign assets rose by 6.03 billion manat ($3.5 billion), or 22.6%.

At the end of September 2025, the net foreign assets of Azerbaijani banks stood at 26.75 billion manat ($15.73 billion), compared with 32.78 billion manat ($19.28 billion) at the end of September 2026.

Meanwhile, banks’ net domestic assets totaled 23.22 billion manat ($13.65 billion) as of October 1. This figure increased by 707.6 million manat ($416.2 million), or 3.1%, in September and by 1.98 billion manat ($1.16 billion), or 9.4%, year on year.

As a result, the banking sector’s net foreign assets exceeded its net domestic assets by 9.56 billion manat ($5.62 billion) as of October 1. Net foreign assets were approximately 1.4 times the level of net domestic assets.

According to the monetary survey, net foreign assets grew faster than net domestic assets both month-on-month and year-on-year. The annual growth rate of net foreign assets reached 22.6%, compared with 9.4% for net domestic assets.

Net foreign assets have also increased from the outset of 2026. The figure stood at 26.65 billion manat ($15.67 billion) at the end of January and reached 32.78 billion manat ($19.28 billion) by the end of September, representing an increase of 6.14 billion manat, or approximately 23%.

Net domestic assets also rose over the same period, from 21.54 billion manat ($12.67 billion) at the end of January to 23.22 billion manat ($13.65 billion) at the end of September.

As of the reporting date, 21 banks were operating in Azerbaijan. The banking sector’s total assets amounted to 63.62 billion manat ($37.42 billion), total liabilities stood at 55.78 billion manat ($32.81 billion), and balance-sheet capital reached 7.84 billion manat ($4.61 billion).

In September, total banking-sector assets increased by 1.8%, total liabilities by 1.9%, and balance-sheet capital by 1.1%.

Net foreign assets represent the difference between banks’ foreign assets and foreign liabilities. An increase in this indicator means that foreign assets are growing relative to foreign liabilities.

World.title: Kazakhstan's ferroalloy exports to Netherlands rise 17% in Jan-Aug
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. Kazakhstan’s ferroalloy exports to the Netherlands rose by 17.0% year-on-year in volume terms during January-August 2026, reaching 10,196 tonnes compared with 8,718 tonnes in the same period of 2025, according to Trend’s calculations based on data from the Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan.

In value terms, ferroalloy exports to the Netherlands grew by 7.27% year-on-year to $12.76 million from $11.90 million recorded in the first eight months of 2025.

In August 2026 alone, Kazakhstan shipped 2,241 tonnes of ferroalloys to the Netherlands, valued at $2.83 million.

In total, Kazakhstan exported 1.05 million tonnes of ferroalloys in January-August 2026, down 16.8% compared with 1.26 million tonnes in the same period of 2025.

In value terms, ferroalloy exports declined by 6.16% year-on-year to $1.36 billion from $1.45 billion. China remained the largest destination for Kazakh ferroalloys, receiving 631,220 tonnes worth $704.5 million during the first eight months of 2026.

Japan ranked second, importing 127,485 tonnes valued at $213.2 million.

In value terms, other major destinations included the United States, with 72,179 tonnes worth $135.7 million; Germany, with 28,042 tonnes worth $53.5 million; Russia, with 37,759 tonnes worth $47.7 million; Italy, with 20,716 tonnes worth $33.5 million; and South Korea, with 22,518 tonnes worth $31.3 million. Indonesia, Spain, the Netherlands and the Czech Republic were also among the main buyers.

In August 2026, Kazakhstan exported 102,127 tonnes of ferroalloys worth $145.49 million.

Kazakhstan’s foreign trade turnover reached $102.96 billion in January-August 2026, up 12.8% in nominal terms compared with the same period of 2025.

Exports totaled $60.39 billion, increasing by 19.5% in nominal terms, while imports reached $42.57 billion, up 4.5%.

Crude oil and crude oil products obtained from bituminous minerals accounted for 49.8% of Kazakhstan’s exports in January-August 2026. Other major export commodities included refined copper and unwrought copper alloys (6.4%), radioactive chemical elements and radioactive isotopes (5.1%), copper ores and concentrates (4.4%), and ferroalloys (2.2%).

Passenger cars and other motor vehicles accounted for the largest share of imports, at 3.3%. Other major imported commodities included telephone equipment (2.7%), pharmaceutical products (2.5%), petroleum gases and other gaseous hydrocarbons (2.4%), and electric generating sets and rotary converters (2.2%).

Italy was Kazakhstan’s largest export destination, accounting for 18% of exports, followed by China (17.6%), Russia (8.5%), Türkiye (7.9%), France (6.1%) and the Netherlands (5.9%).

Russia was Kazakhstan’s largest import partner, accounting for 31% of imports, followed by China (29.8%), Germany (4.6%), the United States (3.9%), South Korea (2.5%) and Türkiye (2.1%).

World.title: Azerbaijani, Georgian PMs attend inauguration of ART Riverfront Hotel Tbilisi (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. Prime Ministers Ali Asadov of Azerbaijan and Irakli Kobakhidze of Georgia attended the inauguration of ART Riverfront Hotel Tbilisi.

Located on the banks of the Kura River in the Georgian capital, the hotel combines modern design with an artistic concept. It offers 152 rooms, a restaurant, conference halls and a range of other amenities.

The hotel’s opening is expected to contribute to strengthening investment, tourism and economic cooperation between Azerbaijan and Georgia.

ART Riverfront Hotel Tbilisi is owned by Azerbaijan-based Absheron Hotel Group, which operates under PASHA Hospitality, part of PASHA Holding.

World.title: Heydar Aliyev Foundation VP Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva attend official opening of Art Weekend (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. The official opening of the Fly to Baku. Art Weekend. Sense the Future NOW festival was held at the Heydar Aliyev Center on October 30.

Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and Founder of IDEA Public Union, together with Alena Aliyeva, attended the opening ceremony of the festival.

The Heydar Aliyev Center presented several exhibitions as part of the "Art Weekend" opening.

Addressing the opening ceremony, Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and Founder of IDEA Public Union, said that renowned artists from various countries joined the event. “And over the next few days, you will discover many paintings, installations, sculptures, and performances. All to show the beauty of nature and also its strength and its rigidity.

In 2012, we have established a Caucasus "Big Five" that include endangered species of animals, which are the brown bear, grey wolf, the Caucasian leopard, the imperial eagle, and the gazelle. And since then, we have worked together with local departments and international organizations to preserve these endangered species of animals and to reintroduce them into the wild and also to increase their habitat. And it has been quite successful.

In order to understand nature and to love it, the best way is to spend more time in the nature. Then you can really connect to it. And also, we want to make sure that everybody remembers that they can make a huge difference by themselves, even with very small actions. So, this is what the Sense the Future NOW festival means to us,” Leyla Aliyeva added.

The event also featured the national dances performed by Azerbaijan State Children's Philharmonic

Expressing his gratitude to Leyla Aliyeva on behalf of international art representatives, who have come to Baku to participate in the festival Fly to Baku. Art Weekend. Sense the Future NOW, Art curator Simon de Pury said: “Back in 2012, I had the great pleasure to meet you there in London. And I remember you said there are two things that I'm really very, very interested in. One is, I really want the artists from Azerbaijan to get a wide acknowledgement, to get widely seen around the world and to get a lot of international exposure. And so we discussed and did do an exhibition in 2012, Fly to Baku, which incorporated some of the greatest and most interesting living artists of Azerbaijan.

We did the first exhibition in London. It was a huge success and subsequently, that exhibition travelled to many cities. It went to Paris, it went to Moscow, it went to several cities around the world.

Then, in 2016, we did a great retrospective dedicated to the American artist George Condo. And that exhibition was a big success here in the Heydar Aliyev Centre. And that is when I discovered this incredible building Zaha Hadid was one of the greatest architects of our time. And I think that the building in which we are now is her magnus opus. In my view, it's her best work in a brilliant career.”

The event featured the immersive theatrical performance authored and directed by Parviz Mammadrzayev, with the visual atmosphere created for "Art Weekend" by Laman Yusifli. Through choreography, music, and visual storytelling, the play embodies a poetic journey that explores the fragile relationship between humanity and nature.

Following the ceremony, the Azerbaijan State Dance Ensemble performed "Jangi" and "Yalli," dances showcasing the country’s ancient dance traditions.

Held for the second consecutive year at the initiative of Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and Head of the IDEA Public Union, the festival's exhibition program brings together diverse artistic approaches, generations, and geographies, offering audiences an opportunity to reflect on themes such as memory, cultural heritage, nature, biodiversity, identity, and the future.

The “Big Five of the Caucasus” is one of the key themes of this year’s “Art Weekend,” exploring the region’s biodiversity and the role of animals in cultural memory, mythology and collective identity.

Another project presented in the Heydar Aliyev Center is “Legendary Creatures: An Azerbaijani Bestiary”. Connecting the “Big Five” with mythological creatures from Azerbaijani folklore, it highlights the importance of preserving wildlife and cultural heritage.

The exhibition features six works by six artists, including carpet art, sculpture, photography, metalwork and mixed media.

All the works are presented to the public for the first time as part of “Art Weekend.”

A contemporary art exhibition “When Nature Speaks. Heirs” features the Caucasian leopard, brown bear, grey wolf, golden eagle and goitered gazelle, exploring the relationship between humanity and nature, highlighting heritage, responsibility and the natural world we leave to future generations. It brings together artists working in installation, sculpture, ceramics, textiles and mixed media.

Attendees then toured an exhibition titled “The Skin of Truth” by Chinese artist Zhang Ji feature works from the artist’s “The Skin of Truth” and “Ultima” series, blending architectural motifs from different religious and cultural traditions with contemporary painting. Inspired by landmarks such as the Great Mosque of Córdoba and the Alhambra Palace, Zhang Ji uses a syringe instead of a brush to create raised surfaces reminiscent of bas-relief sculpture. His works have been exhibited in the United States, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, China, France, Spain, Switzerland, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and other countries, and included in collections worldwide.

The Heydar Aliyev Center also presents “What If Women Ruled the World?” by renowned American artist Judy Chicago and Italian artist Michelangelo Pistoletto’s Mirror of Eternity.

Since 2022, the What If Women Ruled the World?” project has developed a global archive spanning several countries. Visitors in Baku will be able to contribute to its next chapter by answering questions in an interactive recording booth.

Italian artist Michelangelo Pistoletto’s Mirror of Eternity project employs artificial intelligence to combine human portraits, generating new faces that have never existed before. Participants upload their portraits to the system, which then merges them with another person’s portrait to create a new image. Each portrait thus exists not as a fixed record of memory, but as an evolving digital entity transformed through successive encounters. The project explores the relationship between humanity, memory, technology, and the ever-changing nature of life.

The Fly to Baku. Art Weekend. Sense the Future NOW festival will run until November 1.

World.title: Uzbekistan’s average monthly wages rise 18%
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. Uzbekistan’s average monthly nominal accrued wage reached 7.27 million soums (about $606) in January-September 2026, up 18% year over year, according to data from the country’s Statistics Agency. The figures exclude agricultural enterprises and small businesses.

Tashkent recorded the highest average monthly wage, at 12.3 million soums (around $1,026), an increase of 18.3% compared with the same period in 2025. The figure was about 69% above the national average.

Navoi region ranked second, with an average monthly wage of 8.82 million soums (approx. $736), followed by Tashkent region at 6.89 million soums (about $574). Bukhara region recorded an average of 5.84 million soums (around $487), while wages in Samarkand region reached 5.37 million soums (approx. $448).

Qashqadaryo region reported the lowest average monthly wage, at approximately 4.97 million soums (about $414), followed by Surkhandarya region at 4.99 million soums (around $416). Namangan region recorded an average of 5.40 million soums (approx. $450).

In terms of annual growth, Namangan region led the country, with average wages increasing by 20.3%. Jizzakh region followed at 19.8%, while Tashkent region recorded 19.1% growth. Samarkand region posted the slowest increase, at 11.5%.

According to Trend’s calculations, the national average monthly wage increased by approximately 1.11 million soums (about $92.60) compared with the same period last year. Tashkent’s average was about 2.48 times the wage recorded in Qashqadaryo region, highlighting substantial regional differences in nominal earnings.

The longer-term trend also shows sustained wage growth. The national average rose from 3.73 million soums (around $311) in January-September 2022 to 7.27 million soums (approx. $606) in the same period of 2026, an increase of approximately 94.8% over four years.

However, nominal wage growth does not necessarily translate into an equivalent increase in purchasing power. The real improvement in workers’ living standards depends on inflation, while differences in regional economic activity, employment structure and the composition of surveyed businesses may also affect average wage figures.

World.title: Dead dolphin tests positive for H5 bird flu
World.content:
Another dead dolphin has tested positive for H5 bird flu.

South Australia's chief veterinary officer Skye Fruean said the case was in a common dolphin that washed ashore at Encounter Bay on the state's Fleurieu Peninsula this week.

She said there was low risk of an extensive outbreak among dolphins, although there is concern for land-based sea mammals like seals and sea lions.

"It's going to be a chance encounter that that dolphin's unfortunately come into contact with a wild bird that's infected," Dr Fruean said.

" You're not going to see a big die-off of dolphins from bird flu. "

South Australia has now registered 340 positive H5 bird flu events.

Events are not individual case reports, but rather refer to confirmed positive tests affecting at least one animal from a species in a single location.

Dr Fruean said no recent events had shown signs of mass mortality.

Monitoring latest marine threat Throughout the algal bloom crisis, citizen scientists off the coast of South Australia helped with research. Now, with deadly bird flu impacting wildlife, they are taking to the ocean to keep watch.

"We've been really pleased that we've seen a bit of a slowdown of how often we're getting positive cases, but we're certainly still getting [them] consistently," she said.

"There haven't been any where we've seen really significant numbers [of individual deaths].

"We have had some pretty significant impacts on the crested tern populations in particular."

A vaccination program has finished for selected birds at Cleland Wildlife Park and is halfway completed for birds at Zoos SA facilities.

The greater crested tern has been among the species impacted the most by H5N1 in South Australia. (iNaturalist: leafymouse/Greater crested tern/CC BY-NC 4.0)

The federal government has also confirmed that vaccines would be released for a little penguin program for South Australia.

Dr Fruean said operational preparations were underway to commence that program in penguin colonies living on Granite Island, Penneshaw and Emu Bay.

"I don't have a start date yet for little penguin vaccination plans, but certainly that [operational] work is still continuing," she said.

World.title: RFDS pilots make highway landings as key Nullarbor airstrip still unsealed
World.content:
The Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS) continues to face risky landings along a remote stretch of outback highway after a long wait to seal a key airstrip on the Nullarbor Plain.

Sitting 1,200 kilometres east of Perth on the WA-SA border, the Eucla Airstrip is 500km west and 700km east from the nearest available hospitals.

But its unsealed runway renders it unusable after wet weather, posing problems for RFDS pilots and their remote patients.

While $3.3 million was allocated in the 2024 state budget for an upgrade, bureaucratic and planning delays have prevented work from getting underway.

Wet weather landings

The consequences of the delays were highlighted on October 7, when rain from a strong storm front closed the airstrip.

With a patient requiring urgent transfer from Eucla's nursing post to Kalgoorlie Hospital, the RFDS aircraft was required to land on the Eyre Highway.

The upgrades will involve sealing the Eucla airstrip to reduce closures due to wet weather. (Supplied: WA government)

Police closed the highway in both directions for about two and a half hours to allow the aircraft to land and take off.

RFDS pilot Elias Hoch said the road landing required extra preparation, including a low pass to check the road surface, traffic and nearby signposts before touching down.

The road is about 9 metres wide, leaving little room for error, and the aircraft had to be pushed backwards by members of the public to face into the wind for take-off.

Police have to close the Eyre Highway for more than two hours each time a plane needs to land. (Supplied: Syloan Henderson-Wilson/RFDS WA)

"A road is quite a lot skinnier than even quite a narrow runway, so it throws off your depth perception a little bit," Mr Hoch said.

"And that sort of adds a little layer of challenge to the landing."

Ongoing delays

Shire of Dundas president Laurene Bonza said the council had spent about 15 years lobbying for the upgrade.

"We have had a funding commitment from the state government about two years ago and that's not progressing very quickly at all," she said.

Laurene Bonza says the long-awaited airstrip upgrade needs a clear path from planning to construction. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"So we keep getting further away from actually getting it done. The money that I've said we can have now won't be enough unless they're going to give us a bit more."

A state government spokesperson said the funding remained available, but the project required a full redesign, environmental clearance and confirmation of native title permissions to proceed.

As little as 3mm of rain can make the Eucla airstrip unserviceable. (Supplied: Shire of Dundas)

But Cr Bonza said native title clearance had been completed four times over, and extensive investigation rendered the redesigns unnecessary.

"It feels like we're doing the same surveys and we haven't actually made any real progress on getting the job done," she said.

The president said the repeated delays meant the project's initial $4.5 million cost was likely to rise.

Residents frustrated by delays

Eucla Roadhouse owner Rasa Patupis, who has lived on the border for 60 years, said she had pushed for the upgrade for almost 30 of them.

"One patient who had suspected appendicitis, it took them 11 hours to get to Kalgoorlie by ambulance, which is not, obviously, a good idea," she said.

"We've written letters to the ministers appropriate at the time, we've done personal requests. It's just been a list that just seems to fall on deaf ears."

Ms Patupis said it had been frustrating to see infrastructure developed in more remote locations, as their wait continued.

Rasa Patupis has lived in Eucla for 60 years. (ABC Goldfields: Rhiannon Stevens)

"What would it mean? Some sort of assurance if something's happened out there with my staff, the locals or a traveller, that we can feel assured that we can get these people out in time-critical times," she said.

Katherine O'Dea, who grew up on the Nullarbor, said local families had previously helped maintain the runway using their own equipment.

"We had to get safety people out to stop cars from coming on the highway or driving on the highway when we're expecting a plane to come in," she said.

" It can genuinely be a matter of life and death as to whether the airstrip is functional or otherwise. "

Ms O'Dea said those operations were a "logistical nightmare", and believes the airstrip should have been sealed years ago.

World.title: Israel's Arab parties emerge from deadlocked election as kingmakers
World.content:
When schoolteacher Ranya Farhat voted in the Israeli election for the very first time this week she, like many Arab Israelis, did not believe it would affect the outcome.

But on Tuesday a record turnout of Arabs, many of whom identify as Palestinian citizens of Israel, tipped the political scales and turned the Arab-majority parties into kingmakers in a deadlocked result.

Votes from Bedouin communities also surged, with some drawing attention on social media for riding camels and donkeys to polling places.

"It's making a difference this time," Ms Farhat says.

Their main motivation was toppling Benjamin Netanyahu's government and sending a clear message about its policies towards the Palestinian population, both in Israel and in the occupied territories.

Ms Farhat believes hatred towards Arabs had reached a "persistent" all-time high under the current government, driven by extremist cabinet members.

"Voting serves as a demand for full equality in citizenship, asserting that these rights are an obligation of the state, rather than a 'grant' contingent upon political loyalty," she says.

In Tarabin, a Bedouin village in the Negev Desert, where Netanyahu's Likud party had the majority vote in the past two elections, turnout nearly doubled and secured a win for the United Arab List party.

Analysis: The battle for Palestinian-Israeli votes could decide Israel's political future With neither voting bloc able to form government following Israel's election, Benjamin Netanyahu is attacking the legitimacy of Palestinian-Israeli votes.

Some of these communities are not recognised by the government and are often cut off from access to basic services. They are among the most economically isolated in the country.

But it was the turnout among first-time voters and women, like Ms Farhat, that was a particular surprise to Amnon Be'eri-Sulitzeanu, co-executive director of the NGO, Abraham Initiatives, which engages with Arab communities.

These groups, along with the Bedouin communities, are typically considered to be the "weaker links".

"It's a democratic achievement … a clear sign of eagerness … for civic and political engagement of the Arab citizens," Mr Be'eri-Sulitzeanu says.

" It exceeded our wildest dreams. "

The kingmakers that will be hard to ignore

Netanyahu's coalition and that of his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, failed to secure majority in the election. They are now scrambling to find new alliances to form government.

Gadi Eisenkot has said the results, which did not deliver either party a majority, are a vote for change. (Reuters: Shir Torem)

Both had vowed not to work the Arab-majority parties but after they secured a record 19 seats in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, their significant leverage will be hard to ignore.

Amir Badran, a member of the Hadash party (now part of Joint List), describes the situation as "political checkmate".

"Nobody wants to collaborate or to make any coalition with Arabs, just for the simple fact that they are Arabs, nothing more," he says.

"Now, they are a huge political force … and none of the blocs are able to do a coalition without the Arab votes.

" So, we are the kingmakers. "

Where to next in the Israeli election? The result of the Israeli election with neither Netanyahu nor the opposition gaining majority, means weeks of messy and complicated negotiations.

But Mr Badran fears the sentiment towards Arabs means this could be their last chance to vote.

"The racism reached a point that Arab minorities can clearly see the day coming … where Arabs do not have the right to vote," he says.

Amnon says the Arab community has "had enough of politics … that doesn't bring concrete achievements".

"They want to be engaged in the political system … and to play the political game … and engage in constructive politics and bring results," he says.

The Arab parties, despite previous objections to working with Jewish-Israeli parties over Gaza and the West Bank, are making moves to help oust Netanyahu.

The United Arab List (UAL), a party with roots in the Islamic Movement, recruited former lawmaker and deputy public security minister Yoav Segalovitz — a Jewish Zionist — as the number two candidate.

Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen and party member Ahmad Tibi said they were extending a hand to the opposition and would do what they could to bring down Netanyahu and his coalition.

But Mr Be'eri-Sulitzeanu says the opposition fell into Netanyahu's trap and "made this commitment that is not moral, not democratic and makes no political sense, that they won't sit with the Arabs".

What drove voters to the polls

Netanyahu's camp has been running an anti-Arab campaign, which has ramped up with allegations the parties "stole" the election.

It has used the slogan "Right or Palestine" — a phrase that rhymes in the original Hebrew "yemin o falastin" — in an attempt to paint the opposition as against Israel.

Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed the election was "stolen". (Reuters: Ammar Awad)

Before the polls had even closed, the Netanyahu camp began claiming Arabs were "stealing" the election and posting AI-generated content urging right-wing voters to "get out" in an "emergency".

Then came the calls for an investigation and later allegations of foreign interference involving Qatar. Mansour Abbas, head of UAL welcomed the probe to preserve the "purity" of the elections.

Israeli election official demands probe into foreign interference claims The fallout from Israel's inconclusive election takes another dramatic turn amid allegations of foreign interference.

Eisenkot supported the investigations, but accused Netanyahu of manipulating public opinion, delaying publication of the results and casting doubt on the legitimacy of the incoming Knesset.

The vilification of Israeli Arabs ensued across social media, and politicians from Zionist Israeli parties played up the language of danger and fear.

The anti-Arab sentiments are not new to Arab-Israelis who voted out of frustration with the current government's policies.

Most of this community are descendants of families that remained in the newly established Israel in 1948, and have faced decades of hostility and racism.

Many complain of facing worse conditions in their municipalities when compared to Jewish counterparts, including funding cuts, higher crime rates, poorer education levels and fewer economic opportunities.

"They wanted, plain and simple, to send this government home and to change the unbearable situation," Be'eri-Sulitzeanu says.

"People felt an urgency to do something about this situation … there was no need for anyone to tell them, drive them, convince them."

For some, the fate of Palestinians in Gaza or the West Bank was a deciding factor in their voting, but others focused on issues affecting them.

Aram Hosen Kewan, from the town of Umm al-Fahm in northern Israel, worked the phones this election to encourage members of his community to vote and says many of the conversations centred on issues affecting Arabs in Israel, not Gaza.

"The space to be Palestinian in Israel is always shrinking," he says.

"If the right wing continues, it will not end in Gaza. It will continue to the West Bank, after this to the Arab citizens.

"I'm more worried than scared, because every Palestinian had the feeling that he's next in line.

"I always say, 'We are one people, three societies in Palestine.'"

Mr Be'eri-Sulitzeanu is outraged at the government's reaction to the turnout, given that it had previously criticised Arabs for not voting.

"There's a risk that the level of disappointment will be so high we won't see this level of engagement in the future."

"If their extended hand is not met with a [gesture] from the bloc … then next time I'm afraid they will not vote in such numbers."

Voters hope outcome serves 'causes that matter to the people'

In Kafr Qasim in central Israel near the West Bank border, the mood is mixed.

There are no celebrations on the street as people go about their daily lives, unsure whether the vote will lead to change.

Some are optimistic and happy to have woken up to a result that felt inclusive.

Ahmed Issa, who owns a shop in the Kafr Qasim village. (ABC News: Ron Bavarsky)

Ahmed Issa, who owns a shop in the village, stood outside the day after the vote in pride.

"We are here and we have participated … the results make us proud, and Arabs have kept their promise."

He feels the government's "racism" means citizens like him are being ignored and says he doesn't have rights in the country.

"Arabs are suffering from a haemorrhage of violence, home demolitions, and a lack of support from the current government."

Others are weary. They are aware they are not accepted by any camp and believe the reaction and lack of allies prove how marginalised they are even if they have the numbers.

Azzam Sarsour, standing on a busy street in Kafr Qasim in central Israel near the West Bank border. (ABC News: Ron Bavarsky)

Azzam Sarsour, standing on a busy street, says all his relatives came out to vote hoping for change, but that he won't bother next time after seeing the Jewish parties refuse to sit with the Arab parties.

"We voted for nothing. Even if the Arab parties won 40 seats, it would mean nothing. To be honest, I'm considering leaving this country," he says.

One shopkeeper remarks the election was two days before the anniversary of the Kafr Qasim massacre, which had become a symbol of injustice for Palestinians in Israel and a reminder of the fraught history and context that shapes how the discussion is unfolding.

For Aram Hosen Kewan, any change will be better than the current situation, saying even if the parties don't differ when it comes to Gaza, he'd take a "government who kills 10 people in a day, not a government who kills 100 people in a day".

Despite the scepticism, Ms Farhat is still hoping for change.

"Hopefully, the outcome will serve the causes that matter to the people, rather than reflecting a ruler's selfish desire to cling to power at the expense of the people's interests," she says.

World.title: The Republican senator campaigning on her clashes with Trump
World.content:
As the US midterm elections get closer, Donald Trump's polling numbers keep diving further underwater.

And Republican Senate candidates are becoming more vocal about their differences with the president.

Michigan's Mike Rogers, an early tariffs supporter, is now calling for an end to the Canada trade war.

New Hampshire's John Sununu, who initially praised Trump's decision to attack Iran, now criticises the plan as flawed.

And Ohio's Jon Husted, who has championed data centres for years, now says they should only be built where the locals want them.

But in Maine, Susan Collins can lay claim to a long history of disagreements with Trump.

Susan Collins's supporters say she's been an effective champion for Maine. (ABC News: Brad Ryan)

The veteran Republican, a fixture of the Senate since Bill Clinton was president, even voted to convict Trump after he was impeached over the January 6 insurrection.

"I'm not exactly his favourite senator," she said during one recent debate.

"I vote very independently," she told another.

Talking up her differences with Trump is a central part of Collins's strategy to keep her seat. It could be the key to helping his Republican Party keep control of the Senate.

Lost support

Republicans see the Maine Senate seat as one they cannot afford to lose.

The local polls are hairbreadth tight, but Trump is unpopular in Maine. About twice as many Mainers disapprove of his performance than approve, according to Civiqs' public opinion tracker.

So the question is: Has Collins done enough to convince Mainers she will stand up to Trump when it counts?

For Lee Umphrey, who had consistently voted for Collins up until this year, the answer is no.

"I've known her a long time, she's done a lot of good, and for organisations like ours she has been very reliable," said Umphrey, who runs a community development corporation in Bangor, where Collins lives.

Lee Umphrey has a signed photo with Susan Collins among others on his office wall, but says the goodwill she built up in Maine has faded under Donald Trump. (ABC News: Brad Ryan)

"[But] this is really a referendum on President Trump's executive power and the abuses connected to that."

He listed examples including the Elon Musk-led slashing of government services, cuts to Medicaid health insurance under the "Big Beautiful Bill", tariffs on Canada, and the war in Iran.

'Women felt betrayed'

To some extent, Collins split with Trump on all four examples listed by Umphrey.

She voiced opposition to some DOGE cuts, voted against the Big Beautiful Bill, criticised the Canada tariffs, and supported Democrat-led resolutions to end the war.

She points to wins like her successful efforts to boost rural health funding in the Big Beautiful Bill and to remove tariffs from some Canadian products, including rock salt used on Maine's icy roads in winter.

Maine is a key state in the battle for a Senate majority, and pollsters rate the race as a toss-up. (Portland Press Herald: Gregory A Rec via AP)

Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, mocks what he sees as meek efforts for meagre concessions.

"She's like an arsonist who helped set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out," he said in one recent debate.

Her critics argue she too often caves to pressure.

"I'm sure that she has done good things for the state of Maine and for the country, but of late, ever since Trump has been on the scene, she's mostly been complicit," said Mary Ann Larson, part of a group that holds weekly protests against Collins and Trump.

Mary Ann Larson has been taking part in weekly protests against Susan Collins and Donald Trump since early 2025. (ABC News: Brad Ryan)

Like many in Maine, Larson has not forgotten Collins's role in appointing Supreme Court judges that overturned abortion rights, including her critical vote to confirm Trump-nominee Brett Kavanaugh's appointment in 2018.

"So many women felt betrayed by that," Larson said. "We're half the population and we basically were disenfranchised by that vote."

Loading

Local issues

Collins has a history of outperforming the polls.

When she was last up for election six years ago, polls predicted she would lose. But she won by nine percentage points.

Democrats' hopes for her defeat were high again earlier this year, as candidate Graham Platner attracted a huge groundswell of grassroots support.

But he was forced out of the race in July after being accused of sexual assault (which he denies).

One of the biggest blows to Collins's campaign came in September, when ProPublica published an investigation into alleged bribery.

Jackson called it "corruption of the highest order" but Collins denied wrongdoing, and the allegations do not look to have significantly dented her re-election effort.

Some of Collins's enduring electoral success is attributed to her work on low-key local issues and dealings with constituents.

Some locals offer personal stories when asked for their views on the senator, like Bangor local Lisa Thomas, who said she had bumped into Collins several times at the shops.

Lisa Thomas still uses the pot roast recipe Susan Collins gave her years ago. (ABC News: Brad Ryan)

"About four years ago we were talking about pot roasts, and she gave me her mother's recipe. I've used it ever since, and it's great," said Thomas.

"Each time I see her, I always come to shake her hand and say, 'I appreciate you, I appreciate what you stand for, for goodness and equality.'"

Broken promises

Thomas was collecting a Susan Collins lawn sign at a family day for conservatives at a Bangor church, co-sponsored by the Republican Party.

Handing out the signs was 19-year-old volunteer Sofia Pride, who described Collins as "easy to support whichever side of the political spectrum you're on".

"I've always looked up to her," she said, recalling how Collins used to phone into a public radio show Pride worked on when she was at high school.

Sofia Pride, a volunteer for Susan Collins's campaign, remembers the senator phoning into the radio show she worked on in her freshman year of high school. (ABC News: Brad Ryan)

But when asked about Trump, Pride said: "I'm going to pass on the question if that's OK. I think it's not about him right now. It's about having Senator Collins win this race, and he's chosen not to be involved in it, and I think that says a lot."

Some attendees said they would vote for Collins despite having reservations about Trump.

"When he ran in 2024, he promised us no new wars," said three-time Trump voter Michael Capeci.

"Then he made the decision to go to war in Iran for supposed nuclear weapons that I don't think even exist.

"But I strongly support Susan Collins because she's delivered a lot of good money to the state of Maine and she's done so much to keep businesses open and get economic development and federal funds into the state."

Michael Capeci will vote for Susan Collins despite feeling let down by Donald Trump's attack on Iran. (ABC News: Brad Ryan)

Trump's 11th-hour gift

Collins's campaign has focused on promoting her as a fighter for local causes as much as it has promoted her fights with Trump.

And the Trump administration delivered a gift to boost those messages in the final days of the campaign.

Last week, Collins announced the White House had agreed to another reduction on tariffs on Canadian products, including those deemed crucial to Maine's famed blueberry and apple industries.

The move could indicate Trump and his team fear his unpopularity could finally spell the end of Collins's electoral luck.

"There's a growing resentment that while he's doing well and the stock market's happy and his rich friends are happy, people on the street are hurting," said Umphrey, the community development head.

"We're seeing this all the time with diesel fuel, regular gasoline, food costs, healthcare costs all going up.

"I think any goodwill that Senator Collins has built up because of her good work is going to fade away, because it's pretty severe."

World.title: Inside fraternities and why they are so important to US colleges
World.content:
New York state police have announced they will take charge of future sexual assault investigations at Cornell University in the latest fallout over the university's handling of an alleged gang rape on campus.

It comes as the university's faculty undertook a vote of no confidence in the school's administration over how it handled the allegation, with the results expected on November 6.

The alleged Cornell University incident in 2024 is not isolated, with the Associated Press reporting police were investigating allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity party at the University of Chicago on October 11.

A female student at the University of Arizona alleged she was sexually assaulted by two men at a fraternity house on August 26, according to AP.

A few weeks later, on October 8, the University of Arizona suspended fraternity activity after reports of hazing and sexual misconduct.

According to the AP, previous hazing at the university's fraternities included forcing new members to consume large quantities of alcohol, as well as live goldfish.

Australian attitudes to fraternities, also known as frats, have been mostly shaped by popular culture, but what are fraternities really? And why are they so ingrained in higher education in the US?

Cornell has closed the Chi Phi chapter house during an investigation into alleged sexual assault. (Reuters: Angelina Katsanis)

What are fraternities?

Social fraternities or sororities are exclusive clubs for undergraduate students who can live together, socialise together and participate in traditions, usually in a same-sex environment.

Kimberly Davis, data analyst at Pennsylvania State University's Piazza Centre for Fraternity and Sorority Research, said fraternities were "often built around a shared identity" and members could maintain fraternity relationships "long after graduation".

Female students typically join sorority chapters, which function similarly to fraternities. (Reuters: Bing Guan)

"For some students, that level of connection is especially appealing during a period of life that can feel uncertain and transitional," Dr Davis said.

The first fraternity-like organisation was founded in 1776 at the College of William and Mary in Virginia, but they became much more popular across the US by the mid 1800s, according to Dr Davis.

Why are fraternities so important to US universities?

Dr Davis said on a practical level, fraternities provided additional residential options for university campuses.

She said fraternities were also "valuable partners" for universities to foster leadership development, student involvement in community activities, service and philanthropy.

"The friendships and communities that fraternities create also offer benefits for universities," she said.

Chi Phi organisation's website says its mission "is to build better men through lifelong friendships, leadership opportunities and character development". (AP: Heather Ainsworth)

"Alumni who have favourable fraternity experiences often associate their experiences with the university, which in turn encourages alumni to stay connected to the institution through alumni mentor ship and financial donations."

What are the problems with frats?

Loading...

According to a 2019 survey by the Association of American Universities, 10 per cent of undergraduate women who reported being raped said the incident occurred at a fraternity house, and 20 per cent of women reporting unwanted sexual touching said it occurred in a fraternity house.

6.4 per cent of men and 6.7 per cent of transgender, gender queer or questioning students who reported being raped said the incident occurred in a fraternity house, and just under 10 per cent of men and 12.6 per cent queer students reported unwanted sexual touching.

Dr Davis said fraternities did not contribute to a culture of sexual violence by design, but "that does not mean that fraternity environments cannot contribute to risk".

"Some organisational environments can normalise attitudes and behaviours that increase the risk of sexual violence," she said.

"A chapter that prioritises accountability, healthy relationships, and intervention can create a very different environment from one that normalises excessive alcohol use or tolerates harmful behaviour."

Cornell gang-rape investigation reopened A US prosecutor has reopened an investigation into allegations a woman was gang-raped by seven students at a Cornell University fraternity.

As well as sexual assault allegations, fraternities are also often associated with hazing.

The University of Colorado defines hazing as any activity that humiliates, degrades, abuses, or endangers someone, regardless of consent, as condition for entering an organisation.

The Pennsylvania State University Piazza Centre is named after student Timothy Piazza, who died as the result of a hazing incident at the university's Beta Theta Pi fraternity.

Mr Piazza was given at least 18 drinks in 82 minutes, according to prosecutors, and fell down the fraternity house stairs, becoming unconscious.

He later died from a head injury after a delayed response by bystanders.

"Timothy Piazza was one of four IFC fraternity men who died in hazing incidents in 2017 alone; that was an especially deadly year and the catalyst for many revised state hazing laws," Dr Davis said

Hazing prevention organisation HazingInfo's database indicates about five deaths per year have been reported in the US since 2000.

Do we have anything like them in Australia?

In Australia, the frat niche is filled by residential colleges, which provide accommodation, meals, academic support and social activities for residents.

Southern Cross University professor Elizabeth Mackinlay said instances of sexual harassment, assault and violence persisted at Australian residential colleges.

Report reveals bizarre college rituals The parents of Stuart Kelly, whose brother died in a one-punch attack in Sydney, believe he was targeted in a sadistic college hazing ritual before he killed himself. A new report has triggered fresh calls for an inquest into his death.

She said under-reporting continued at a concerning level, because students feared potential consequences for them and those responsible.

Professor Mackinlay said what Australian residential colleges and US fraternities had in common was hazing.

Hazing, abuse and misogyny have been reported at some residential colleges, including at Sydney University when, in 2018, allegations emerged of sexual assault, excessive alcohol consumption and other incidents.

In 2024, the City of Sydney council recommended the abolition of the University of Sydney's Residential Colleges after an incident at St Paul's College "where 6 students were expelled and a further 21 suspended after engaging in acts of 'serious humiliation' and sexual violence against a student".

Professor Mackinlay said the issues reported at Cornell University, the University of Arizona and St Paul's College she experienced herself during her time at university in the late 80s and 90s.

"The alcohol abuse, the degradation, rape, everything happened," she said.

" Nobody reported it. Leadership in the student group took part. "

Professor Mackinlay said the culture of hazing and alcohol abuse had to change and "cultural norms around respectful relationships have to be in place and reinforced".

"If there's gender-based violence, there's a good chance that you're going to have to sit at the breakfast table in halls the next morning with the perpetrator there," she said.

World.title: Flesh-eating Buruli ulcer cases are rising. Here's how to protect yourself
World.content:
It starts as a small, painless lump on the skin that is easy to ignore.

But under the seemingly innocuous lump, flesh-eating bacteria are burrowing through fat and muscle.

Warning: Readers are advised that this article includes an image of an open wound.

The skin over the lump then dies, turns black and eventually becomes an open sore that, if untreated, grows.

This is a typical case of Buruli ulcer, a condition that until recently was primarily found in West Africa.

Victoria is now considered the Buruli ulcer centre of the world, with a record 426 confirmed cases last year.

Buruli ulcer is typically acquired in summer and autumn.

It is endemic in the Mornington Peninsula, Bellarine Peninsula, Geelong and some Melbourne suburbs.

It is also found in other parts of Australia: pockets of coastal Queensland, where it is sometimes called Daintree ulcer, and around Darwin.

Most recently, cases have popped up on the New South Wales south coast around Batemans Bay.

Visitors to these popular tourism areas might unknowingly get infected, go home and, months later, develop a Buruli ulcer where local doctors may not be aware of the condition.

So, coming into summer holidays, how can you protect yourself from the disease?

What causes Buruli ulcer?

Buruli ulcer is caused by the microbe Mycobacterium ulcerans.

It can be transmitted to humans via mosquitoes, so ulcers usually appear in areas near bites, such as on arms and legs.

Loading...

Once in the skin, the bacteria secrete a cocktail of molecules that numb the area, slowly kill surrounding tissues and suppress the immune system.

"These things make it quite an impressive pathogen, and often, it's been there for a while before people actually know they've got it," Daniel O'Brien, an infectious diseases physician at Barwon Health in Geelong and Royal Melbourne Hospital, says.

The progression of lump to ulcer happens in about 90 per cent of Buruli ulcer cases he sees.

In less than 1 per cent of cases, the bacteria reach bone.

How is Buruli ulcer diagnosed and treated?

Buruli ulcer advances so slowly that the first symptoms usually are not noticed until five or six months after the infection.

It is diagnosed by sending a swab off for PCR testing to see whether the ulcer contains M. ulcerans bacteria.

Treatment starts with a six-to-eight-week course of antibiotics, but the drugs themselves can be problematic. They interact with many other medications and produce side effects so awful that about 20 per cent of patients cannot finish the whole course.

M. ulcerans infections can start off looking like nasty spider bites that do not heal, Dr O'Brien says, but eventually turn into ulcers. (Supplied)

Dr O'Brien is leading a team trialling a new antibiotic that can be taken over just 10 days, which he says is less harsh on the body, yet still effective against M. ulcerans.

For most people, antibiotics will be enough, but if there is too much tissue damage or the wound is not healing properly, surgery is needed.

Even with treatment and good wound care, it can take months — even a year — for an ulcer to fully heal.

Dr O'Brien says outcomes for patients are generally better if the ulcer is diagnosed early.

For that reason, he recommends getting a health practitioner to look at any suspicious lumps sooner rather than later, especially if you live or holidayed in an area known to have the bacterium, and to specifically ask about Buruli ulcer.

How can I protect myself from Buruli ulcer?

While Buruli ulcer prevalence is rising, Dr O'Brien says it is important to remember that the disease is still uncommon in humans.

" If you protect yourself from the environment … you really minimise your risk of acquisition. "

While mosquitoes are a main source of Buruli ulcers, they are not the only one.

Brushtail and ringtail possums are also known to get infected, and can develop nasty ulcers on their paws, face and tail.

A 2025 study found that analysing the poo of possums could help predict regions where Buruli ulcer might crop up next, with human cases usually appearing up to three years after the first positive possum poo test.

That is because possums shed the bacteria in droppings, introducing it to the soil, which can then get into cuts in our skin.

Dr O'Brien's advice is to:

cover up as much as possible

wear mosquito repellent on exposed skin

cover any wounds while handling soil, and if you injure yourself, wash it immediately with soap and water, then apply antiseptic

avoid handling sick or injured possums

A recent study found reducing mosquito numbers in Buruli ulcer areas also lowered human case numbers, so it is a good idea to tip out standing water where mosquitoes breed and put out mosquito traps.

It is also important to note that research shows not all possums in Buruli-endemic areas carry the bacteria, and it is illegal to trap, relocate or cull possums without a licence.

And, in good news for ringtails and bushies, an edible possum vaccine in the works could help reduce infections and ulcers in the future.

Hear more about Buruli ulcer on Outbreaks, a special series on Science Friction.

World.title: US approves $3 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
World.content:
The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $US2.1 billion ($3 billion) in what would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second Trump administration.

The US State Department made the announcement on Friday, local time, amid Ukraine's urgent calls for more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia's military fires at the country.

The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.

Delayed missile deliveries have ‌added ⁠to Ukraine's tensions with the US after President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for Kyiv's unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy (left) and Donald Trump at the UN General Assembly in September. (AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

On Thursday, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian ‌city of Dnipro, while five died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a missile strike killed one person in Kyiv, officials said.

Mr Zelenskyy said this week that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the US to sign off on critical ​missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.

Deadlier drones herald horrifying new warfare Russia's new jet-powered drones are ripping through the skies at hundreds of kilometres an hour, and Ukraine's defences are struggling to keep up.

But despite Ukraine's urgency, it will likely not receive the missile interceptors quickly.

Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles — which are yet to be manufactured — are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.

One of the people said Ukraine's Ministry of Defence is encouraging the Pentagon to bring forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in a statement.

Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, with the capital Kyiv coming under fire. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

The program uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia's invasion, according to a Pentagon website.

The JUMPSTART program was used in August to buy 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth $US825 million ($1.17 billion) made by Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire.

Trump's threats to Ukraine It is hard to see Donald Trump's shifting position on Ukraine as a clear strategic change, and not one driven principally by soaring fuel prices ahead of the US mid-term elections.

Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.

The US ‌has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.

In July, the US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $US58.6 billion ($83 billion) to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.

Lockheed has said that deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity ​by the end of ​2030 and increase jobs ⁠at its Camden, Arkansas, plant by 50 per cent to about 1,850 from 1,200.

Lockheed previously announced Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would go to 2,000 units ​annually.

Pentagon negotiators are ⁠pressing contractors to move much faster, with tentative production agreements struck this year at the centre of ​efforts to increase missile output.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Bunnings shelves Halloween straightjacket costume after criticism
World.content:
Bunnings has removed a straitjacket costume from its online marketplace as mental health advocates urge retailers to stop selling Halloween outfits that portray people with mental illness as "insane".

The costume, listed on Bunnings Marketplace, was a straitjacket with arm ties and the words "Property of the county mental institution — approach with caution!" printed on the back.

SANE Australia, a non-profit organisation for people with complex mental health issues, said it was unacceptable for corporations to publicly support mental health causes while profiting from products that reinforce stigma.

"The time has well and truly come for us to stop turning a blind eye to these kinds of tropes in the community," CEO Rachel Green told ABC Victoria Statewide Drive.

" You wouldn't see people buying and wearing a cancer patient costume, for example. So why is a costume dressing up as someone with a mental illness considered acceptable? "

Rachel Green says it's unacceptable for businesses to publicly support mental health while profiting from products that reinforce stigma. (Supplied: SANE Australia)

Sandy Jeffs, a SANE ambassador and author who lives with schizophrenia and was a patient at Melbourne's former Larundel Psychiatric Hospital, said the costumes were insulting and "downright mad-shaming".

"Halloween, it's fun for people, but I suppose it's when it goes to negative tropes like introducing straitjackets as a costume — it goes into a dark place," she said.

"They're there to laugh at, to make fun of, to really demonise a whole cohort of people who don't deserve to be demonised or to be laughed at and shamed.

" We're just ordinary people with a very extraordinary illness … dealing with the stigma that surrounds these conditions every day. "

If you or anyone you know needs help: Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

Lifeline on 13 11 14

Headspace on 1800 650 890

When contacted by the ABC, a spokesperson for Bunnings said the item had since been removed from sale.

"We understand the concerns raised, and once the listing was brought to our attention, it was removed from Bunnings Marketplace," a spokesperson said.

The same costume is available for sale at Kmart, which, like Bunnings, is owned by Wesfarmers, as well as at Dick Smith, Amazon and a number of smaller costume stores.

The ABC has contacted Wesfarmers for comment.

Not the first time

It's not the first time SANE has called out retailers for selling costumes it considers stigmatising.

SANE said a social media campaign in 2024 prompted Big W to remove Halloween costumes from sale.

Ms Green said Spotlight was among the retailers that quickly pulled the costume at the time, but had since made it available for sale again.

The costume remained available on the Spotlight website on Saturday. (Supplied: Spotlight)

She said the costumes mattered for families dealing with serious mental illness.

"It does matter for the family who've got a 25-year-old who's got early signs of psychosis and is really struggling and needs to have that support wrapped around them," Ms Green said.

"How are they going to feel with people walking around on Saturday dressed in a costume that's a caricature of a bygone era."

The ABC has contacted Spotlight for comment.

World.title: Updated inner-south Victorian sells for $50,000 below reserve
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Updated inner-south Victorian sells for $50,000 below reserve Wes Mountain October 31, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

An updated three-bedroom Victorian in South Yarra sold for $1.75 million in post-auction negotiations – $50,000 below reserve – as a small number of homes went to auction over a quiet Cup weekend. Minutes from Hawksburn train station and a short walk to both Toorak and Williams roads, the preserved Victorian weatherboard at 3 Hopetoun Grove features a striking red door. Inside, floating floorboards lead past two front bedrooms built around period chimneys into a sitting room and a rear open-plan kitchen and living area, with full-length windows looking onto a small yard and terrace. With a primary bedroom and ensuite upstairs above the living area, the property was listed with a reserve of $1.8 million. Marshall White Stonnington agent and auctioneer Fiona Counsel said the auction opened with a $1.7 million vendor bid, followed by a single $1.71 million genuine bid from a local couple with a young family, on which it was passed in.



Counsel said the vendors, upsizing to a new property, agreed to “meet the market”, with the buyers happy to meet them halfway and sell for $1.75 million, as the potential for another rate hike on Tuesday loomed over the weekend. “I think from the vendor’s perspective… they factored that in when it came to the negotiation,” she said. The well-preserved Victorian facade hides an expansive updated interior. Marshall White Stonnington She said she didn’t think the Cup Day long weekend had been a factor in interest on the day. “We were comfortable to go on race week,” she said. “Everyone was here that was expected to be here.”



The property was one of 418 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. Further south, a three-bedroom freestanding villa in Hughesdale, with 433-square-metres of land on the title, sold for $950,000 at auction, soaring $100,000 over its $850,000 listed reserve. Split between living and dining areas to the front, and its three large bedrooms to the rear, 2/142 Poath Road was one of two units on the block, with mostly original interiors and a large yard ready to be updated by a new owner. Ray White Oakleigh agent and auctioneer Jonathon Eaves said a $720,000 genuine bid opened the auction, from which three bidders pushed the price up in $20,000 increments to $800,000.



Related Article Melbourne house prices Melbourne suburbs where house prices have fallen the most From there, bids slowed to $10,000 and eventually $5000 increments after being declared on the market at $850,000. It eventually reached $950,000 – $100,000 over its reserve and more than $200,000 above the opening bid. The successful buyers were a young couple, purchasing their first home in the area, while the vendors sold to transition to the next stage of their lives. Eaves thought the sale was an indication that some parts of the market were still selling well, but said the threat of another rate hike did factor into reluctance from at least one buyer to put his hand up at auction. “But you’ve just got to look at it and say, ‘can I afford it? Is it a good home?’” he said.



“And can I see that potentially, in 10 years, this property will be worth more?” Property alerts are now available in The Age app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.
