World.title: Two dead, one injured in three-car crash on Mid North Coast
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Two people have died and one injured following a three-car crash in Suffolk Park on NSW’s Mid North Coast on Saturday.

Emergency services were called to Broken Head Road near Byron Bay at 10.30am where they found the driver of a vehicle, believed to be a woman aged in her 50s, and the driver of a second vehicle, a man believed to be in his 60s, had died at the scene. They are yet to be formally identified.

A woman in her 60s who was a passenger in the second vehicle was treated at the scene by NSW Ambulance paramedics and airlifted to Gold Coast University Hospital in a critical condition.

The occupants of a third vehicle were uninjured.

World.title: The King and the colonies: Why Charles will have to confront slavery
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: King Charles has been greeted with joyous music, smiling dancers and a shot of rum on a journey through the Caribbean that looks like an endless celebration. But every stop takes the King closer to a meeting in Antigua where he will have to navigate the grim history of slavery in his talks with Commonwealth leaders from former British colonies. Charles has expressed sorrow about slavery, but has stopped short of a formal apology, given that he is guided by British policy that rules out paying reparations for the damage done over centuries. At this meeting, however, several leaders from the Commonwealth appear determined to force a debate about a response from Britain over its imperial past. And the response, they say, is not only about money. They want an apology. The King with Guyana’s Minister of Agriculture Minister, Zulfikar Mustapha, and Mangroves Restoration and Management project coordinator Kene Moseley at the Kingston Seawall Esplanade in Georgetown. Chris Jackson/Getty Images “What benefit do we have from this man coming to our country?” asked Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee, after the King flew out of the island nation a few days ago. “We know what we are giving, but what are we getting, you know? And if all that we’re getting is an opportunity to smile and wave and say hello, I think for a lot of Bahamians that just wasn’t worth it.”



One seasoned observer, Alan Lester, professor of historical geography at the University of Sussex, believes this sets up an opportunity for a unified statement and an apology that helps Britain build better relations with the Commonwealth. Without an agreement, however, it could merely lead to more acrimony. The King began his Caribbean tour on Tuesday in the Bahamas, where he displayed some dance moves in a parade, and then visited Guyana, where he tasted the local rum. Charles shook traditional cowbells as he paraded with Junkanoo dancers in Nassau, Bahamas. AP Photo/Tim Aylen Charles sniffs a glass of a special Guyanese rum created in his honour in Georgetown. Getty Images He arrives in Antigua on Sunday for events that include a cricket match among famous West Indies champions and several Commonwealth leaders. The argument about slavery will shape the agenda after a formal event on Wednesday to open the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, or CHOGM.



Of course, the King has proven his skill at delicate diplomacy in the past, not least in handling Donald Trump during two state visits – the American president’s trip to London last year and the King’s visit to Washington DC this year. On both occasions, the King made pointed remarks about liberty, climate change and Ukraine with no display of tension with Trump. The talks on slavery could be more difficult because the King may be outnumbered. Caricom, which represents 15 states and several territories around the Caribbean, is calling for significant action on slavery because of the evidence that European nations enslaved Africans, shipped them across the Atlantic, stripped them of their humanity and set up the financial systems to treat them as chattels. Jevon Thompson, of the Ethiopian African Black International Congress, carries a protest sign calling for reparations and a public apology while Charles was in Nassau on Wednesday. AP Photo/Tim Aylen The Caribbean manifesto, issued in June, notes that Britain paid compensation to slave owners when it abolished slavery, but did not compensate those who had been enslaved. Setting out a 10-point plan for justice, the group seeks a formal apology, a development program for Indigenous people, repatriation for descendants of slaves who might seek to return to Africa, the restitution of cultural heritage, help to remedy a crisis in public health and help with education and training. A key goal is compensation for gender-based violence, given estimates that 6 million African women were transported across the Atlantic as slaves, almost one-third of the 20 million who were forcibly removed.



Caricom also seeks support with psychological rehabilitation and sovereignty over technology development. The final point of the 10-point plan is debt cancellation, monetary compensation and decolonisation. “The crimes against humanity committed against African people by enslaving nations have left an enduring legacy of psychological trauma, financial dependency and socioeconomic disparities,” it says. “The demand for monetary compensation and debt cancellation is a call for financial redress.” Charles greets people in Georgetown, Guyana, on Friday. Getty Images The Caribbean nations do not name the amount due in reparations. Crucially, their claim is against all European empires, not just the British. But they note reports that estimate “Britain’s black debt” ranges from £7.5 trillion to as much as £18 trillion. That is roughly $14 trillion to $34 trillion. Given that Britain’s annual economic output is just over £3 trillion, and its net public debt is climbing toward 100 per cent of annual GDP, the full bill for slavery looks unpayable.



British Prime Minister Andy Burnham rejects it completely. “I am clear we do not and will not pay reparations,” his spokesman told the media last Tuesday. Some academics have dismissed the case for reparations based on history. Nigel Biggar, a professor emeritus of moral theology at Oxford University, has argued that the demands ignore Britain’s achievement in abolishing slavery. “Black Africans had been busy enslaving other Africans and selling them to the Romans and then to the Arabs long before Europeans arrived on the scene,” Biggar wrote last year. Related Article Royal family King Charles dances in the Bahamas as calls for slavery reparations grow louder He cited estimates that the Arab slave trade as a whole, which lasted from the seventh century until well into the 20th century, transported about 17 million slaves, most of them African. This is not just an argument for leaders from Africa and the Caribbean. Pacific leaders have also engaged on the issue because of the “blackbirding” of islanders to work on sugar cane and other farms in Australia and other colonies. Former prime minister Scott Morrison sparked a storm in 2020 by saying Australia had no history of slavery, with some historians arguing that colonial businessmen such as Ben Boyd shipped slaves from Melanesia to Australia in the 1800s.

A two-bedroom unrenovated apartment in Randwick sold on Saturday for $1.01 million, $40,000 below the reserve to a first-time buyer. Four groups registered to bid for the keys to 7/1 Church Street but when the auction opened, just two participated – a first-home buyer and a builder planning to renovate and keep it as an investment. The first-home buyer made the opening bid at $900,000. Bids continued in increments of $25,000 until it reached $1 million when it stalled. The first-home buyer then bid a further $10,000 against himself and the property sold. The property, which was sold as a deceased estate, had a guide of $950,000 and a reserve of $1.05 million.



There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. The successful bidder, who has been renting in Zetland, had been looking for only two weeks. Related Article NSW residential property Sydney house prices are falling – just not in the suburbs you’d expect “I am finding 70 per cent of buyers I have met in the last month or two are all new – they have been looking since August,” sales agent for Ray White Eastern Beaches, Angus Gorrie said. “They are coming out of the woodwork because they have seen the market has dropped.



“But anyone who has been looking since May is still looking.” The property was one of 682 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. The apartment is on the top floor of an older-style building and is a 10-minute walk from Centennial Park. Domain In Baulkham Hills, a fully renovated five-bedroom home sold for $2,825,000 – $25,000 above the reserve. Three groups registered to vie for the keys to 3 Valda Place – including one after the auction started – with bidding kicking off at $2.65 million. Two were active. Bidding proceeded in increments of $50,000 until it reached $2.75 million when it stalled briefly. Two more $25,000 bids followed and the hammer fell.



The property had a guide of $2.7 million and a reserve of $2.8 million. The successful bidders were a local family who “fell in love” with the high-quality build and its position in the coveted Crestwood pocket. The vendors were a family moving out of Sydney. Richard Matthews sales agent Jesse di Loreto said the sale price was a strong result for the area and an indication that buyer confidence was returning. “A lot of people who have been holding off for the past six months are coming back. World.title: Five years after Cleo Smith was found alive, experts weigh in on her recovery
World.content:
NationalWACrime Five years after Cleo Smith was found alive, experts weigh in on her recovery Aaron Bunch October 31, 2026 — 1:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The image of little Cleo Smith, returned to her mother’s arms and clutching a pink balloon, touched the hearts of a nation that had feared the worst. Her safe recovery 18 days after being snatched in the dead of night from a family tent in remote Western Australia instantly captured national and then international attention. Cleo Smith is carried inside a friend’s house by her mother on November 4 in Carnarvon, Western Australia. Getty Images Cleo’s rescue, which was filmed, and the hunting down of her abductor, Terence Darrell Kelly, now 41, entered folklore as “the greatest story in WA policing history”. For her mother Ellie Smith and stepfather Jake Gliddon, it no doubt triggered unimaginable relief.



Yet it could so easily have ended badly. Five years on, experts agree the cherubic four-year-old was lucky to have survived and may still face troubled times ahead. “I’m amazed she was found alive and safe,” criminal psychologist Tim Watson-Munro tells AAP. “We all hoped for the best but we feared the worst. “They can disappear in the twinkling of an eye.”



Kelly, who confessed to impulsively snatching Cleo while high on methamphetamine, was sentenced to 13 years and six months behind bars for this crime. He drove Cleo 75km southeast to his Carnarvon home, where she was held until police found her alone in a bedroom playing with toys in the early hours of November 3. Cleo Smith’s family have appeared in a tell-all interview on 60 Minutes. 60 Minutes Asked gently three times by Detective Cameron Blain to tell him who she was, she finally answered: “My name is Cleo.” The tender exchange was recorded on the officer’s body-worn camera and eventually went viral.



“It was a very moving moment,” Mr Watson-Munro recalls. “The nation was fixated on this case; it was a high-priority press story. “Everyone was praying for Cleo ... hoping she would be all right.” Kelly was arrested nearby, about the same time Cleo was discovered, after a massive police investigation and intense media interest. “The longer the period of time between an abduction and the person’s arrest, the less likely it is the child will survive,” Mr Watson-Munro says.



“It’s very fortunate Cleo did survive.” While most missing children are recovered safely, genuine stranger abductions are rare and carry vastly different survival odds, according to the FBI. Four-year-old Cleo Smith in hospital after her rescue in Carnarvon. WA Police More than 75 per cent of those cases which prove fatal involve a rescue window of just three hours. Almost 90 per cent allow no longer than 24 hours. Kelly had gone to the Blowholes campsite, 960km north of Perth, to look for items to steal before coming across the Smith family’s two-room tent, where Cleo and her younger sister were asleep in a separate compartment.



A loner obsessed with dolls, he made the opportunistic decision to take Cleo as her parents slept nearby. He lifted her up, along with her sleeping bag, and carried her to his car before driving south to his home. Terence Kelly kidnapped Cleo Smith from her family’s tent. Getty/Supplied Cleo’s parents awoke hours later to find her missing and then endured 18 days of not knowing if she was alive or dead. Now nine years old, Cleo is reportedly thriving and a keen member of her local swimming club and an accomplished young gymnast.



Ellie Smith told Nine’s 60 Minutes in June Cleo was a happy child who loved her sister Isla and her many friends at school. Mr Watson-Munro says Cleo’s young age at the time and the fact she was abducted during a happy family camping trip in a remote part of Australia captivated the public. “Anything to do with abduction and children always raises people’s antennae a bit because they can relate strongly to the situation,” he says. Criminologist and clinical psychologist Michelle Noon says people identify with Cleo and her family because they were ordinary people enjoying a family activity. “That’s what can really start to terrify people,′ she says.



“We’ve all had those experiences as children and we have those experiences with our own families. “When people start thinking like that, we see really strong public interest and also really strong public impact.” Coming during the COVID-19 pandemic, Cleo’s rescue was the “antidote we all needed in terms of a good news day”, Dr Noon says. “What was refreshing about Cleo’s case is we got some answers and it gave the community something to hold onto at a time when there was lots of uncertainty in the world.” Cleo was what experts call an “ideal victim” and her family camping trip was a “respectable project” - the two requirements for a case to cross into public consciousness.



“When a crime has those qualities, to use a technical term, people really freak out,” Dr Noon says. “It draws you in and it makes you hold your kids a little tighter and a little closer. “In this case, we’re just so lucky she found her way home in her own way, and that despite what happened.” Dr Noon says while discussing Cleo’s case in the public domain, it is important to be mindful she will eventually be able to access information published about her. “She’s going to be a young person coming into a world where she’s not famous; her experience is infamous,” she says.



“We call that secondary victimisation and it’s all the stuff that happens because you’ve been a victim of crime that impacts you.” Kelly, who received a discount for his early guilty plea, was sentenced in April 2023 and will be eligible for parole after serving 11-and-a-half years. A 2024 legal appeal against his sentence failed.

World.content:
SportFitness Hyrox athlete who soiled herself ‘traumatised’ by backlash Emily Smith October 31, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: An Australian extreme fitness athlete who soiled herself during a race said she was “traumatised” by the backlash to the incident. Joanna Wietrzyk apologised to her fellow competitors, saying she “didn’t really think about those around me” when she became unwell during the Hyrox event in Beijing in September. The 24-year-old pushed on to win the event and later said she had suffered a bacterial infection from food poisoning. Pictures and videos from the competition showed faeces running down Wietrzyk’s legs, on to the mats and communal equipment.



The athlete retroactively withdrew from the race, but organisers faced intense criticism for allowing her to continue despite the potential health risks to other competitors. They insisted that affected lanes were deep-cleaned and contaminated equipment was removed, but Moritz Fürste, Hyrox’s co-founder, apologised and said the company made a mistake by not reacting immediately. New rules have been put in place giving organisers the power to remove athletes if their bodily fluids pose a contamination risk. Australian Joanna Wietrzyk has apologised following the notorious Hyrox incident. Getty Images In an interview with the BBC, Wietrzyk said the backlash she received after the incident was “traumatic”.



“Yes, I did make the wrong decision, but I don’t believe I should have received such backlash and such scrutiny online … At the end of the day, I’m only human,” she said. She added that it had been a “mentally and emotionally taxing period”, with her family also receiving threats online. “[It] was very eye-opening for me to see the effect of social media nowadays, especially from someone who’s 24, just out there racing,” she said. The athlete revealed she planned to return to competition but was “nervous” to do so. “I don’t want it to become my identity,” she said. Wietrzyk said that despite suffering from food poisoning she went into the race “feeling fresh, feeling really, really good”.



“It was a very sudden experience,” she said. She had completed two runs and the SkiErg, a machine that simulates skiing, and was midway through the burpee broad jumps exercise when she became unwell. Related Article Fitness ‘I regret the decision’: Hyrox athlete apologises, forfeits event after soiling herself “It wasn’t until about halfway through the race where everything did transpire ... In that moment, right then and there, as a very competitive person … and an elite athlete that I am, my only focus is on racing,” she said. “Obviously I did put other people at risk,” she admitted.



“It was my decision to continue racing, so I take full responsibility for that. I didn’t really think about those around me … The decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision, and I’m truly sorry for everyone that I did affect.” Some athletes at the event were refunded their entry fees. In a Hyrox event, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing high-intensity fitness exercises using shared equipment. Wietrzyk, from Melbourne, holds the world record in the women’s solo event and was invited to compete in the elite group of the 16-24 age category. She won in Beijing with a time of 1hr 1min 23sec. She will compete in Hamburg, Germany, on Friday. The Telegraph, London

World.title: Western Sydney Airport is made for western Sydney. So how does travel there stack up? We tested it
World.content:
Three reporters travel to the new Western Sydney Airport from western Sydney. What method of travel wins?

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

With Sydney’s new airport up and running, a key question has lingered amidst the excitement: how does one get there? Armed with fake luggage and a keen eye for bus routes, the Herald’s western Sydney reporters set a challenge to see who could make it to the airport the quickest via public transport for a real flight. Our goal was to arrive the recommended two hours before a Jetstar flight to the Gold Coast. In theory, it’s easy: get the metro. But the Western Sydney International Airport metro line is not due to be completed until December 2027 at earliest, so there are currently limited public transport options, in addition to driving. We picked the three largest western Sydney hubs – Parramatta, Penrith and Campbelltown – as the starting points for our journeys. 9am: My plan to get this flight has just changed for a third time. I’d initially wanted to take WSI’s much-advertised $25, 50-minute “super shuttle” bus service that runs direct between Parramatta and the airport. But it’s only running twice a day – and the first service leaves after my flight is meant to take off. Next best option was getting a FlixBus, the infamously cheap European green bus company now operating in Australia. Its website boasted about a $3 ticket for a bus leaving at just the right time. But now it has disappeared from the website.



10.30am: It’s going to take me longer, but I’m getting the train to St Marys to join the dedicated free shuttle bus. The train is empty, and I’ve made a discovery: I thought the FlixBus service had disappeared because it was full, but it turns out the company just cancelled the service for today. 10.55am: St Mary’s train station is incredibly noisy because it’s almost surrounded by a construction site for the new metro station – the one that was meant to be ready by the time the airport opened to connect the rest of Sydney to WSI. It’s not. 11.06am: After heaving my luggage through the main street of St Marys, I arrive at the new WSI shuttle bus stop, which is admittedly not much of a bus stop. Three men are constructing a shelter (which is amusing, considering this airport opening was not exactly a surprise) that has left about two dozen passengers waiting for the bus in the sun. The bus arrives as I pull up and join the queue. It’s free, but you need to tap an Opal card to record passenger numbers. The WSI shuttle bus area at St Marys will be functional -- eventually. Anthony Segaert 11.16am: It turns out that despite this bus being full, I’m the only one with a suitcase. The other people on this bus are here for fun. A group of elderly women tell me they’ve heard the airport is beautiful and want to explore it for fun. Another couple tells me they read in the Herald that there weren’t many food options at the airport, so they considered bringing their own lunch for a visit. 11.20am: We’ve just turned off Mamre Road onto Luddenham Road, and it’s a reminder of how developed this area is yet to be: the bus is hurtling along this narrow two-lane track that is crumbling at the sides. 11.39am: We’re here, at just over the hour mark.



9am: Normally, a trip to the Western Sydney Airport from Penrith would only be about a 25-minute drive for me. It’s convenient and faster than travelling to Sydney Airport in Mascot, which often takes me over an hour. So, while many from Sydney’s east may dread travelling to Badgerys Creek, I’m very excited to do so. Normally. Today, however, I’m catching a bus to the new airport and my expectations for a smooth and quick trip are low. Google Maps tells me it will take me one hour and 11 minutes to arrive. 10.40am: While I’m waiting for my 11.05am bus (I’m very early), another airport bus pulls up at 10.40am. One person gets on. Five minutes before my bus comes two other people who look lost join me. There’s a bit of a language barrier, but they mime a plane landing, and I’m able to figure out they’re also travelling to the airport. They seem excited to see the planes, and it’s a good reminder of how many people have been looking forward to visiting the airport. 11.06am: My bus arrives almost right on time and three other people get on. I put my suitcase on the luggage rack and pick one of the many seats available. No one else has luggage. Exactly six minutes later we make our first stop. If this is how often the bus will be stopping it’s going to be a long journey. I wish I had a coffee. 11.27am: We finally make it onto the Northern Road and start driving away from Penrith and towards the airport. It’s still very quiet with only three other passengers on board. I fear I might fall asleep. One person stands up to get off, and the bus driver gets cranky at him for not getting his Opal card out fast enough. I make sure mine is still in my pocket. Ellie Busby arrives at Western Sydney International Airport – with the shortest journey. Kate Geraghty 11.40am: I’m just under 10 minutes away from the airport and my verdict on the journey so far is: it wasn’t as bad as I expected. The few passengers onboard were quiet, the air conditioning on the bus was working, and the bus didn’t stop at all the places listed on the bus route, which made the trip feel fairly quick. I’ve definitely had worse bus trips. But maybe I’m just used to commuting from Penrith to Sydney Airport and this feels like a walk in the park in comparison.



11.48am: End of the line. The remaining two passengers and I disembark into the very hot sun after what ended up being a 42-minute bus ride. Despite what Google Maps told me, I don’t have to walk 30 minutes to get to the airport from the bus station. It’s a huge relief, and I’m already looking forward to experiencing the airport’s airconditioning. And getting a coffee. 9am: My flight is at 2.10pm, and I don’t like hanging about at the airport for too long, so I figure I need to get there at roughly midday. The 845 bus route arrives at the airport by 12.21pm, which feels close enough. It leaves Campbelltown Mall at 11.18am, so I have time to kill. 11am: I need to be at Hurley Street before Dumaresq Street Bus Stop and it will be a quick five-minute walk. Excellent. Past the Dumaresq Street Cinema (which is offering $9.50 tickets to any movie session, an absolute bargain), I find my bus stop and am dismayed. It has no shelter, I am early, and the sun is sweltering. The sign for the bus from Campbelltown to WSI is the only piece of shade. Mostafa Rachwani 11.18am: After 10 minutes contemplating every detail of the bus stop sign as I hide in its very small shadow, the 845 finally arrives, and I jump on, full of hope and wonder. The bus is essentially empty except for someone in a Mad Mex fast-food chain uniform and a school student sitting in the back playing games on his phone.



I clunkily drag my bag to a seat in the middle of the bus. There are no luggage racks on this bus, so my bags sit neatly next to me on the bus seat. Google Maps tells me this trip will be more than an hour long, so I lean back and lament the lack of a footrest. 11.30am: Despite my reservations, this bus ride has so far been about as smooth as possible. Maybe it is the relatively new roads in Sydney’s far south-west, perhaps it’s this expert bus driver, but there are very few bumps or stops on this route. We stop around Narellan and almost everyone gets off and one man, Daniel Schembri, gets on. He’s wearing an Australian Rugby League jersey, and tells me he’s not actually going to the airport. He’s going to St Mary’s and using the airport route as a “shortcut” through western Sydney. Related Article Western Sydney International Construction noise, coffee and boredom: How to spend all day at Western Sydney Airport “It would take me hours to take a bus or train to get from Campbelltown back home to St Mary’s,” he says. “But this route is a shortcut, I just change over at the airport, and I’m on my way.” “It’s a bullshit route though,” Schembri adds. “Because they should do this every ten minutes when there are flights. That way more people can use it.” 11.45am: I’ve gotten deathly bored now. We’ve made only two stops, and are flying past mostly green fields. Thankfully the bus is air-conditioned and comfortable, but at this point not much else is happening. I check the route, and it says there is still nearly half an hour left.

World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Updated inner-south Victorian sells for $50,000 below reserve Wes Mountain October 31, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. An updated three-bedroom Victorian in South Yarra sold for $1.75 million in post-auction negotiations – $50,000 below reserve – as a small number of homes went to auction over a quiet Cup weekend. Minutes from Hawksburn train station and a short walk to both Toorak and Williams roads, the preserved Victorian weatherboard at 3 Hopetoun Grove features a striking red door. Inside, floating floorboards lead past two front bedrooms built around period chimneys into a sitting room and a rear open-plan kitchen and living area, with full-length windows looking onto a small yard and terrace. With a primary bedroom and ensuite upstairs above the living area, the property was listed with a reserve of $1.8 million. Marshall White Stonnington agent and auctioneer Fiona Counsel said the auction opened with a $1.7 million vendor bid, followed by a single $1.71 million genuine bid from a local couple with a young family, on which it was passed in.



Counsel said the vendors, upsizing to a new property, agreed to “meet the market”, with the buyers happy to meet them halfway and sell for $1.75 million, as the potential for another rate hike on Tuesday loomed over the weekend. “I think from the vendor’s perspective… they factored that in when it came to the negotiation,” she said. The well-preserved Victorian facade hides an expansive updated interior. Marshall White Stonnington She said she didn’t think the Cup Day long weekend had been a factor in interest on the day. “We were comfortable to go on race week,” she said. “Everyone was here that was expected to be here.”



The property was one of 418 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. Further south, a three-bedroom freestanding villa in Hughesdale, with 433-square-metres of land on the title, sold for $950,000 at auction, soaring $100,000 over its $850,000 listed reserve. Split between living and dining areas to the front, and its three large bedrooms to the rear, 2/142 Poath Road was one of two units on the block, with mostly original interiors and a large yard ready to be updated by a new owner. Ray White Oakleigh agent and auctioneer Jonathon Eaves said a $720,000 genuine bid opened the auction, from which three bidders pushed the price up in $20,000 increments to $800,000.



Related Article Melbourne house prices Melbourne suburbs where house prices have fallen the most From there, bids slowed to $10,000 and eventually $5000 increments after being declared on the market at $850,000. It eventually reached $950,000 – $100,000 over its reserve and more than $200,000 above the opening bid. The successful buyers were a young couple, purchasing their first home in the area, while the vendors sold to transition to the next stage of their lives. Eaves thought the sale was an indication that some parts of the market were still selling well, but said the threat of another rate hike did factor into reluctance from at least one buyer to put his hand up at auction. “But you’ve just got to look at it and say, ‘can I afford it? Is it a good home?’” he said.



“And can I see that potentially, in 10 years, this property will be worth more?” Property alerts are now available in The Age app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.

World.title: The King and the colonies: Why Charles will have to confront slavery
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: King Charles has been greeted with joyous music, smiling dancers and a shot of rum on a journey through the Caribbean that looks like an endless celebration. But every stop takes the King closer to a meeting in Antigua where he will have to navigate the grim history of slavery in his talks with Commonwealth leaders from former British colonies. Charles has expressed sorrow about slavery, but has stopped short of a formal apology, given that he is guided by British policy that rules out paying reparations for the damage done over centuries. At this meeting, however, several leaders from the Commonwealth appear determined to force a debate about a response from Britain over its imperial past. And the response, they say, is not only about money. They want an apology. The King with Guyana’s Minister of Agriculture Minister, Zulfikar Mustapha, and Mangroves Restoration and Management project coordinator Kene Moseley at the Kingston Seawall Esplanade in Georgetown. Chris Jackson/Getty Images “What benefit do we have from this man coming to our country?” asked Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee, after the King flew out of the island nation a few days ago. “We know what we are giving, but what are we getting, you know? And if all that we’re getting is an opportunity to smile and wave and say hello, I think for a lot of Bahamians that just wasn’t worth it.”



One seasoned observer, Alan Lester, professor of historical geography at the University of Sussex, believes this sets up an opportunity for a unified statement and an apology that helps Britain build better relations with the Commonwealth. Without an agreement, however, it could merely lead to more acrimony. The King began his Caribbean tour on Tuesday in the Bahamas, where he displayed some dance moves in a parade, and then visited Guyana, where he tasted the local rum. Charles shook traditional cowbells as he paraded with Junkanoo dancers in Nassau, Bahamas. AP Photo/Tim Aylen Charles sniffs a glass of a special Guyanese rum created in his honour in Georgetown. Getty Images He arrives in Antigua on Sunday for events that include a cricket match among famous West Indies champions and several Commonwealth leaders. The argument about slavery will shape the agenda after a formal event on Wednesday to open the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, or CHOGM.



Of course, the King has proven his skill at delicate diplomacy in the past, not least in handling Donald Trump during two state visits – the American president’s trip to London last year and the King’s visit to Washington DC this year. On both occasions, the King made pointed remarks about liberty, climate change and Ukraine with no display of tension with Trump. The talks on slavery could be more difficult because the King may be outnumbered. Caricom, which represents 15 states and several territories around the Caribbean, is calling for significant action on slavery because of the evidence that European nations enslaved Africans, shipped them across the Atlantic, stripped them of their humanity and set up the financial systems to treat them as chattels. Jevon Thompson, of the Ethiopian African Black International Congress, carries a protest sign calling for reparations and a public apology while Charles was in Nassau on Wednesday. AP Photo/Tim Aylen The Caribbean manifesto, issued in June, notes that Britain paid compensation to slave owners when it abolished slavery, but did not compensate those who had been enslaved. Setting out a 10-point plan for justice, the group seeks a formal apology, a development program for Indigenous people, repatriation for descendants of slaves who might seek to return to Africa, the restitution of cultural heritage, help to remedy a crisis in public health and help with education and training. A key goal is compensation for gender-based violence, given estimates that 6 million African women were transported across the Atlantic as slaves, almost one-third of the 20 million who were forcibly removed.



Caricom also seeks support with psychological rehabilitation and sovereignty over technology development. The final point of the 10-point plan is debt cancellation, monetary compensation and decolonisation. “The crimes against humanity committed against African people by enslaving nations have left an enduring legacy of psychological trauma, financial dependency and socioeconomic disparities,” it says. “The demand for monetary compensation and debt cancellation is a call for financial redress.” Charles greets people in Georgetown, Guyana, on Friday. Getty Images The Caribbean nations do not name the amount due in reparations. Crucially, their claim is against all European empires, not just the British. But they note reports that estimate “Britain’s black debt” ranges from £7.5 trillion to as much as £18 trillion. That is roughly $14 trillion to $34 trillion. Given that Britain’s annual economic output is just over £3 trillion, and its net public debt is climbing toward 100 per cent of annual GDP, the full bill for slavery looks unpayable.



British Prime Minister Andy Burnham rejects it completely. “I am clear we do not and will not pay reparations,” his spokesman told the media last Tuesday. Some academics have dismissed the case for reparations based on history. Nigel Biggar, a professor emeritus of moral theology at Oxford University, has argued that the demands ignore Britain’s achievement in abolishing slavery. “Black Africans had been busy enslaving other Africans and selling them to the Romans and then to the Arabs long before Europeans arrived on the scene,” Biggar wrote last year. Related Article Royal family King Charles dances in the Bahamas as calls for slavery reparations grow louder He cited estimates that the Arab slave trade as a whole, which lasted from the seventh century until well into the 20th century, transported about 17 million slaves, most of them African. This is not just an argument for leaders from Africa and the Caribbean. Pacific leaders have also engaged on the issue because of the “blackbirding” of islanders to work on sugar cane and other farms in Australia and other colonies. Former prime minister Scott Morrison sparked a storm in 2020 by saying Australia had no history of slavery, with some historians arguing that colonial businessmen such as Ben Boyd shipped slaves from Melanesia to Australia in the 1800s.

A two-bedroom unrenovated apartment in Randwick sold on Saturday for $1.01 million, $40,000 below the reserve to a first-time buyer. Four groups registered to bid for the keys to 7/1 Church Street but when the auction opened, just two participated – a first-home buyer and a builder planning to renovate and keep it as an investment. The first-home buyer made the opening bid at $900,000. Bids continued in increments of $25,000 until it reached $1 million when it stalled. The first-home buyer then bid a further $10,000 against himself and the property sold. The property, which was sold as a deceased estate, had a guide of $950,000 and a reserve of $1.05 million.



There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. The successful bidder, who has been renting in Zetland, had been looking for only two weeks. Related Article NSW residential property Sydney house prices are falling – just not in the suburbs you’d expect “I am finding 70 per cent of buyers I have met in the last month or two are all new – they have been looking since August,” sales agent for Ray White Eastern Beaches, Angus Gorrie said. “They are coming out of the woodwork because they have seen the market has dropped.



“But anyone who has been looking since May is still looking.” The property was one of 682 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. The apartment is on the top floor of an older-style building and is a 10-minute walk from Centennial Park. Domain In Baulkham Hills, a fully renovated five-bedroom home sold for $2,825,000 – $25,000 above the reserve. Three groups registered to vie for the keys to 3 Valda Place – including one after the auction started – with bidding kicking off at $2.65 million. Two were active. Bidding proceeded in increments of $50,000 until it reached $2.75 million when it stalled briefly. Two more $25,000 bids followed and the hammer fell.



The property had a guide of $2.7 million and a reserve of $2.8 million. The successful bidders were a local family who “fell in love” with the high-quality build and its position in the coveted Crestwood pocket. The vendors were a family moving out of Sydney. Richard Matthews sales agent Jesse di Loreto said the sale price was a strong result for the area and an indication that buyer confidence was returning. “A lot of people who have been holding off for the past six months are coming back. The Hills district has been quite resilient,” he said. Property alerts are now available in the SMH app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.

World.title: Five years after Cleo Smith was found alive, experts weigh in on her recovery
World.content:
NationalWACrime Five years after Cleo Smith was found alive, experts weigh in on her recovery Aaron Bunch October 31, 2026 — 1:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The image of little Cleo Smith, returned to her mother’s arms and clutching a pink balloon, touched the hearts of a nation that had feared the worst. Her safe recovery 18 days after being snatched in the dead of night from a family tent in remote Western Australia instantly captured national and then international attention. Cleo Smith is carried inside a friend’s house by her mother on November 4 in Carnarvon, Western Australia. Getty Images Cleo’s rescue, which was filmed, and the hunting down of her abductor, Terence Darrell Kelly, now 41, entered folklore as “the greatest story in WA policing history”. For her mother Ellie Smith and stepfather Jake Gliddon, it no doubt triggered unimaginable relief.



Yet it could so easily have ended badly. Five years on, experts agree the cherubic four-year-old was lucky to have survived and may still face troubled times ahead. “I’m amazed she was found alive and safe,” criminal psychologist Tim Watson-Munro tells AAP. “We all hoped for the best but we feared the worst. “They can disappear in the twinkling of an eye.”



Kelly, who confessed to impulsively snatching Cleo while high on methamphetamine, was sentenced to 13 years and six months behind bars for this crime. He drove Cleo 75km southeast to his Carnarvon home, where she was held until police found her alone in a bedroom playing with toys in the early hours of November 3. Cleo Smith’s family have appeared in a tell-all interview on 60 Minutes. 60 Minutes Asked gently three times by Detective Cameron Blain to tell him who she was, she finally answered: “My name is Cleo.” The tender exchange was recorded on the officer’s body-worn camera and eventually went viral.



“It was a very moving moment,” Mr Watson-Munro recalls. “The nation was fixated on this case; it was a high-priority press story. “Everyone was praying for Cleo ... hoping she would be all right.” Kelly was arrested nearby, about the same time Cleo was discovered, after a massive police investigation and intense media interest. “The longer the period of time between an abduction and the person’s arrest, the less likely it is the child will survive,” Mr Watson-Munro says.



“It’s very fortunate Cleo did survive.” While most missing children are recovered safely, genuine stranger abductions are rare and carry vastly different survival odds, according to the FBI. Four-year-old Cleo Smith in hospital after her rescue in Carnarvon. WA Police More than 75 per cent of those cases which prove fatal involve a rescue window of just three hours. Almost 90 per cent allow no longer than 24 hours. Kelly had gone to the Blowholes campsite, 960km north of Perth, to look for items to steal before coming across the Smith family’s two-room tent, where Cleo and her younger sister were asleep in a separate compartment.



A loner obsessed with dolls, he made the opportunistic decision to take Cleo as her parents slept nearby. He lifted her up, along with her sleeping bag, and carried her to his car before driving south to his home. Terence Kelly kidnapped Cleo Smith from her family’s tent. Getty/Supplied Cleo’s parents awoke hours later to find her missing and then endured 18 days of not knowing if she was alive or dead. Now nine years old, Cleo is reportedly thriving and a keen member of her local swimming club and an accomplished young gymnast.



Ellie Smith told Nine’s 60 Minutes in June Cleo was a happy child who loved her sister Isla and her many friends at school. Mr Watson-Munro says Cleo’s young age at the time and the fact she was abducted during a happy family camping trip in a remote part of Australia captivated the public. “Anything to do with abduction and children always raises people’s antennae a bit because they can relate strongly to the situation,” he says. Criminologist and clinical psychologist Michelle Noon says people identify with Cleo and her family because they were ordinary people enjoying a family activity. “That’s what can really start to terrify people,′ she says.



“We’ve all had those experiences as children and we have those experiences with our own families. “When people start thinking like that, we see really strong public interest and also really strong public impact.” Coming during the COVID-19 pandemic, Cleo’s rescue was the “antidote we all needed in terms of a good news day”, Dr Noon says. “What was refreshing about Cleo’s case is we got some answers and it gave the community something to hold onto at a time when there was lots of uncertainty in the world.” Cleo was what experts call an “ideal victim” and her family camping trip was a “respectable project” - the two requirements for a case to cross into public consciousness.



“When a crime has those qualities, to use a technical term, people really freak out,” Dr Noon says. “It draws you in and it makes you hold your kids a little tighter and a little closer. “In this case, we’re just so lucky she found her way home in her own way, and that despite what happened.” Dr Noon says while discussing Cleo’s case in the public domain, it is important to be mindful she will eventually be able to access information published about her. “She’s going to be a young person coming into a world where she’s not famous; her experience is infamous,” she says.



“We call that secondary victimisation and it’s all the stuff that happens because you’ve been a victim of crime that impacts you.” Kelly, who received a discount for his early guilty plea, was sentenced in April 2023 and will be eligible for parole after serving 11-and-a-half years. A 2024 legal appeal against his sentence failed.

World.title: Hyrox athlete who soiled herself ‘traumatised’ by backlash
World.content:
SportFitness Hyrox athlete who soiled herself ‘traumatised’ by backlash Emily Smith October 31, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: An Australian extreme fitness athlete who soiled herself during a race said she was “traumatised” by the backlash to the incident. Joanna Wietrzyk apologised to her fellow competitors, saying she “didn’t really think about those around me” when she became unwell during the Hyrox event in Beijing in September. The 24-year-old pushed on to win the event and later said she had suffered a bacterial infection from food poisoning. Pictures and videos from the competition showed faeces running down Wietrzyk’s legs, on to the mats and communal equipment.



The athlete retroactively withdrew from the race, but organisers faced intense criticism for allowing her to continue despite the potential health risks to other competitors. They insisted that affected lanes were deep-cleaned and contaminated equipment was removed, but Moritz Fürste, Hyrox’s co-founder, apologised and said the company made a mistake by not reacting immediately. New rules have been put in place giving organisers the power to remove athletes if their bodily fluids pose a contamination risk. Australian Joanna Wietrzyk has apologised following the notorious Hyrox incident. Getty Images In an interview with the BBC, Wietrzyk said the backlash she received after the incident was “traumatic”.



“Yes, I did make the wrong decision, but I don’t believe I should have received such backlash and such scrutiny online … At the end of the day, I’m only human,” she said. She added that it had been a “mentally and emotionally taxing period”, with her family also receiving threats online. “[It] was very eye-opening for me to see the effect of social media nowadays, especially from someone who’s 24, just out there racing,” she said. The athlete revealed she planned to return to competition but was “nervous” to do so. “I don’t want it to become my identity,” she said. Wietrzyk said that despite suffering from food poisoning she went into the race “feeling fresh, feeling really, really good”.



“It was a very sudden experience,” she said. She had completed two runs and the SkiErg, a machine that simulates skiing, and was midway through the burpee broad jumps exercise when she became unwell. Related Article Fitness ‘I regret the decision’: Hyrox athlete apologises, forfeits event after soiling herself “It wasn’t until about halfway through the race where everything did transpire ... In that moment, right then and there, as a very competitive person … and an elite athlete that I am, my only focus is on racing,” she said. “Obviously I did put other people at risk,” she admitted.



“It was my decision to continue racing, so I take full responsibility for that. I didn’t really think about those around me … The decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision, and I’m truly sorry for everyone that I did affect.” Some athletes at the event were refunded their entry fees. In a Hyrox event, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing high-intensity fitness exercises using shared equipment. Wietrzyk, from Melbourne, holds the world record in the women’s solo event and was invited to compete in the elite group of the 16-24 age category. She won in Beijing with a time of 1hr 1min 23sec. She will compete in Hamburg, Germany, on Friday. The Telegraph, London

World.title: Western Sydney Airport is made for western Sydney. So how does travel there stack up? We tested it
World.content:
Three reporters travel to the new Western Sydney Airport from western Sydney. What method of travel wins?

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

With Sydney’s new airport up and running, a key question has lingered amidst the excitement: how does one get there? Armed with fake luggage and a keen eye for bus routes, the Herald’s western Sydney reporters set a challenge to see who could make it to the airport the quickest via public transport for a real flight. Our goal was to arrive the recommended two hours before a Jetstar flight to the Gold Coast. In theory, it’s easy: get the metro. But the Western Sydney International Airport metro line is not due to be completed until December 2027 at earliest, so there are currently limited public transport options, in addition to driving. We picked the three largest western Sydney hubs – Parramatta, Penrith and Campbelltown – as the starting points for our journeys. 9am: My plan to get this flight has just changed for a third time. I’d initially wanted to take WSI’s much-advertised $25, 50-minute “super shuttle” bus service that runs direct between Parramatta and the airport. But it’s only running twice a day – and the first service leaves after my flight is meant to take off. Next best option was getting a FlixBus, the infamously cheap European green bus company now operating in Australia. Its website boasted about a $3 ticket for a bus leaving at just the right time. But now it has disappeared from the website.



10.30am: It’s going to take me longer, but I’m getting the train to St Marys to join the dedicated free shuttle bus. The train is empty, and I’ve made a discovery: I thought the FlixBus service had disappeared because it was full, but it turns out the company just cancelled the service for today. 10.55am: St Mary’s train station is incredibly noisy because it’s almost surrounded by a construction site for the new metro station – the one that was meant to be ready by the time the airport opened to connect the rest of Sydney to WSI. It’s not. 11.06am: After heaving my luggage through the main street of St Marys, I arrive at the new WSI shuttle bus stop, which is admittedly not much of a bus stop. Three men are constructing a shelter (which is amusing, considering this airport opening was not exactly a surprise) that has left about two dozen passengers waiting for the bus in the sun. The bus arrives as I pull up and join the queue. It’s free, but you need to tap an Opal card to record passenger numbers. The WSI shuttle bus area at St Marys will be functional -- eventually. Anthony Segaert 11.16am: It turns out that despite this bus being full, I’m the only one with a suitcase. The other people on this bus are here for fun. A group of elderly women tell me they’ve heard the airport is beautiful and want to explore it for fun. Another couple tells me they read in the Herald that there weren’t many food options at the airport, so they considered bringing their own lunch for a visit. 11.20am: We’ve just turned off Mamre Road onto Luddenham Road, and it’s a reminder of how developed this area is yet to be: the bus is hurtling along this narrow two-lane track that is crumbling at the sides. 11.39am: We’re here, at just over the hour mark.



9am: Normally, a trip to the Western Sydney Airport from Penrith would only be about a 25-minute drive for me. It’s convenient and faster than travelling to Sydney Airport in Mascot, which often takes me over an hour. So, while many from Sydney’s east may dread travelling to Badgerys Creek, I’m very excited to do so. Normally. Today, however, I’m catching a bus to the new airport and my expectations for a smooth and quick trip are low. Google Maps tells me it will take me one hour and 11 minutes to arrive. 10.40am: While I’m waiting for my 11.05am bus (I’m very early), another airport bus pulls up at 10.40am. One person gets on. Five minutes before my bus comes two other people who look lost join me. There’s a bit of a language barrier, but they mime a plane landing, and I’m able to figure out they’re also travelling to the airport. They seem excited to see the planes, and it’s a good reminder of how many people have been looking forward to visiting the airport. 11.06am: My bus arrives almost right on time and three other people get on. I put my suitcase on the luggage rack and pick one of the many seats available. No one else has luggage. Exactly six minutes later we make our first stop. If this is how often the bus will be stopping it’s going to be a long journey. I wish I had a coffee. 11.27am: We finally make it onto the Northern Road and start driving away from Penrith and towards the airport. It’s still very quiet with only three other passengers on board. I fear I might fall asleep. One person stands up to get off, and the bus driver gets cranky at him for not getting his Opal card out fast enough. I make sure mine is still in my pocket. Ellie Busby arrives at Western Sydney International Airport – with the shortest journey. Kate Geraghty 11.40am: I’m just under 10 minutes away from the airport and my verdict on the journey so far is: it wasn’t as bad as I expected. The few passengers onboard were quiet, the air conditioning on the bus was working, and the bus didn’t stop at all the places listed on the bus route, which made the trip feel fairly quick. I’ve definitely had worse bus trips. But maybe I’m just used to commuting from Penrith to Sydney Airport and this feels like a walk in the park in comparison.



11.48am: End of the line. The remaining two passengers and I disembark into the very hot sun after what ended up being a 42-minute bus ride. Despite what Google Maps told me, I don’t have to walk 30 minutes to get to the airport from the bus station. It’s a huge relief, and I’m already looking forward to experiencing the airport’s airconditioning. And getting a coffee. 9am: My flight is at 2.10pm, and I don’t like hanging about at the airport for too long, so I figure I need to get there at roughly midday. The 845 bus route arrives at the airport by 12.21pm, which feels close enough. It leaves Campbelltown Mall at 11.18am, so I have time to kill. 11am: I need to be at Hurley Street before Dumaresq Street Bus Stop and it will be a quick five-minute walk. Excellent. Past the Dumaresq Street Cinema (which is offering $9.50 tickets to any movie session, an absolute bargain), I find my bus stop and am dismayed. It has no shelter, I am early, and the sun is sweltering. The sign for the bus from Campbelltown to WSI is the only piece of shade. Mostafa Rachwani 11.18am: After 10 minutes contemplating every detail of the bus stop sign as I hide in its very small shadow, the 845 finally arrives, and I jump on, full of hope and wonder. The bus is essentially empty except for someone in a Mad Mex fast-food chain uniform and a school student sitting in the back playing games on his phone.



I clunkily drag my bag to a seat in the middle of the bus. There are no luggage racks on this bus, so my bags sit neatly next to me on the bus seat. Google Maps tells me this trip will be more than an hour long, so I lean back and lament the lack of a footrest. 11.30am: Despite my reservations, this bus ride has so far been about as smooth as possible. Maybe it is the relatively new roads in Sydney’s far south-west, perhaps it’s this expert bus driver, but there are very few bumps or stops on this route. We stop around Narellan and almost everyone gets off and one man, Daniel Schembri, gets on. He’s wearing an Australian Rugby League jersey, and tells me he’s not actually going to the airport. He’s going to St Mary’s and using the airport route as a “shortcut” through western Sydney. Related Article Western Sydney International Construction noise, coffee and boredom: How to spend all day at Western Sydney Airport “It would take me hours to take a bus or train to get from Campbelltown back home to St Mary’s,” he says. “But this route is a shortcut, I just change over at the airport, and I’m on my way.” “It’s a bullshit route though,” Schembri adds. “Because they should do this every ten minutes when there are flights. That way more people can use it.” 11.45am: I’ve gotten deathly bored now. We’ve made only two stops, and are flying past mostly green fields. Thankfully the bus is air-conditioned and comfortable, but at this point not much else is happening. I check the route, and it says there is still nearly half an hour left.
